articles.title: Should I buy a Rumawip or other affordable housing unit?
articles.excerpt: Tens of thousands of affordable homes sit unsold while city prices hit records. Sean explains who these schemes really serve, and how they change the price of the homes around them.
articles.viewerQuestion: Is an affordable housing unit a good buy, and how do these schemes affect other buyers?
articles.answer: If you qualify and the location suits you, it can be very good value, because these homes are heavily subsidised. But Sean says the schemes have produced unsold homes while their cost is passed on to the open-market homes around them.

articles.title: Twins are coming. Should we stretch for a RM1 million family house?
articles.excerpt: A 30-year-old banker with twins on the way wants a RM1 million Kota Damansara house shared with his brother. Sean suggests renting on and buying an apartment one income can carry first.
articles.viewerQuestion: Should he commit to the house and work hard to pay for it, or keep renting until his early 40s?
articles.answer: Keep renting for now, and buy a home on his own that fits one person's budget, around RM500,000 to RM600,000, ideally a subsale with a three-bedroom layout. Live there for five to eight years, then upgrade to a bigger family home once the twins start school.

articles.title: I need an apartment to care for my mother. Why is the developer's price higher than subsale?
articles.excerpt: A 58-year-old in Johor Bahru wants an apartment to live in with his mother, and finds the developer's unsold units dearer than subsales. Sean explains the gap and how to choose between new and subsale.
articles.viewerQuestion: Why do the developer's new units cost more than subsale units, does it signal a problem, and should he buy new or subsale?
articles.answer: The gap doesn't mean the building has problems: developers rarely sell leftover units below what earlier buyers paid. Since he knows exactly which unit he wants, choose on cash and condition: new units come with developer packages and less money upfront, while a subsale is usually cheaper, can be negotiated and may already be furnished.

articles.title: Landed or condo: which holds its value better?
articles.excerpt: A reader assumes landed homes are guaranteed to appreciate while condos age. Sean explains why that view is hindsight, where condos win, and the price ceiling open landed homes run into.
articles.viewerQuestion: In a sought-after area such as Bukit Jalil, Hartamas or PJ, how would a condo's value hold up against a landed home over the long run?
articles.answer: Landed terrace houses do appreciate fastest, but "guaranteed" is hindsight. Condos in good locations grow a little more slowly yet earn far more rent, and older landed homes without security face a ceiling on what buyers will pay.

articles.title: Should we move from our Bangi house to a new Cyberjaya condo to cut the commute?
articles.excerpt: Two civil servants want to swap their Bangi terrace for a RM575,000 Cyberjaya condo to shorten the school run. Sean says high-rise prices there have fallen, so compare 20 projects, or simply rent.
articles.viewerQuestion: Should they rent out or sell the Bangi house, is RM3,200 a month a burden, and what are Cyberjaya's prospects if they sell in 20 years?
articles.answer: First check the numbers they left out: their joint income and how much is still owed on the Bangi house. Cyberjaya high-rises have generally lost value, so before committing RM3,200 a month for 29 years, compare about 20 projects nearby, consider Putrajaya, or simply rent in Cyberjaya, which is cheap for the space you get.

articles.title: Why is the bank's valuation different from the price I agreed?
articles.excerpt: Your loan depends on what the bank's valuer says the property is worth, not what you agreed to pay. Sean explains why the two differ, and why some new units stay unsold for years.
articles.viewerQuestion: What is the difference between bank value and market value, and why does it matter to a buyer?
articles.answer: Market value is what buyers are willing to pay; bank value is a valuer's calculation, mostly based on what similar properties nearby have actually sold for. Where there are no comparable transactions, such as the last units of a new township, the bank may value well below the asking price, and your loan shrinks with it.

articles.title: Loan approved but I backed out. Can I get my booking fee back?
articles.excerpt: A buyer paid a RM1,000 booking fee after being told to 'just try the loan'. It was approved, he couldn't afford it, and the developer kept the fee. Sean explains when fees are refunded.
articles.viewerQuestion: Is it fair that the booking fee isn't refunded, and how can he get it back?
articles.answer: The developer isn't obliged to refund it: booking fees are refunded only when the loan is rejected, not when you change your mind. His best option is a polite letter asking for part of it back, and next time to work out his loan eligibility before visiting any sales gallery.

articles.title: Can I borrow on the valuation, not the price, to cover my subsale costs?
articles.excerpt: A first-time buyer wants a Maluri subsale for RM245,000 but a loan on its RM280,000 valuation, to avoid using savings. Sean explains why banks lend on the SPA price, and what to do instead.
articles.viewerQuestion: Is it possible to borrow on the higher valuation so the purchase is effectively 100% financed, and how does the process work?
articles.answer: Not simply: banks lend up to 90% of the price written in the SPA, not the valuation, and every fee and tax follows that SPA figure too. If the down payment and costs would wipe out your savings, either save a little longer, look at EPF withdrawals or genuine full-financing schemes, or accept that the property may be beyond your budget for now.

articles.title: Should I buy from a big branded developer or a smaller newcomer?
articles.excerpt: Big listed developers sell a lifestyle; smaller ones compete on facilities, price and discounts. Sean compares two brochures and lists the questions to ask at any sales gallery.
articles.viewerQuestion: Does the developer's brand matter, and how should a buyer compare projects from big and small developers?
articles.answer: For an investment, the brand matters less than the numbers: tenure, price per sq ft against the neighbours, the net price after rebates, and the rent it can earn. Big developers sell a lifestyle and command a premium; smaller ones often offer more space and discounts for the money. For your own home, buy what feels right within your budget.

articles.title: Three of us bought a house we can barely afford. Should we refinance or sell our apartment?
articles.excerpt: Three single brothers bought a RM1 million terrace house and have nothing left to renovate it. Sean calls the purchase a mistake and compares refinancing their Klang apartment with selling it.
articles.viewerQuestion: Should they refinance or sell the Klang apartment to pay for renovation, and was the house a risky buy?
articles.answer: Yes, the house was a mistake: it needs three incomes to service and they paid above subsale prices. Now they can either refinance the apartment, freeing about RM124,000 while the rent roughly covers the new instalment, or sell it for about RM200,000 after the loan and rent somewhere until the keys come. Sean would refinance and keep it, if they can handle a vacant month.

articles.title: My building now allows only one Airbnb operator. What can I do?
articles.excerpt: A first-time buyer got the keys to a city-centre unit meant for Airbnb, then the building demanded a RM100,000 deposit from operators and let only one operate. Sean explains why, and how to get the unit earning.

articles.answer: A large deposit for operators is reasonable and keeps a building manageable, and he cannot challenge the arrangement until a joint management body is formed. Meanwhile his unit earns nothing, so sign with the approved operator or furnish it and rent it out long-term.

articles.title: Could a bulk purchase get me my second property sooner?
articles.excerpt: A 27-year-old spent his savings on a compact terrace house in Subang Jaya and wants an investment unit next. Sean explains why developers have unsold units, and why entry price decides who wins on rent.
articles.viewerQuestion: Will a non-gated terrace house keep rising in value, how can he buy a second property with little cash, and if a bulk-purchase group buys many units in one project, won't they all compete for the same tenants?
articles.answer: The house is a good buy, though open, non-gated terraces will rise more slowly as security matters more to buyers. With his cash used up, his next unit has to be bought on credit: a discounted unit whose rent covers the instalment, completing in a few years while he saves for the furnishing.

articles.title: Should I buy now the condo I'll downsize to in 20 years?
articles.excerpt: A 36-year-old father of three wants a Bukit Jalil condo to rent out now and retire into later, but it needs RM150,000 down. Sean says no: sell the old apartment, regain two 90% loans and buy for cash flow.
articles.viewerQuestion: Does it make sense to buy now, rent it out even at a small loss, and move in at retirement? Or should he sell the Shah Alam apartment?
articles.answer: Don't buy it. Nobody knows what he will need, earn or be able to do at 56, and putting RM150,000 into a 70% loan for an own-stay project is the wrong tool. Sell the apartment, which frees a 90% loan for each of them, and buy for cash flow instead.

articles.title: Is buying an auction property worth the risk?
articles.excerpt: Auction prices can be the market's most genuine, but your deposit is lost if financing fails. Sean explains how auctions work and what to check before you bid.
articles.viewerQuestion: How does buying at auction work, and should a first-time buyer try it?
articles.answer: It can be a genuine bargain, but only for buyers with capital and knowledge. You pay 10% to bid and must settle the rest within 90 to 120 days, on a loan based on your winning price, so first-time buyers without savings are better off with new properties.

articles.title: What should I check before buying in a mixed development or township?
articles.excerpt: Living above the office and the mall sounds convenient, but whether it works depends on who controls the shops. Sean explains, from his time on a township team, what makes a mixed development and township succeed.
articles.viewerQuestion: What decides whether a mixed development or township is a good place to buy?
articles.answer: Ask who owns the shops. A mall owned and managed by one party can control its tenant mix and marketing; one sold off unit by unit to hundreds of owners often can't, and declines. In townships, back a developer with a long-term master plan, and judge value rather than brand.

articles.viewerQuestion: Should an unmarried couple buy a property together in joint names?
articles.answer: No. Joint names use up both partners' 90% loans on one property, and nobody plans for a break-up. If you must, set the terms out in writing; better still, buy in one name with the other as guarantor.

articles.excerpt: A 55-year-old earning RM32,000 a month wants a third and fourth rental property to pass on. Sean says judge each by yield, and use cash to buy subsale at the right price.

articles.answer: Yes, both are doable at her income, but a 15-year loan means rent will rarely cover the instalment. Judge each unit by its yield, look at subsale, auction and bulk purchases rather than buying from the developer, and put enough cash down that the rent covers the instalment.

articles.title: Cash back on a new launch, or a lower loan with positive cash flow?
articles.excerpt: Developers now offer free legal fees, furniture and even cash back, but the extras inflate the loan. Sean explains how rebates work and when cash in hand beats a unit whose rent covers its instalment.
articles.viewerQuestion: Is it better to take a new launch with big rebates and cash back, or pay a down payment to borrow less and have rent cover the instalment?
articles.answer: Rebates are built into a higher price and loan, so a new launch rarely has positive cash flow: rent follows the market, not your instalment. If you have cash, paying down to borrow less is safer. Cash back only helps if you use it to cover the monthly gap, not to spend.

articles.title: Should I buy three condos mostly in cash and stop working at 35?
articles.excerpt: A Malaysian working in Singapore plans to come home, put RM200,000 down on each of three RM300,000 condos and live off the rent. Sean shows why fixed deposits beat that plan, and what to do instead.
articles.viewerQuestion: Is it a good plan to buy three RM300,000 condos in Kuala Lumpur with RM200,000 down on each, borrowing only RM100,000 apiece, and live on the roughly RM500 a month each would leave?
articles.answer: No. Putting RM600,000 in cash into three condos for about RM1,500 a month is a poor return; the same cash in fixed deposits at about 3% earns that without tenants. Buy with loans while he still has a salary to qualify, keep his capital invested, and don't stop working altogether.

articles.title: Can I complain if my new home isn't ready when I get the keys?
articles.excerpt: A friend collected his keys to find the facilities unfinished. Sean explains the protection homebuyers have under the Housing Development Act, and the tribunal where they can claim without a lawyer.
articles.viewerQuestion: What can a buyer do when a new home or its facilities are not delivered as promised?
articles.answer: Buyers of residential property are protected by the Housing Development Act, and a developer should hand over only when an architect certifies the facilities are ready. articles.excerpt: A buyer's RM620,000 condo is about to be handed over with 270 of 770 units unsold, and rent nearby falls short of the instalment. Sean explains how developers clear stock, and why he would furnish, rent and hold.

articles.answer: Don't sell at a loss. Fully furnish it at handover, rent it out to cover most of the instalment, and hold until the market recovers enough to sell without a loss. Developers rarely cut prices openly, but they do sell leftover units privately through bulk purchasers, which is the competition CG faces.

articles.title: With populations shrinking, does property still have a future in Malaysia?
articles.excerpt: A viewer asks whether falling birth rates and crashes in China and Hong Kong mean property is a bad bet. Sean explains why he still backs Malaysian property, and where demand will move.
articles.viewerQuestion: Should people still be encouraged to own property, and will falling populations eventually crash prices?
articles.answer: In Malaysia, yes. The country still has a large young workforce, the government leans on construction and new highways to grow the economy, and buyers here need far less upfront than elsewhere. Smaller families will change what people want, towards smaller homes in convenient city locations, but prime areas will stay out of reach to buy and become places people rent.

articles.answer: For many families a large apartment lives better than a terrace house: one level, no stairs, cooler rooms and facilities for the children, at a price close to a comparable terrace in the city. Landed homes still win on parking right at the door, freedom to renovate and, so far, capital growth.

articles.title: My developer delivered late. What can I claim, and from when?
articles.excerpt: A court case ruled that late-delivery damages run from the booking date, not the SPA date. Sean explains how LAD works, how buyers can claim, and what ending booking fees could mean for buyers and developers.

articles.answer: If a developer hands over late, the standard SPA for new homes entitles you to liquidated ascertained damages calculated daily, and the homebuyer tribunal is open to any buyer without a lawyer. articles.title: With RM70,000 at 25, should I start a business or buy property first?
articles.excerpt: A 25-year-old with RM70,000 saved wants to escape the rat race, either with a self-service laundry or rental properties. Sean says start the business first: property keeps you rich rather than making you rich.

articles.answer: Start the business first, carefully and if possible while keeping his job. At 25 with no commitments he can afford to fail, and running a business teaches him far more than a salary does. Once the business makes money, buy properties whose rent covers the instalment, and use them to store that wealth.

articles.title: Is a leasehold condo with 60-odd years left too risky to buy?
articles.excerpt: A couple love a leasehold condo but worry it will be hard to sell with 60 to 70 years left on the lease. Sean says the lease is the smaller risk; buying together unmarried is the bigger one.

articles.answer: The lease isn't the real risk. If the rent covers the instalment, they can always rent the unit out and wait, so they can buy if they like it. What worries Sean is buying jointly without an agreement.

articles.title: What can I learn from Sean's worst property deal?

articles.title: I just got my keys. How do I let out the unit?
articles.excerpt: After the keys come four decisions: how long to let for, what rent to ask, how far to furnish, and who will manage tenants. Sean's checklist for new landlords.

articles.title: Why do strata buildings run down, and what can owners do about it?
articles.excerpt: Most of us will end up living in strata property, yet few owners understand how a building is run. Sean talks to David Foo, whose firm serves about 500 neighbourhoods, about fees, committees and upkeep.
articles.viewerQuestion: What makes some strata buildings well kept while others run down, and what can owners and committees do?
articles.answer: A strata building is run like a company: owners are shareholders, the committee is the board and the building manager is the chief executive. Buildings decline when collection lags behind rising costs and committees try to save rather than maintain. Pay on time, attend AGMs, and expect the committee to set targets and use numbers.

Maintain, don't hoard

articles.title: Salaried, on commission or self-employed: what trips up a loan?

articles.answer: Know which income group you are in, because each is judged on different records: payslips and EPF for employees, commission statements and tax returns for agents, and company accounts and bank statements for business owners. articles.title: Should I use tricks to qualify for a bigger housing loan?

articles.answer: No. A rejection means your income cannot carry the commitment for 30 to 35 years. Everyone in the sale earns their cut once you sign, but if the rent doesn't cover the loan, you alone carry the shortfall, and selling may still leave you owing the bank.

articles.excerpt: A 34-year-old in oil and gas earns RM11,000 but has only months of savings and likes a new PJ project costing RM3,000 a month. Sean says it is that unit she cannot afford, not property.

articles.answer: Not now. Her income qualifies for a loan, but what is left each month cannot carry a RM3,000 commitment. Stay put, build savings and income, and when ready, buy a cheaper unit for investment first while she still values flexibility.

articles.title: I'm in my 70s. What should my daughter do with our paid-off house?
articles.excerpt: A mother in her 70s has mapped out what her daughter should do with their landed home after she passes. Sean explains why cash and careful plans may not serve the next generation.
articles.viewerQuestion: Is it sensible for the daughter, after her mother has passed away, to rent out the house for about RM3,000, buy a RM300,000 to RM350,000 condo near work, and do her own repairs to save money?
articles.answer: Sean wouldn't lock the daughter into a plan. She could simply keep living in the house, and should first work out what she wants; if she does invest, a loan works better than cash, and she should buy as soon as a unit's rent covers its instalment rather than wait.
points: Cash loses value faster than it seems
Property bought in cash is a weak investment
Property pays when you borrow

articles.title: Should I sell my paid-off leasehold flat and rent near work instead?
articles.excerpt: A 41-year-old paid off a PJ leasehold apartment now worth less than she paid, and has RM600,000 in cash. Sean says keep it and rent it out, rent near work, and buy only with an investor's eye.
articles.viewerQuestion: Should she sell the leasehold flat or rent it out, and rent near work or buy another property, new or subsale?
articles.answer: Keep the flat and rent it out rather than sell before an expected upturn. Rent a place near work rather than tie a long loan to a job that may change; if she buys, buy a subsale near work as an investment, with a yield of 6% or more.

articles.title: My shop lot has tripled in value but is hard to rent. Should I sell?
articles.excerpt: A 41-year-old's paid-off Butterworth shop lot, bought for RM240,000, has an RM800,000 offer but half of it sits empty. Sean says hold for now, check the real value and rent, and pay someone to manage it.
articles.viewerQuestion: Should she sell the shop lot or keep it, and if she sells, what should she buy in the Klang Valley?
articles.answer: Hold it for now. It costs almost nothing to keep, protects her money against inflation and can be refinanced in an emergency. Check its real value and the going rent, pay a contractor or property manager instead of relying on her father, and only sell when a clearly better deal comes along.

articles.title: Should parents buy property for their children?
articles.excerpt: Some parents pay the down payment on their children's homes; some children ask for their parents' EPF. Sean explains when help teaches responsibility, and when it breeds entitlement.
articles.viewerQuestion: Should parents buy property for their children, and should children ask them to?
articles.answer: Parents can help, but use it to teach: pay the down payment and let the child pay the instalments, as savings for the future. Children should stand on their own feet; borrowing a sum and repaying it is fine, but asking for parents' savings to invest is not.

articles.title: My parents will give me RM700,000. Can I buy a RM1.35m condo?
articles.excerpt: A 30-year-old earning RM7,500 has RM700,000 to RM800,000 from his parents for a RM1.35 million tenanted condo. Sean says the gift doesn't change what he can afford.
articles.viewerQuestion: With his parents' money and the rent, is this a sensible first property, and should he put in a bigger down payment or keep the cash in a flexi loan?
articles.answer: No. On his own income he can comfortably carry a property of about RM500,000, and the gift only makes a RM1.35 million unit look affordable. He should buy his first property as an investment without his parents' money, and ask them to hold on to it for now.

articles.title: My parents will pay half. Must I buy a home to live in?
articles.excerpt: A first-time investor's parents will pay half the price, but only for a home to live in. Sean explains how to protect a one-income household and handle the condition.

articles.title: My sight may fail. Keep buying property, or slow down and live?
articles.excerpt: A 31-year-old with two properties has a genetic condition that may affect his sight. His parents urge him to slow down. Sean agrees: pause until the second unit is rented, build reserves, and spend time with family.
articles.viewerQuestion: Should he keep buying properties for financial security, or take his parents' advice to slow down and enjoy the present?
articles.answer: Slow down, but don't stop. He can't qualify for another loan until the Batu Kawan unit is rented anyway, so spend the time building reserves and furnishing money, plan for the worst case with his sight, and make time with his family. Buy a third only once he has more than he needs.

A third loan is harder

articles.title: How should I use price per square foot when comparing projects?
articles.excerpt: Price per square foot lets you compare projects and areas, but it shifts with floor level, unit size and property type. Sean explains how to read it, and a marketing trick to watch for.
articles.viewerQuestion: What does price per square foot tell me, and how should I use it?
articles.answer: Psf is the price divided by the size, and it gives you an index to compare a project with its area and its neighbours. But compare like with like: psf is higher on upper floors and for smaller units, and lower for landed homes, so a low headline psf may not mean a cheap unit.

articles.title: Do I need to own a property before I propose?
articles.excerpt: Many young men feel they must buy a home before proposing, and stretch for a landed house to do it. Sean questions the norm, and warns against making a dream home the first property.
articles.viewerQuestion: Is it necessary to own a property before proposing, and what kind of first home makes sense for a couple?
articles.answer: No. It is fine to rent while saving, and if you do buy, buy within your budget rather than a dream home. An RM800,000 landed house needs about RM4,000 a month for 30 years, which can absorb one partner's entire salary and put the relationship under strain.

articles.title: Is my property an asset or a liability? Traders vs investors

Investors buy and keep for rent; traders buy and sell for capital gains, and must play by the tax rules.

articles.title: If my rental loses RM400 a month, isn't a fixed deposit better?
articles.excerpt: A viewer works out that a zero-down condo yielding 5% still costs RM400 a month after maintenance, and asks why not use fixed deposits or EPF instead. Sean explains why leverage changes the sum.

articles.answer: Compared without a loan, fixed deposits and EPF would win. But property is bought with the bank's money: with nothing or little down, the tenant pays RM24,000 a year into your loan while you cover a few thousand, and that rent also counts as income for the next loan. Just don't buy a unit whose known rent can't cover the instalment.

Sean builds equity slowly with units whose rent covers the instalment, uses a management company, and judges a price against the area's median rather than looking for the cheapest unit.

articles.title: Out of bankruptcy at 41. Should I take a loan to rebuild my credit?

articles.answer: Don't take the personal loan. Wait the 12 months, apply for a credit card when he can and use it responsibly, and meanwhile close the monthly gap by earning more and spending less. Borrowing at 20% to clear 18% card debt only moves the debt from one name to another.

articles.answer: Refinancing is better than selling a unit that pays its way every month, but under the newer cash-out rules a conventional refinance may release only about RM30,000, and the existing debts may also hold back approval. So check every route, and settle the high-interest debt quickly even if that means selling.

articles.answer: Keep their flat as the family home and safety net. articles.title: We'll retire with six properties. What should we sell, and when?

articles.title: Moving home to retire: keep, sell or refinance our two houses here?
articles.excerpt: A family returning after 20 years abroad owns a landed house in Desa ParkCity and a stagnant leasehold townhouse in PJ. Sean says keep the first, sell the second, and choose a home by the life they want back.

Before buying anything, visit about 20 properties across types, areas and both sides of Malaysia, learn the four ways to buy, and never pay above the median price. Keep the money in shares meanwhile; property prices won't run away in a year.

articles.title: Is buying a second property within a year too aggressive?

articles.answer: Not too aggressive for her income and finances, and the building rents well. Demographics will hurt outlying areas and big houses, not city units with job-driven demand.

articles.answer: The rebates are retail-price sales tactics that everybody gets, and a newer project only wins when the entry price makes sense. Let the existing unit run, use your second 90% loan slot only when you can afford it, and keep the capital a third property would need in global equities.

articles.title: I retire next year with no children. Should I sell all my properties?
articles.excerpt: A single woman retiring next year owns a PJ terrace and three paid-off rented units, plus a condo under construction. Sean says set a budget for the life she wants, then sell or refinance to fund it.

articles.answer: Don't let the market decide. Work out what her retirement will cost, then choose how to fund it: hold everything for the rent, sell one unit every few years, or refinance each unit only as far as its rent can repay and keep the cash. articles.title: My condo is worth less than my loan. Sell at a loss or rent it out?

articles.viewerQuestion: If he mainly wants to sell, should he spend money to rent it out first, or just cut the price and sell?
articles.answer: If he can afford the gap between the sale price and what he still owes, sell, accept the loss and put his credit and cash into a location with real demand. Only hold and furnish it to rent if he can't cover that gap, because there the rent will never exceed the instalment.

articles.title: I'm 25 and working in the UK. Should I buy a RM750,000 unit in KL Sentral?
articles.excerpt: A 25-year-old graduate in the UK has modelled a KL Sentral unit at over RM1,000 per sq ft. Sean suggests five years building his career first, and explains valuations, exit plans and how deals are crafted.
articles.viewerQuestion: Is the valuation margin a good sign, is this a good investment, and how can he make it cash-flow positive?
articles.answer: There's no rush. At 25, Sean would spend the next five years raising his skills and income, then buy with more capital, more options and a clearer idea of where he will live. If he buys now, a higher valuation doesn't mean he has already made money, and cheaper areas may suit an overseas owner better.

Owning from abroad adds risk

articles.title: Should I buy a Rumawip or other affordable housing unit?
articles.excerpt: Tens of thousands of affordable homes sit unsold while city prices hit records. Sean explains who these schemes really serve, and how they change the price of the homes around them.

question.context: A May 2026 news report found tens of thousands of completed homes priced below RM300,000 still unsold in Malaysia. Developers must build a share of affordable homes such as Rumawip, often 30% of a project's units at a ceiling price of RM300,000, while prices in prime areas keep rising.
question.text: Is an affordable housing unit a good buy, and how do these schemes affect other buyers?

answer.quote: People want affordable houses in the location that they want.
answer.summary: If you qualify and the location suits you, it can be very good value, because these homes are heavily subsidised. But Sean says the schemes have produced unsold homes while their cost is passed on to the open-market homes around them.

reasons.title: A good location makes it a bargain
reasons.body: Land and other costs are subsidised, so a RM300,000 Rumawip stands out in an area where open-market units cost about RM900 per sq ft. Market rent there usually covers the instalment, and one Rumawip unit in Bangsar South was auctioned at RM370,000.

reasons.title: The income limit is high
reasons.body: A married couple can qualify for Rumawip on a household income of up to RM15,000 a month and a single buyer on RM10,000, well above the median. If you qualify, Sean sees renting the unit out as your right, though he doesn't encourage it.

reasons.title: Open-market buyers pay for it
reasons.body: If each affordable unit costs RM450,000 to build and sells at RM300,000, a developer building 300 of them loses RM45 million and spreads it over the other 700 units. Some buyers now pay more for a project without affordable housing.

reasons.title: Compare it with open-market homes
reasons.body: A developer Sean interviewed points out that many lower-income buyers struggle to get a loan or find 10% down, while an open-market unit at RM350,000 may need no down payment and carries no restriction on renting or selling later.

actions: Check whether you qualify, and what restrictions apply to renting or reselling the unit.
Judge the location first: a subsidised home is good value only where people want to live.
Before buying to rent out, compare the rent nearby with your instalment.
When buying an open-market unit, ask whether the project includes affordable housing.
Compare against open-market units at a similar price, which may come with discounts and fewer restrictions.
articles.caveat: This is Sean's view of the market in May 2026, not advice on a particular scheme, and criteria differ between federal and state schemes. For the hardcore poor, he argues, government rental housing near the city would help more than ownership.
articles.sourceNote: Summarised from Sean's full English captions for this May 2026 episode, which includes clips from his earlier interviews with developers. The quoted line is Sean's own words; everything else is paraphrased. Income limits and price ceilings are as stated in May 2026 and differ between schemes.

articles.title: Twins are coming. Should we stretch for a RM1 million family house?
articles.excerpt: A 30-year-old banker with twins on the way wants a RM1 million Kota Damansara house shared with his brother. Sean suggests renting on and buying an apartment one income can carry first.

question.asker: From J, a viewer who wrote in by email
question.context: J is 30 and earns about RM7,000 a month; his fiancée's commission income ranges from RM4,000 to RM12,000, and they are expecting twins. They rent a single-storey house in PJ for RM1,300 and have about RM100,000 in savings. He wants a RM1 million leasehold double-storey house in Kota Damansara as a family home for his father and siblings too, which would take about RM200,000 up front with touch-ups and RM4,000 a month, shared with his brother.
question.text: Should he commit to the house and work hard to pay for it, or keep renting until his early 40s?

answer.quote: You don't actually need it now, it's only for romantic reasons.
answer.summary: Keep renting for now, and buy a home on his own that fits one person's budget, around RM500,000 to RM600,000, ideally a subsale with a three-bedroom layout. Live there for five to eight years, then upgrade to a bigger family home once the twins start school.

reasons.title: Newborns strain both money and time
reasons.body: With savings used up and RM4,000 a month to pay, every sick day and every difficult boss becomes a crisis. Babies may also mean daycare costs, and they don't need a landed house, only space for their carers.

reasons.title: Shared names need a clear exit
reasons.body: If his brother puts in money, agree his share and the price at which J would buy him out later. A leasehold house can lose value nearer 60 years left, though leases in Selangor have often been extended.

reasons.title: If he buys, keep the savings
reasons.body: If the seller agrees to a higher selling price, the bank may lend more for renovation and costs. Keep the savings in a flexi loan account as an emergency fund.

reasons.title: A landed home costs more than the instalment
reasons.body: Roofs, plumbing, gates and air conditioners all need fixing. A three-bedroom apartment can house his father and sister just as well, and is far easier to run.

actions: Stay in the current rental through the birth and the first year.
Shortlist PJ apartments or homes within one income's budget, ideally where rent covers 85% to 90% of the instalment.
Work out the new monthly budget, including childcare, before committing to anything.
If buying with his brother, put the ownership split and buy-out terms in writing first.
Plan to upgrade to a family home once the twins reach primary school.
articles.caveat: If they are comfortable with the stress and the bank approves a larger loan that preserves their savings, buying the landed house is workable. Sean admits he has seen many big family homes left empty, so his view reflects his own experience.
articles.sourceNote: Summarised from Sean's full English captions for Asking Sean #203. The quoted line is verbatim; everything else is paraphrased. Figures are as the viewer stated them in February 2023.

articles.title: I need an apartment to care for my mother. Why is the developer's price higher than subsale?
articles.excerpt: A 58-year-old in Johor Bahru wants an apartment to live in with his mother, and finds the developer's unsold units dearer than subsales. Sean explains the gap and how to choose between new and subsale.

question.asker: From Mr M, a viewer who wrote in by email
question.context: Mr M, 58, lives in Johor Bahru. After his father died, he and his siblings take turns caring for their mother, who has limited mobility; his three-bedroom townhouse is full with his wife and two teenage children. He plans to buy an 810 sq ft apartment to live in with his mother and later retire to, in a project that still has unsold units from the developer. Subsale units are listed at about RM280,000 to RM350,000, and the new developer units cost noticeably more.
question.text: Why do the developer's new units cost more than subsale units, does it signal a problem, and should he buy new or subsale?

answer.quote: It's just not common for developers to sell lower than market.
answer.summary: The gap doesn't mean the building has problems: developers rarely sell leftover units below what earlier buyers paid. Since he knows exactly which unit he wants, choose on cash and condition: new units come with developer packages and less money upfront, while a subsale is usually cheaper, can be negotiated and may already be furnished.

reasons.title: Developers protect earlier buyers
reasons.body: Cutting the price of unsold units would anger existing owners and damage the developer's name for future projects. Original buyers also got 10% to 15% discounts at launch, so their net prices sit close to today's subsale asking prices.

reasons.title: Units in one building aren't equal
reasons.body: Floor, view, orientation, block and furnishing all change the price, and later blocks may be priced differently from earlier ones. Compare like with like before deciding a unit is cheap or dear.

reasons.title: New or subsale changes the cash you need
reasons.body: A subsale needs about 18% upfront for the down payment, valuation and legal fees. Buying new can mean little cash upfront with packages such as free SPA legal fees and MOT, but a higher price.

reasons.title: An apartment suits an elderly parent
reasons.body: One level means no stairs for weak knees, unlike most landed homes without a ground-floor bedroom. Dual-key layouts, with a studio beside the main unit, can also let a parent live close but separately.

actions: List recent subsale prices for units like the one you want, by floor and view, before comparing with the developer.
Ask the developer what package comes with an unsold unit, such as free legal fees, MOT and defect warranty.
Make an offer below the asking price on subsale units; owners who expected bigger gains may accept.
Check rents in the building, since they show demand and how easily the unit could be let later.
Plan for clinics, hospitals and your mother's daily needs as much as for the home itself.
articles.caveat: If a developer ever dumps units well below market, that is a warning about the developer, not a bargain. Sean didn't address the bumiputera-lot consent fee the agent offered to arrange, so check that separately with a lawyer.
articles.sourceNote: Summarised from Sean's full English captions for Asking Sean #221. The quoted line is verbatim; everything else is paraphrased. Figures are as the viewer stated them in September 2023.

articles.title: Landed or condo: which holds its value better?
articles.excerpt: A reader assumes landed homes are guaranteed to appreciate while condos age. Sean explains why that view is hindsight, where condos win, and the price ceiling open landed homes run into.

question.asker: From Lau, a viewer who wrote in by email
question.context: Lau believes that because land is limited, a landed home in KL is almost guaranteed to appreciate over 20 to 30 years. Condos, on the other hand, age: however well managed, the building and facilities start to look old.
question.text: In a sought-after area such as Bukit Jalil, Hartamas or PJ, how would a condo's value hold up against a landed home over the long run?

answer.quote: The moral of the story is it's very easy to look back.
answer.summary: Landed terrace houses do appreciate fastest, but "guaranteed" is hindsight. Condos in good locations grow a little more slowly yet earn far more rent, and older landed homes without security face a ceiling on what buyers will pay.

reasons.title: Landed wins on growth, condos win on rent
reasons.body: Official statistics rank landed terrace houses first for capital appreciation, with apartments close behind; corner lots do best of all. But a two- to three-bedroom condo in PJ rents for about RM2,500 to RM2,800, a rate tenants will not pay for a terrace, because condos offer security, facilities and less space to clean and maintain.

reasons.title: Yesterday's safe bet was once the fringe
reasons.body: Subang Jaya, PJ and Damansara Utama were on the edge of development 20 to 30 years ago, and people who bought early apartments in Mont Kiara, Hartamas or Puchong made money too. Townships launch terraces first because they sell easily; condos come later, once land is scarce.

reasons.title: Open landed homes hit a price ceiling
reasons.body: Individual-title terraces sit on public roads that often become shortcuts, and guarding them depends on a residents' association. A household paying RM1.2 to 1.5 million earns around RM18,000 to RM20,000 a month and expects security. Sean believes unguarded landed homes will hit a price cap, and notes many older owners downsize into 1,500 to 1,800 sq ft condos.

reasons.title: Big landed homes are hard to sell
reasons.body: Luxury homes bought for RM800,000 years ago are now listed at RM3 to 4 million and struggling to sell. On a RM3 million home, a buyer needs about RM300,000 down plus RM300,000 to RM400,000 for renovation before moving in, which only the top 5% or so of Malaysians can afford.

actions: Decide first whether you want capital growth or rental income; they point to different property types.
If you buy landed, favour guarded or strata projects and avoid lots facing a main road or a likely shortcut.
Look at today's early-stage townships, rather than chasing locations that have already made their money.
Before buying a large landed home, ask who could afford to buy it from you in 20 years.
Consider renting the dream home and putting your capital into rental apartments instead, as Sean suggests.
articles.caveat: With unlimited capital, Sean says he would happily buy landed and commercial property in prime city areas; these trade-offs bite hardest for buyers stretching to afford. He also warns against copying US house-flipping advice, since Malaysian financing works very differently.
articles.sourceNote: Summarised from Sean's full English captions for Asking Sean #241. The quoted answer is verbatim; everything else is paraphrased. Rents and prices are as Sean stated them in February 2024.

articles.title: Should we move from our Bangi house to a new Cyberjaya condo to cut the commute?
articles.excerpt: Two civil servants want to swap their Bangi terrace for a RM575,000 Cyberjaya condo to shorten the school run. Sean says high-rise prices there have fallen, so compare 20 projects, or simply rent.

question.asker: From E, a viewer who wrote in by email
question.context: E, 40, and her husband are civil servants who have lived in a Bangi terrace house since 2014, now valued at about RM430,000 to RM530,000. Their son's playschool is in Cyberjaya and E works in Putrajaya, a journey of about 90 minutes. They are looking at a Cyberjaya condo due in 2025, with a loan of about RM575,000 over 29 years and about RM3,200 a month including maintenance, though E retires in 19 years.
question.text: Should they rent out or sell the Bangi house, is RM3,200 a month a burden, and what are Cyberjaya's prospects if they sell in 20 years?

answer.quote: We rent things that depreciates in value.
answer.summary: First check the numbers they left out: their joint income and how much is still owed on the Bangi house. Cyberjaya high-rises have generally lost value, so before committing RM3,200 a month for 29 years, compare about 20 projects nearby, consider Putrajaya, or simply rent in Cyberjaya, which is cheap for the space you get.

reasons.title: Selling may free less than you think
reasons.body: In the first years of a loan most of each instalment goes to interest, so a house bought around RM400,000 may still owe about RM380,000 after ten years. After any RPGT on the gain, the cash arrives six to eight months after the sale.

reasons.title: Cyberjaya high-rises have struggled
reasons.body: The town has jobs and amenities, but rental demand hasn't followed, and many condos end up at auction. A friend of Sean's bought at RM450,000 ten years ago; similar units now go for about RM280,000.

reasons.title: Rent what loses value
reasons.body: Where high-rise prices are falling, rents are low too, so a bigger unit or even a landed home can be rented for less than the RM3,200 instalment. Distances in Cyberjaya are also quick to drive, so living right beside the school isn't essential.

reasons.title: Sales galleries are built to close
reasons.body: Sean once designed sales galleries and says most buyers who walk in end up booking. Comparing other projects, and Putrajaya, which has performed better, protects against an emotional purchase.

actions: Work out your joint income and check the instalment is no more than about a third of it.
Find out how much you still owe on the Bangi house and what it would sell for after costs.
Visit about 20 projects around Cyberjaya and Putrajaya, including subsales, before booking.
Price what RM2,500 to RM2,600 a month would rent in Cyberjaya, and compare it with buying.
If you keep the Bangi house to rent out, don't expect a landed home's rent to cover a loan.
articles.caveat: If one specific school is non-negotiable, living nearby matters more. Sean notes Cyberjaya's landed homes have done well; his concern is its high-rise market.
articles.sourceNote: Summarised from Sean's full English captions for Asking Sean #220. The quoted line is verbatim; everything else is paraphrased. Figures are as the viewer and Sean stated them in August 2023. Sean says he used to design property sales galleries.

articles.title: Why is the bank's valuation different from the price I agreed?
articles.excerpt: Your loan depends on what the bank's valuer says the property is worth, not what you agreed to pay. Sean explains why the two differ, and why some new units stay unsold for years.

question.context: Before a bank lends, a professional valuer prepares a report on what the property is worth, and the bank decides how much to finance from it. Many buyers assume the bank's value equals the market price, but the two often differ.
question.text: What is the difference between bank value and market value, and why does it matter to a buyer?

answer.quote: market value is the value determined by the market
answer.summary: Market value is what buyers are willing to pay; bank value is a valuer's calculation, mostly based on what similar properties nearby have actually sold for. Where there are no comparable transactions, such as the last units of a new township, the bank may value well below the asking price, and your loan shrinks with it.

reasons.title: Valuers compare recent transactions
reasons.body: Of the methods valuers use, comparison with similar properties is the most common for homes and shops. A price has to be backed by nearby sales at that level.

reasons.title: New launches can outrun valuations
reasons.body: If a developer prices its final units at RM1 million where nothing nearby has sold for that, banks may value them at only RM700,000 to RM800,000. Those units can stay unsold until subsale transactions catch up.

reasons.title: Government valuations affect stamp duty
reasons.body: If the authorities value a property you bought for RM1 million at RM1.2 million, stamp duty is charged on the higher figure.

actions: Ask the bank for its valuation before you commit to a price.
Check recent transacted prices nearby, not just the asking price.
Be wary of new units priced well above anything sold in the area.
Budget for a shortfall if the valuation comes in below your price.
articles.caveat: Sean also describes deals that rely on a valuation above the agreed price; those are left out here, and buyers should take legal advice on any arrangement where the SPA price differs from what is paid.
articles.sourceNote: Summarised from Sean's English captions for this July 2019 video. The captions are of poor quality, so only points that are clear are included; figures on valuation fees and auction pricing, and his examples of zero-down and cash-back deals, are left out. The quoted line is verbatim; everything else is paraphrased.

articles.title: Loan approved but I backed out. Can I get my booking fee back?
articles.excerpt: A buyer paid a RM1,000 booking fee after being told to 'just try the loan'. It was approved, he couldn't afford it, and the developer kept the fee. Sean explains when fees are refunded.

question.asker: From Kumar, a viewer who wrote in by email
question.context: Kumar paid a RM1,000 booking fee on a new launch condo in Damansara Perdana, dealing with the developer directly after bad experiences with agents. He doubted he could afford it, but the developer's representative encouraged him to apply for a loan first. The loan was approved, he decided the instalment was too high and declined it, and the developer refused to refund the fee. The bank wouldn't issue a rejection letter.
question.text: Is it fair that the booking fee isn't refunded, and how can he get it back?

answer.quote: Refund is only allowed when your loan application is rejected.
answer.summary: The developer isn't obliged to refund it: booking fees are refunded only when the loan is rejected, not when you change your mind. His best option is a polite letter asking for part of it back, and next time to work out his loan eligibility before visiting any sales gallery.

reasons.title: The fee reserves the unit
reasons.body: It pays for the paperwork and loan coordination and holds the unit for you. If anyone could book and later walk away with a full refund, people could tie up whole blocks for months at no cost.

reasons.title: 'Try the loan first' is a sales hook
reasons.body: Being told you can apply and get a refund if it doesn't work out is a common line. It is only true if the bank turns you down, which is why knowing your eligibility in advance protects you.

reasons.title: Rejections hurt your record
reasons.body: A rejected application is visible to other banks and can harm your next application for about four to six months. Experienced investors ask a bank officer for an informal assessment before submitting anything.

reasons.title: Losing RM1,000 beats a 35-year mistake
reasons.body: Many buyers go ahead with a purchase they can't afford rather than lose the booking fee. Sean is glad Kumar chose to lose the fee instead.

actions: Write a polite letter to the developer explaining you are a first-time buyer and asking for part of the fee back.
Before visiting any sales gallery, find out how much loan you qualify for, and only look at projects within it.
Ask a bank officer for an informal assessment of your profile before submitting a formal application.
Read the booking form's refund terms before paying, and don't rely on what you are told verbally.
Where possible, buy from the developer's own sales staff, who are more likely to still be around at handover.
articles.caveat: Some developers have dropped booking fees altogether and let you proceed once your loan qualifies, so practices differ. Sean says strictly speaking booking fees aren't permitted, but they remain common in the market.
articles.sourceNote: Summarised from Sean's full English captions for Asking Sean #237. The quoted answer is verbatim; everything else is paraphrased. Figures and practices are as Sean described them in January 2024.

articles.title: Can I borrow on the valuation, not the price, to cover my subsale costs?
articles.excerpt: A first-time buyer wants a Maluri subsale for RM245,000 but a loan on its RM280,000 valuation, to avoid using savings. Sean explains why banks lend on the SPA price, and what to do instead.

question.asker: From M, a viewer who wrote in by email
question.context: M is a first-time buyer looking at a subsale apartment in Maluri listed at RM260,000, with a market valuation of about RM280,000. M doesn't want to use up savings on the 10% down payment and other costs, and hopes to negotiate the price down to RM245,000 while borrowing RM280,000, using the difference for the down payment, fees and renovation.
question.text: Is it possible to borrow on the higher valuation so the purchase is effectively 100% financed, and how does the process work?

answer.quote: Maybe you cannot afford the property.
answer.summary: Not simply: banks lend up to 90% of the price written in the SPA, not the valuation, and every fee and tax follows that SPA figure too. If the down payment and costs would wipe out your savings, either save a little longer, look at EPF withdrawals or genuine full-financing schemes, or accept that the property may be beyond your budget for now.

reasons.title: The SPA price sets the loan
reasons.body: Stamp duty, legal fees and any RPGT are all calculated on the SPA price. Writing a higher price raises the owner's and buyer's costs, so owners often refuse, and any such arrangement depends on the bank's own valuation, the owner's written consent through the lawyers, and your income qualifying for the larger loan.

reasons.title: Valuations come from the bank
reasons.body: An agent's figure isn't enough: the bank asks its panel valuers, who may quote different amounts. Even a high valuation only helps if you qualify for the bigger loan.

reasons.title: A subsale needs about 18% in cash
reasons.body: Beyond the 10% down payment come legal fees, stamp duty and other charges, paid in stages over a six- to nine-month process. It's easy to lose track, so budget for the whole amount from the start.

reasons.title: Owning costs more than the instalment
reasons.body: Maintenance, repairs and building levies add up. If the instalment is well above what you'd pay in rent, and you're single with an uncertain future, renting and investing first may be the better path.

actions: Budget about 18% of the price in cash before committing to a subsale.
Check how much you could withdraw from EPF towards a purchase under the current rules.
Ask banks whether you qualify for any genuine full-financing scheme for first homes.
If buying would leave no emergency fund, set a savings target, such as another RM10,000 in six to eight months, before buying.
Have any unusual price arrangement checked by your own lawyer before signing anything.
articles.caveat: If the price is a rare bargain and you can live without savings for a year or two, buying now can still be your choice; Sean asks whether your health, family and sleep can handle that. Sean also stresses he is not an agent and sells no property.
articles.sourceNote: Summarised from Sean's full English captions for Asking Sean #214. The quoted line is verbatim; everything else is paraphrased. Figures are as the viewer and Sean stated them in June 2023. EPF withdrawal rules have changed since, so check the current ones.

articles.title: Should I buy from a big branded developer or a smaller newcomer?
articles.excerpt: Big listed developers sell a lifestyle; smaller ones compete on facilities, price and discounts. Sean compares two brochures and lists the questions to ask at any sales gallery.

question.context: Viewers shopping for new launches ask whether to stick with big, publicly listed developers or consider smaller and newer ones. Sean compares brochures from one of each: a two-room unit from a big name in Petaling Jaya and a three-room unit from a smaller developer in Kuala Lumpur, both at about RM750,000.
question.text: Does the developer's brand matter, and how should a buyer compare projects from big and small developers?

answer.quote: investors only look at numbers
answer.summary: For an investment, the brand matters less than the numbers: tenure, price per sq ft against the neighbours, the net price after rebates, and the rent it can earn. Big developers sell a lifestyle and command a premium; smaller ones often offer more space and discounts for the money. For your own home, buy what feels right within your budget.

reasons.title: Big names sell a lifestyle
reasons.body: Branded developers market the surroundings, lakes and landscaping, and their brand reassures buyers. Smaller developers tend to compete on facilities, price and discounts.

reasons.title: Brochures leave things out
reasons.body: Developers don't advertise what works against them, such as leasehold tenure or how many car parks come with a unit. Ask directly.

reasons.title: Built-up may include extras
reasons.body: Some developers count air-conditioner ledges or balconies in the built-up area, which lowers the apparent price per sq ft. It is marketing, not cheating, but compare like with like.

reasons.title: Construction time changes the deal
reasons.body: Whether a project takes three, four or five years matters: you are paying today for a unit completed years later, and rebates often vary with the construction stage.

actions: Ask whether the land is freehold or leasehold, and how many car parks are included.
Check the price per sq ft of neighbouring projects on property portals.
Ask what the built-up area includes, and the construction period.
Work out the net price after every discount and rebate.
Visit the site to see what is next door, such as a school, market or busy junction.
articles.caveat: This 2017 comparison predates the wave of stalled projects during COVID, after which Sean has stressed a developer's financial strength more.
articles.sourceNote: Summarised from Sean's full English captions for this September 2017 video, which he says is not sponsored. The projects compared are not named here. The quoted line is verbatim; everything else is paraphrased.

articles.title: Three of us bought a house we can barely afford. Should we refinance or sell our apartment?
articles.excerpt: Three single brothers bought a RM1 million terrace house and have nothing left to renovate it. Sean calls the purchase a mistake and compares refinancing their Klang apartment with selling it.

question.asker: From S, a viewer who wrote in by email
question.context: S, 43, and his brothers, 45 and 37, are single and earn about RM12,000 a month between them. In 2013 S and his younger brother bought a Klang apartment from the developer for RM265,000; about RM180,000 of the loan is left, similar units are listed at about RM320,000 to RM380,000, and it would rent for about RM1,000 to RM1,300 furnished. Last year all three bought a double-storey terrace house in Shah Alam from the developer for about RM1.04 million with an 85% loan over 30 years, so all live together. Keys are due at the end of 2024, when the RM4,300 instalment starts, and they have no money left for renovation.
question.text: Should they refinance or sell the Klang apartment to pay for renovation, and was the house a risky buy?

answer.quote: Buying the property was a very, very big mistake.
answer.summary: Yes, the house was a mistake: it needs three incomes to service and they paid above subsale prices. Now they can either refinance the apartment, freeing about RM124,000 while the rent roughly covers the new instalment, or sell it for about RM200,000 after the loan and rent somewhere until the keys come. Sean would refinance and keep it, if they can handle a vacant month.

reasons.title: New homes are priced ahead
reasons.body: Developers price in future growth: similar subsale terraces nearby sell for about RM850,000 to RM900,000, so they paid about RM100,000 more and shouldn't expect quick gains. A sale soon wouldn't clear the loan comfortably either.

reasons.title: Refinancing frees cash but raises the instalment
reasons.body: At a RM380,000 valuation, an 80% loan of about RM304,000 clears the RM180,000 owed and leaves about RM124,000. The new instalment of roughly RM1,200 to RM1,300 is close to the rent, but an empty month comes out of their pockets.

reasons.title: Selling takes months
reasons.body: A sale takes about six months to complete for freehold and about nine for leasehold, so they'd need to time it and rent a place in between. Refinancing and then selling within three months isn't realistic, because the paperwork alone takes that long.

reasons.title: Shared ownership carries extra risk
reasons.body: If one brother loses his job, marries or wants his share out, the others must cover or buy him out. A rise in interest rates would also push the RM4,300 instalment higher.

actions: Ask your bank's mortgage department for a valuation from its panel valuers, and compare it with listings on property portals.
Decide on a basic renovation budget first; for a bare terrace house, Sean estimates about RM70,000 to RM80,000 for essentials.
If you refinance, keep the extra cash as a buffer for months when the apartment is empty.
If you sell, park what's left after renovating in a flexi or semi-flexi loan account to cut interest.
Agree in writing how the brothers will share costs, and what happens if one wants to leave.
articles.caveat: Sean's preferred option suits brothers who can tolerate the apartment sitting empty for a while; if they can't, selling is the safer choice. With hindsight, he would have rented a large house and let out the apartment instead of buying.
articles.sourceNote: Summarised from Sean's full English captions for Asking Sean #225. The quoted line is verbatim; everything else is paraphrased. Figures are as the viewer and Sean stated them in October 2023, and the refinancing sums are Sean's rough examples.

video.title: ASKING SEAN #225 | BROTHERS BOUGHT A HOUSE THEY COULD NOT AFFORD

articles.title: My building now allows only one Airbnb operator. What can I do?
articles.excerpt: A first-time buyer got the keys to a city-centre unit meant for Airbnb, then the building demanded a RM100,000 deposit from operators and let only one operate. Sean explains why, and how to get the unit earning.

question.asker: From Mr Kong, a viewer who wrote in by email
question.context: Mr Kong bought his first property, a new unit in central Kuala Lumpur, to run as a short-term rental and lined up an Airbnb operator. Soon after he got the keys, building management required a RM100,000 deposit from short-stay operators and restricted their access. His operator pulled out, and he hears only one operator is now allowed in the building.
question.text: Is it fair for management to allow only one operator, and what should he do now?

answer.quote: focus on the problem just move on as quickly as possible
answer.summary: A large deposit for operators is reasonable and keeps a building manageable, and he cannot challenge the arrangement until a joint management body is formed. Meanwhile his unit earns nothing, so sign with the approved operator or furnish it and rent it out long-term.

reasons.title: Short-stay should be plan D
reasons.body: Sean rates a project by whether long-term, medium-term or room rental can cover the instalment, with Airbnb only as a last option. A unit that relies on Airbnb alone has nothing to fall back on.

reasons.title: Short-stay can be banned
reasons.body: Penang has limited it to commercial-title projects, Singapore bans it nationwide, and a building's owners can vote it out. Any of these can end the strategy overnight.

reasons.title: Why a big deposit helps
reasons.body: With seven or eight operators, residents and managers cannot tell whose guests caused damage. A RM100,000 deposit filters for operators with the money to pay for repairs, and fewer of them is easier to manage.

reasons.title: Airbnb buildings need a quick exit
reasons.body: Heavily used buildings can deteriorate like student housing, families won't buy into them, and about 10,000 similar units are coming around Bukit Bintang and KLCC. The time to sell is while rates are high, which is when owners least want to.

actions: Talk to the approved operator, even if its terms are less generous.
If you have no budget to furnish, buy simple furniture online and rent the unit long-term for now.
Use zero-interest instalment plans to furnish if your credit is good.
Raise the operator question at the AGM once the joint management body is formed.
Keep short-stay units for later in your portfolio, after projects whose long-term rent covers the loan.
articles.caveat: If another operator paid the same deposit and was still refused, that would be worth questioning. Sean had heard of the building but had not seen evidence of falling rents there.
articles.sourceNote: Summarised from Sean's full English captions for Asking Sean #271. The quoted line is verbatim; everything else is paraphrased. Figures are as stated in January 2025. The episode is sponsored by Versa, a savings app, and Sean mentions the instalment plans of The Makeover Guys, a renovation company he works with.
