articles.title: Could a bulk purchase get me my second property sooner?
articles.excerpt: A 27-year-old spent his savings on a compact terrace house in Subang Jaya and wants an investment unit next. Sean explains why developers have unsold units, and why entry price decides who wins on rent.

question.asker: From Mr N, a viewer who wrote in by email
question.context: Mr N is 27, earns RM6,500 a month and expects about 20% a year in raises. Last year he bought a compact terrace house in SS19, Subang Jaya, for RM415,000, below the area's median of about RM450,000, spending RM50,000 on the down payment and fees and RM60,000 on renovation, including his EPF Account 2. He has about RM10,000 in cash and RM20,000 in shares left.
question.text: Will a non-gated terrace house keep rising in value, how can he buy a second property with little cash, and if a bulk-purchase group buys many units in one project, won't they all compete for the same tenants?

answer.quote: Entry price determines the success of your investment for property.
answer.summary: The house is a good buy, though open, non-gated terraces will rise more slowly as security matters more to buyers. With his cash used up, his next unit has to be bought on credit: a discounted unit whose rent covers the instalment, completing in a few years while he saves for the furnishing.

reasons.title: Open terraces have a price ceiling
reasons.body: Easy access makes non-gated houses targets when crime rises, and their roads are public, so residents cannot seal them off. As prices approach RM1 million, which needs about RM15,000 a month in income, buyers expect security and facilities, so growth slows.

reasons.title: Unsold units come from ambitious pricing
reasons.body: Developers raise prices as a project sells, and the last 10% can stay unsold. They cannot cut prices openly without upsetting earlier buyers, so they sell the rest at a discount through investment clubs instead.

reasons.title: A lower entry price wins the rental race
reasons.body: In a project of hundreds of identical units, the owner who paid less has a smaller instalment and cash back to furnish properly, so a fully furnished unit beats a bare one at the same rent.

reasons.title: Cash back belongs to the property
reasons.body: Sean warns that cash back is not spending money for a car or a holiday. It should go into furnishing the unit or reducing the loan, or the rent will not perform.

actions: Add CCTV, alarms and better locks to a non-gated home.
Agree with your spouse on how many properties you want and when, before buying more.
Look for a discounted unit whose rent covers the instalment, due to complete in four to five years.
Save for furnishing while it is being built; a three-bedroom fit-out can cost RM50,000 to RM60,000.
Look for completed projects launched before COVID, which often have better materials than new launches.
articles.caveat: If he only wants two or three properties in his lifetime, Sean says taking it slowly and building cash first is fine. Not every developer works with bulk-purchase clubs, so the choice of units is limited.
articles.sourceNote: Summarised from Sean's full English captions for Asking Sean #286. The quoted answer is verbatim; everything else is paraphrased. Figures are as stated in June 2025. Sean is a member of FAR Capital, the bulk-purchase club discussed in this episode, not its owner; his recent purchases came through it, and the episode links to it.

video.title: ASKING SEAN #286 | WHY SO MANY UNSOLD UNIT?

articles.title: Should I buy now the condo I'll downsize to in 20 years?
articles.excerpt: A 36-year-old father of three wants a Bukit Jalil condo to rent out now and retire into later, but it needs RM150,000 down. Sean says no: sell the old apartment, regain two 90% loans and buy for cash flow.

question.asker: From RC, a viewer who wrote in by email
question.context: RC is 36 with three children. He and his wife earn about RM20,000 a month together, and his side business brings in about RM25,000 more. They own a Shah Alam apartment bought for RM345,000 in 2014, rented at about RM1,600, and a RM1.3 million semi-D bought in 2023, both in joint names, so any further loan is capped at 70%. He is thinking of a Bukit Jalil condo to rent out until they downsize in 20 to 25 years, which would need about RM150,000 down and RM2,200 a month.
question.text: Does it make sense to buy now, rent it out even at a small loss, and move in at retirement? Or should he sell the Shah Alam apartment?

answer.quote: Invest in properties using credit. Invest in everything else using cash.
answer.summary: Don't buy it. Nobody knows what he will need, earn or be able to do at 56, and putting RM150,000 into a 70% loan for an own-stay project is the wrong tool. Sell the apartment, which frees a 90% loan for each of them, and buy for cash flow instead.

reasons.title: Twenty years is too far to plan a home
reasons.body: By 56 his income, health and family will all be different; if his side business grows, he may prefer somewhere quite different. A building also needs good management to stay in shape for decades, and the Urban Renewal Act uses 30 years as a checkpoint. Sean expects oversupply in parts of Bukit Jalil.

reasons.title: Joint names used up both 90% loans
reasons.body: Each Malaysian gets two 90% loans for residential property. A couple who buys every home jointly uses both people's slots each time, so their third purchase is capped at 70%. Selling the joint apartment frees a 90% slot for each of them.

reasons.title: At 70%, many units beat this one
reasons.body: With 30% down, which is the international norm, almost any KL project rents for more than its instalment. Putting RM150,000 down on an own-stay project only to break even is a poor use of that cash.

reasons.title: The apartment is ready to sell
reasons.body: Held for about ten years, it falls outside RPGT, which is counted from the SPA date. Sold at RM330,000 to RM350,000, it would roughly clear the loan, and a cut in interest rates would make it easier to sell as more buyers qualify.

actions: Prepare to sell the Shah Alam apartment, and ask agents to test the market now.
Keep the RM150,000 invested, or park it in the semi-D loan account to reduce interest if your bank allows it.
With your two freed 90% loans, buy units where the rent covers the instalment, comparing new, subsale, auction and bulk purchase.
If you want sole names later, ask the bank whether one spouse can refinance the other's share; that spouse's income must qualify for the whole loan.
Shop for a retirement home when you are near retirement; any time can be a good time to buy at the right price.
articles.caveat: If his wife has her own income, Sean encourages putting a property in her name alone. A joint name makes sense mainly for a spouse without income, who otherwise has no claim to the home.
articles.sourceNote: Summarised from Sean's full English captions for Asking Sean #295. The quoted answer is verbatim; everything else is paraphrased. Figures and RPGT rules are as stated in September 2025. Sean owns a unit in Bukit Jalil himself and is a customer of FAR Capital, a bulk-purchase club, not its owner.

video.title: ASKING SEAN #295 | BUYING A HOUSE TO RETIRE IN 20 YEARS TIME?

articles.title: Is buying an auction property worth the risk?
articles.excerpt: Auction prices can be the market's most genuine, but your deposit is lost if financing fails. Sean explains how auctions work and what to check before you bid.

question.context: When an owner misses three consecutive monthly instalments, the bank can send the property to auction, a process that takes six to eight months. Auctions now run online, and many of the units on offer are newer ones from investors who bought more than they could carry.
question.text: How does buying at auction work, and should a first-time buyer try it?

answer.quote: This auction process requires a lot of capital.
answer.summary: It can be a genuine bargain, but only for buyers with capital and knowledge. You pay 10% to bid and must settle the rest within 90 to 120 days, on a loan based on your winning price, so first-time buyers without savings are better off with new properties.

reasons.title: The loan follows the price you pay
reasons.body: To bid on a unit with a RM360,000 reserve price you put up 10%, RM36,000. Win at RM380,000 and you can borrow 90% of that, RM342,000, not 90% of a RM500,000 market value. If the bank lends only 70%, you must find the difference.

reasons.title: Some deals can't be financed
reasons.body: A title under a private caveat can only be bought with cash, and some auctioned houses stand on land owned by someone else. Sean has seen bidders lose their 10% because no bank would lend.

reasons.title: You buy it as it is
reasons.body: Units are sold as is, often unseen inside. Unpaid maintenance fees can be large, up to RM160,000 on one unit left empty for years, so check whether the bank's terms say it will settle them. An occupant, especially an owner who has lost the home, can mean trouble.

reasons.title: Prices fall each round without bids
reasons.body: When nobody bids, the bank lowers the reserve, for example from RM500,000 to RM450,000, RM410,000 and then RM360,000. Genuine bidders can still push a unit back towards market value, so knowing which round to go in is a skill.

actions: Have 10% of the reserve price ready to bid, plus cash to cover any shortfall in financing.
Check how much a bank will lend on that particular unit before you bid.
Read the sale terms for caveats, who owns the land and who pays outstanding maintenance fees.
Use an agent experienced in auctions to arrange a viewing and find out who occupies the unit.
Set a maximum bid and stick to it; an agent can bid for you within your limit.
articles.caveat: If you have little more than an emergency fund, Sean says new properties are the better route. For buyers in their 30s to 50s with capital, auctions are worth comparing with subsale: they are no longer the shady, unregulated halls older buyers warn about, and many units are fairly new.
articles.sourceNote: Summarised from Sean's full English captions for this March 2021 episode. The quoted answer is verbatim; everything else is paraphrased. Sean checked his notes with Jeff, an agent who specialises in auction properties and whom the video recommends. The process is as described in 2021.

video.title: AUCTION PROPERTY

articles.title: I own two properties. How would you buy four more?
articles.excerpt: A 36-year-old with RM700,000 in shares and funds and two properties wants four more. Sean lists the ways investors get around the 70% loan limit, and asks why four.

question.asker: From Vu, a viewer who wrote in by email
question.context: Vu is 36, married and earns about RM12,000 a month. He has about RM700,000 in shares, ETFs and funds and about RM400,000 in EPF. He owns two properties: one rented out since handover three years ago, with rent covering about 90% of its instalment, and one under construction.
question.text: If he wanted to buy four more investment properties, how would Sean go about it?

answer.quote: The goal is never to buy cheap properties
answer.summary: Buy only units bought with little cash whose rent covers the instalment, and get around the 70% loan limit on a third residential loan in one of several ways. But replace 'four more' with a target value or rental income, keep building the share portfolio that is already working, and buy one when a good deal appears.

reasons.title: Leverage is the point of property
reasons.body: Banks fund 90% or more, a tenant pays the loan, and your own capital can be invested elsewhere or parked in the loan account to cut interest while staying withdrawable. Sean would not buy property outright in cash.

reasons.title: The third loan is capped at 70%
reasons.body: Each Malaysian gets two residential loans at up to 90%; from the third, it is 70% however high the income. On a RM500,000 unit that means RM150,000 in cash.

reasons.title: There are ways around the cap
reasons.body: Commercial-title suites can be financed at up to 85%; bulk-purchase discounts of 20% to 30% cover the gap; equity in older units can be refinanced after 10 to 15 years, though cash-out is now restricted; and refinancing existing loans with an insurer-linked lender can, Sean says, free the 90% slots again at a higher rate. Or pay the difference in cash.

reasons.title: Unit counts lead to bad buys
reasons.body: An arbitrary target, such as six properties by 40, pushes people to buy whatever is available. A target like RM20 million in value, or a monthly rental income, rewards buying fewer, better units.

actions: Set a target value or monthly rental income with your spouse instead of a number of units.
Only buy units needing little upfront cash, with about 6% yield or rent above the instalment.
Compare commercial-title financing, bulk purchase and refinancing before paying 30% down.
Keep growing the share portfolio that built your wealth.
Don't announce how many properties you own.
articles.caveat: Sean says he avoids low-cost and welfare housing as investments, though they would make four units cheap. The refinancing rules he describes are as of late 2024 and were tightening.
articles.sourceNote: Summarised from Sean's full English captions for Asking Sean #269. The quoted line is verbatim; everything else is paraphrased. Figures are as stated in December 2024. Sean is a long-term customer of FAR Capital, a bulk-purchase club, not its owner, and refers viewers to a contact for insurer-linked home loans; the episode is sponsored by Versa, a savings app. A subsale method he describes, financing at a bank valuation above the agreed price, is left out here.

video.title: ASKING SEAN #269 | BUILDING BEYOND THE 3RD PROPERTY

articles.title: What should I check before buying in a mixed development or township?
articles.excerpt: Living above the office and the mall sounds convenient, but whether it works depends on who controls the shops. Sean explains, from his time on a township team, what makes a mixed development and township succeed.

question.context: Mixed developments put homes, offices and a mall on one site, and large townships add schools, landed homes and transport over many years. Sean filmed this in a Johor township where he had worked on the development team, as residents were collecting their keys.
question.text: What decides whether a mixed development or township is a good place to buy?

answer.quote: please ask who owns the retail units
answer.summary: Ask who owns the shops. A mall owned and managed by one party can control its tenant mix and marketing; one sold off unit by unit to hundreds of owners often can't, and declines. In townships, back a developer with a long-term master plan, and judge value rather than brand.

reasons.title: The retail mix makes or breaks it
reasons.body: Anchor tenants such as supermarkets and hardware chains draw their own crowds, and a good mix of grocers, bookshops and services is what makes living above a mall convenient.

reasons.title: Strata malls are hard to manage
reasons.body: When retail units are sold to individual owners, management has no say over who rents them, and rebranding or marketing needs hundreds of owners to agree. Several older strata malls struggled for this reason.

reasons.title: Townships grow in stages
reasons.body: A good master plan first builds a self-sustaining mixed core, then adds schools, transport links and landed phases to draw people in over ten years or more.

reasons.title: Brands cost more for a reason
reasons.body: Established township developers price higher because they look after the area for years. For a young investor unsure where to start, choosing a major brand is a safe default, but pay for value, not the name.

actions: Ask whether the retail component is owned by one party or sold as strata units.
Look at the anchor tenants and the mix of shops, not just the building.
Read the township's master plan and what the developer has already delivered.
Check transport links to the places residents work.
Compare prices with neighbouring projects to judge the brand premium.
articles.caveat: Sean's view of this township draws on his time working for its developer; other townships and developers may follow different models.
articles.sourceNote: Summarised from Sean's English captions for this February 2018 video. Sean previously worked on the development team for the township he films here, which is not named in this summary. The quoted line is verbatim; everything else is paraphrased.

articles.title: Should I buy a property with my boyfriend or girlfriend?
articles.excerpt: Couples who buy in joint names find a break-up leaves both of them on the loan. Sean explains why he discourages it, and the arrangement he prefers.

question.context: Sean has seen friends' break-ups turn a property they bought together into a long, sticky problem. Couples usually join names because neither can afford the home alone, and bankers often suggest adding a second name to get a loan approved.
question.text: Should an unmarried couple buy a property together in joint names?

answer.quote: I will not encourage couples to actually buy property by joining names.
answer.summary: No. Joint names use up both partners' 90% loans on one property, and nobody plans for a break-up. If you must, set the terms out in writing; better still, buy in one name with the other as guarantor.

reasons.title: It wastes your 90% loans
reasons.body: Each person can usually get up to 90% financing on their first two residential loans; from the third it is normally 70%. Buying jointly uses both partners' quota on one property, while buying separately lets a couple hold up to four at 90%.

reasons.title: Break-ups don't service loans
reasons.body: If a couple stops talking, the instalments can stop too. The bank sends warning letters to both of you, and both get arrears recorded in CCRIS.

reasons.title: Joining names often means overreaching
reasons.body: If one income qualifies for a RM300,000 home but together you buy a RM700,000 landed house, you take on about RM3,500 a month for 30 years. Lose one income and the home is at risk.

reasons.title: One name, one guarantor
reasons.body: Sean prefers the property in one partner's name, with the other acting as guarantor on the loan if the income falls short. The other partner keeps their own quota for later purchases.

actions: Don't buy a property as proof of your relationship.
If one income can't support the home, look at a cheaper one before adding a second name.
If you do buy jointly, agree in writing, ideally with a lawyer, what happens if either of you loses a job, stops paying or wants to sell.
Consider buying in one name with your partner as guarantor.
articles.caveat: Sean has no objection to joint names between family members who trust each other, though never with a stranger, and a couple with clear written terms can make it work.
articles.sourceNote: Summarised from Sean's full English captions for this November 2018 episode. The quoted answer is verbatim; everything else is paraphrased. The captions are unclear in places, so only clearly stated points are included. Loan margins are as described in 2018, so check current rules with a bank.

articles.title: I'm 55 with a high income. Should I keep buying rental properties?
articles.excerpt: A 55-year-old earning RM32,000 a month wants a third and fourth rental property to pass on. Sean says judge each by yield, and use cash to buy subsale at the right price.

question.asker: From S, a viewer who wrote in by email
question.context: S turns 55 this year, earns about RM32,000 a month gross and plans to work until 60. She owns a fully paid double-storey corner house worth about RM3 million, has about RM1.7 million in EPF and has just bought a RM1.2 million freehold condo for her own use with a 90% loan, about RM1 million over 15 years at 3.85%. She avoids shares and unit trusts, and wants to grow wealth to pass on to her two sons.
question.text: Is it a good move to buy a third property for rent in Kuala Lumpur, and could she take a loan for a fourth in 2026?

answer.quote: The criteria of investment should be yield.
answer.summary: Yes, both are doable at her income, but a 15-year loan means rent will rarely cover the instalment. Judge each unit by its yield, look at subsale, auction and bulk purchases rather than buying from the developer, and put enough cash down that the rent covers the instalment.

reasons.title: Age shortens the loan
reasons.body: Most banks lend until 65 and some until 70, so she gets about 15 years, not 35. A RM900,000 loan at 4% costs about RM3,985 a month over 35 years but about RM6,657 over 15, which needs roughly RM21,000 of income instead of RM12,000.

reasons.title: Yield is the measure
reasons.body: Divide 12 months' rent by the price; it should be at least 1% above the loan rate to cover interest and maintenance. Sean regards 5% to 6% as normal and 7% as a bonus; 10% to 12% usually means risky short-stay units in tourist areas, which many buildings now ban.

reasons.title: Cash lets her buy with certainty
reasons.body: A third loan is capped at 70%, so a RM1 million unit needs about RM300,000 upfront, or RM350,000 to RM360,000 with renovation. With that cash, a subsale lets her see the unit, its rent and condition, and negotiate.

reasons.title: Compare the whole area, not one project
reasons.body: Around Sunway Velocity and the TRX area, look at the median prices and yields of neighbouring condos as well, and at bulk purchase deals, where buyers can pay less upfront for a better price.

actions: Work out each shortlisted unit's yield and drop anything below about 5%.
Decide how much cash you'll put down so the rent covers the 15-year instalment, and keep enough back for medical bills, family and emergencies.
Compare subsale, auction and bulk purchase prices in the same area before considering a developer's price.
Be wary of deals that look too good to be true, including short-stay units promising very high returns.
Involve your sons now so they understand the properties they will inherit.
articles.caveat: Sean couldn't say whether she should spend, invest or keep her cash; that balance between enjoying it, protection and legacy is hers. Younger buyers can take 35-year loans, so the rent-covers-instalment test suits them better than it does her.
articles.sourceNote: Summarised from Sean's full English captions for Asking Sean #235. The quoted line is verbatim; everything else is paraphrased. Figures are as the viewer and Sean stated them in January 2024. Sean mentions The Makeover Guys, a renovation company he works with, and bulk purchase clubs in general.

video.title: ASKING SEAN #235 | TOO LATE TO START INVESTING AT 55?

articles.title: I cancelled my booking. Was it FOMO, or the right call?
articles.excerpt: A 25-year-old booked a RM640,000 unit on a promised 15% return, then cancelled. Sean explains why that was right, and how to tell what you can actually afford.

question.asker: From Xiao Bai, a viewer who wrote in by email
question.context: Xiao Bai is 25, takes home about RM4,600 a month after EPF, has a car loan, and saves RM1,000 to RM1,500 a month with about RM20,000 put aside. He booked a RM640,000 leasehold unit in Bandar Sunway with more than RM30,000 cash back and a 10% rebate. The instalment would be about RM2,700 plus RM370 maintenance, and the agent promised a 15% return. After a month of doubt, he cancelled.
question.text: Was walking away right, or too conservative? And how does he stop worrying that prices will run away before he is ready?

answer.quote: It's a good move that you cancel.
answer.summary: Cancelling was right. The numbers only worked if nothing went wrong, and on his income a property of around RM300,000 to RM400,000 is the safer place to start.

reasons.title: A 15% return is a red flag
reasons.body: A good rental yield in Malaysia is about 5 to 6%. Anything far higher usually comes from student or Airbnb-style room-by-room rental, so ask whether the figure is gross or net. If a developer could really deliver 15%, it would charge more for the unit.

reasons.title: Student-style buildings are hard to exit
reasons.body: Buildings full of students wear out fast, so the sinking fund rises. Only other investors will buy such units, since families do not want to live there, and when a campus moves away, rents fall.

reasons.title: He could not survive a bad year
reasons.body: After the car loan, roughly RM3,500 of his income counts toward borrowing, enough for about RM400,000 to RM500,000. A RM2,700 instalment with little savings leaves nothing to carry the unit through six empty months.

reasons.title: Time yourself, not the market
reasons.body: Sean says any time is a good time to buy if you are ready. The cure for fear of missing out is knowledge: agents earn when you sign, not when you are still paying through a vacancy.

actions: Do your research before paying a booking fee, not after.
Visit about 20 properties in your budget; the sales pitches start to sound alike, which makes you immune to them.
Before buying, have six months of emergency funds, insurance, and a clear career path.
Work out the real price after cash back and rebates; after handover, banks value the unit on that lower figure, so selling early loses money.
Compare price per sq ft across areas. Bandar Sunway near RM1,000 can cost more than Mont Kiara or Bangsar South.
articles.caveat: Buying would not necessarily have been wrong for someone confident of a fast-rising income, such as in sales. Sean went all in on his first property at a similar income and nearly crashed, and says he would tell his younger self to slow down.
articles.sourceNote: Summarised from Sean's full English captions for Asking Sean #321. The quoted answer is verbatim; everything else is paraphrased. Prices are as stated in September 2026.

video.title: ASKING SEAN #321 | CANCELLED BOOKING DUE TO FOMO

articles.title: I own four cars and want a fifth. Should I buy property instead?
articles.excerpt: A 28-year-old in Kuching with RM500,000 in fixed deposits, four cars and a baby on the way asks about landed homes, his rented-out house and his uncle's. Sean says fix the spending first.

question.asker: From TK, a viewer who wrote in by email
question.context: TK is 28, a project manager in Kuching earning RM8,000 a month and spending about RM6,800, much of it on four cars; he is eyeing a fifth for when his baby arrives. He has RM500,000 in fixed deposits and RM100,000 in EPF, and owns a double-storey house bought for RM418,000 with RM80,000 down, rented at RM900 against a RM1,450 instalment, though it could fetch RM1,200. He lives in his uncle's corner house and is weighing that house, a new RM700,000 to RM800,000 double-storey or a RM500,000 to RM600,000 apartment.
question.text: Should he keep his rented house, buy his uncle's, and choose landed or an apartment for his family home, and how much should he put down?

answer.quote: Why do you need four cars in the first place?
answer.summary: Keep the house he owns and, for a family with this many cars, a landed home makes sense. But on RM8,000 with RM6,800 spent each month, the real problem is spending: until he controls it and stops buying cars, the property questions don't matter.

reasons.title: His rented house is earning its keep
reasons.body: New double-storeys nearby sell for about RM620,000, so his RM418,000 house has likely gained. Early in a loan most of each instalment is interest; at RM1,200 rent, about 85% of the RM1,450 instalment, the tenant is effectively paying the bank's interest for him.

reasons.title: His uncle's house depends on the price
reasons.body: Bought for RM280,000 in 2015 with neighbours now at RM400,000, it has risen about 43% in ten years, and corner lots usually fetch 25% to 35% more. Compare his uncle's price plus renovation with RM800,000 for a new house in an area whose water and power supply he doesn't yet know.

reasons.title: Cars lose value; homes gain it
reasons.body: In ten years his cars will be worth half or less, while both houses he knows have risen. In Kuching renting is cheaper than owning, but the saving only helps if it is invested rather than spent on another car.

reasons.title: Count cash flow, not units
reasons.body: A better goal than owning many properties is positive monthly cash flow, such as RM10,000 a month across the portfolio. In Kuching, Sean would buy an apartment only if long-term rent, not Airbnb income, covers the instalment.

actions: Bring monthly spending down, ideally to about half your income, before buying more property, and don't buy the fifth car.
Raise the rent on your existing house to the market rate of about RM1,200 when the tenancy is renewed.
Ask your uncle his price, then compare it plus renovation with buying new.
Take a 90% full flexi loan and park spare cash in it to cut interest, after checking when your bank lets you withdraw it.
Move some of the RM500,000 fixed deposit into options that earn more, such as EPF, which pays about 6%.
articles.caveat: If the uncle would sell near his 2015 price, it is an easy yes. And Sean would buy an own-stay apartment only if nearby rents cover about 85% of its instalment, his rule for judging an own-stay purchase.
articles.sourceNote: Summarised from Sean's full English captions for Asking Sean #293. The quoted answer is verbatim; everything else is paraphrased. Figures are as stated in August 2025.

video.title: ASKING SEAN #293 | INVEST IN PROPERTY OR A NEW CAR?

articles.title: Cash back on a new launch, or a lower loan with positive cash flow?
articles.excerpt: Developers now offer free legal fees, furniture and even cash back, but the extras inflate the loan. Sean explains how rebates work and when cash in hand beats a unit whose rent covers its instalment.

question.context: A conventional purchase needs about 18% of the price in cash, around RM90,000 for a RM500,000 unit. Developers have responded with rebates that grow ever more generous: waived legal fees and stamp duty, free kitchen cabinets or full furnishing, and cash back, where the bank values a unit above the price you actually pay.
question.text: Is it better to take a new launch with big rebates and cash back, or pay a down payment to borrow less and have rent cover the instalment?

answer.quote: your rental is in accordance to market value
answer.summary: Rebates are built into a higher price and loan, so a new launch rarely has positive cash flow: rent follows the market, not your instalment. If you have cash, paying down to borrow less is safer. Cash back only helps if you use it to cover the monthly gap, not to spend.

reasons.title: Free extras raise the loan
reasons.body: A unit worth RM500,000 can carry an SPA price of RM600,000 to RM650,000 once rebates are included. Borrowing RM650,000 instead of RM450,000 makes a big difference to the instalment.

reasons.title: Rent doesn't care what you paid
reasons.body: Owners often set the asking rent from their instalment, but tenants pay what similar units fetch. A unit financed at an inflated price will struggle to break even.

reasons.title: Cash back can bridge the gap
reasons.body: If the instalment is RM3,000 and rent RM1,800, cash back can cover the RM1,200 difference for a few years while rents rise, leaving your own savings free to invest elsewhere.

reasons.title: Sudden cash changes habits
reasons.body: Buyers who receive RM30,000 to RM50,000 in cash back often feel richer and spend it. Without discipline, the buffer is gone before the shortfall begins.

actions: Compare the SPA price with the unit's likely market value after handover.
Check market rents for similar units, not your instalment, to estimate income.
If taking cash back, work out how many months of shortfall it will cover.
Keep cash back in a separate account reserved for the property.
Resist 'book today' offers until you have done the numbers.
articles.caveat: Sean put this to his audience as an open question in April 2020, when cash in hand mattered more. The best case is a unit with both cash back and positive cash flow.
articles.sourceNote: Summarised from Sean's full English captions for this April 2020 'question of the week' video. The quoted line is verbatim; everything else is paraphrased.

video.title: CASH BACK ON HAND VS CASH FLOW POSITIVE ?? | QUESTION OF THE WEEK

articles.title: Should I buy three condos mostly in cash and stop working at 35?
articles.excerpt: A Malaysian working in Singapore plans to come home, put RM200,000 down on each of three RM300,000 condos and live off the rent. Sean shows why fixed deposits beat that plan, and what to do instead.

question.asker: From Mr Lee, a viewer who wrote in by email
question.context: Mr Lee is 35 and has worked in Singapore for about eight years. Gains from shares during COVID went mostly into a Singapore condo whose rent covers all its costs with a little to spare. He also has several hundred thousand ringgit in cash and savings earning interest, and wants to move back to Malaysia and stop working.
question.text: Is it a good plan to buy three RM300,000 condos in Kuala Lumpur with RM200,000 down on each, borrowing only RM100,000 apiece, and live on the roughly RM500 a month each would leave?

answer.quote: Use credit to buy properties, not use capital.
answer.summary: No. Putting RM600,000 in cash into three condos for about RM1,500 a month is a poor return; the same cash in fixed deposits at about 3% earns that without tenants. Buy with loans while he still has a salary to qualify, keep his capital invested, and don't stop working altogether.

reasons.title: The cash would take decades to pay back
reasons.body: RM600,000 for RM1,500 a month takes 400 months to recover. At about 3% a year, the same RM600,000 in fixed deposits pays about RM1,500 a month with no vacancies or bad tenants.

reasons.title: RM300,000 condos are the wrong stock
reasons.body: At that price in Kuala Lumpur, Sean says, you are mostly looking at welfare-type apartments, which he would leave alone.

reasons.title: Loans need an income
reasons.body: Malaysia lets buyers borrow up to 90% and still find units whose rent covers the instalment. That needs a salary or declared income to qualify, so buy before quitting rather than after.

reasons.title: Interest is a cost against rent
reasons.body: Loan interest can be written off against declared rental income, which is one more reason not to pay down so much up front.

actions: Keep the cash in fixed deposits or the investments you already know well.
Buy one ready-built unit of around RM600,000 whose rent covers the instalment, and try it before buying more.
Sign for any properties while still employed, then leave the job once the loans are approved.
Take three to six months off before deciding what to do next, rather than retiring outright.
Find work you would do even unpaid; Sean argues life is only stressful when you do what you dislike.
articles.caveat: If he has no wish to borrow at all, Sean would still put the cash into safer non-property investments first, because they keep the flexibility a family emergency may need.
articles.sourceNote: Summarised from Sean's full English captions for Asking Sean #280. The quoted answer is verbatim; everything else is paraphrased. Figures are as stated in April 2025. Sean recommends buying through FAR Capital, a bulk-purchase club he is a member of, not its owner, and the episode links to it. The episode is sponsored by The Makeover Guys, a renovation company.

video.title: ASKING SEAN #280 | WHY CASH BUY PROPERTY FOR CASH FLOW?

articles.title: Can I use a property's cash back to clear my personal loan?
articles.excerpt: A couple paying RM3,300 a month on a RM300,000 personal loan want to buy a new launch with cash back to settle it. Sean backs the swap, if the cash arrives in time.

question.asker: From Mr M, a viewer who wrote in by email
question.context: Mr M, 32, and his wife earn about RM15,000 a month after tax between them. In 2022 he took a RM300,000, 10-year personal loan to renovate his parents' house, now RM252,000 outstanding at RM3,300 a month, and they also pay RM2,000 rent. A new launch of about RM1 million offers a RM950,000 loan against a net price of roughly RM730,000, so buying jointly would release about RM220,000 to RM250,000 in cash back. The instalment plus maintenance would be about RM4,700, against the RM5,300 they pay now.
question.text: Is buying a property for its cash back a sensible way to clear the personal loan?

answer.quote: In this logic, I would think that it's good.
answer.summary: Yes, in principle: it swaps a personal loan at about 8% for housing loan debt at 3% to 4%, cuts their monthly outgoings and turns rent into ownership. But first find out exactly when the developer pays the cash back, agree with his wife who carries the new instalment, and ask the bank about settling the personal loan early.

reasons.title: The type of loan decides what you pay
reasons.body: Personal loans run at about 6% to 8% and can reach 12%, and credit card balances about 16%, while his newest housing loan is at 3.85%. Sean notes that average property prices have risen about 3.6% a year over 20 years.

reasons.title: Renovation money doesn't all become value
reasons.body: Putting RM300,000 into a house doesn't add RM300,000 to its price; at most perhaps 30% to 40%, and only for approved extensions that add real space. Borrowing at personal loan rates for that is the costly part of the mistake.

reasons.title: Timing can make it a triple burden
reasons.body: Rebates are often paid with each stage of construction, but some developers only pay the cash back at handover. If so, the couple would be servicing the new loan's interest, the rent and the personal loan all at once for years.

reasons.title: It uses up his wife's borrowing power
reasons.body: He only qualifies for about RM750,000 alone, so the plan depends on her name, while she already has a house loan of her own. That limits her future purchases, so the split should be agreed openly.

actions: Ask the developer's senior management, not just the sales staff, exactly when the cash back is paid and put it in writing.
Ask the bank whether settling the RM252,000 personal loan in one lump sum earns any discount, since its interest may already be fixed.
Agree with your spouse, in writing if needed, who pays the new instalment when their name is used to qualify.
Check the rent nearby covers the instalment, as a fallback if you move or need to rent it out.
Learn how hire purchase, personal and housing loan rates are worked out before taking any new loan.
articles.caveat: Heavy rebates only appear when developers struggle to sell; in a hot market they disappear. If the cash back only comes at handover and you can't carry the overlap, the plan can make things worse rather than better.
articles.sourceNote: Summarised from Sean's full English captions for Asking Sean #249. The quoted line is verbatim; everything else is paraphrased. Figures are as the viewer and Sean stated them in May 2024. The episode was sponsored by OpenHouse, a new-launch search app, and Sean mentions FAR Capital, the property investment club he is a member of, which teaches these strategies.

articles.title: Is a cheap unit with good rent worth buying?
articles.excerpt: A buyer is offered two old units in central KL at RM160,000 each, renting to foreign workers at a 6.33% yield. Sean explains why cheap is not the same as money-making.

question.asker: From Mrs. Y, a viewer who wrote in by email
question.context: Mrs. Y has bought a 1,750 sq ft own-stay unit from a large listed developer in KL East, still under construction. She is now offered two 425 sq ft units at RM160,000 each in an old building in Chow Kit, completed in 2000 and refurbished in 2020. They rent for RM1,000 a month, mostly to foreign workers, with a RM130 management fee, and she works out a 6.33% return before maintenance.
question.text: With steady rent but little prospect of the price rising, is it still a good investment?

answer.quote: Don't buy a property just because it's cheap.
answer.summary: No. The cash flow works, but with almost no capital appreciation, a loan slot used up and only about RM200 a month to show for it, Sean says better deals are available and this one is not worth the headspace.

reasons.title: The yield clears the bar, just
reasons.body: Sean's break-even is about 5.4%: a RM100,000 loan over 35 years at 4% costs about RM450 a month. At 6.33% the unit is roughly a point above that, and on a 90% loan of about RM145,000 the surplus comes to around RM200 a month.

reasons.title: There is almost nothing to sell later
reasons.body: Units like these compete on being the cheapest, for tenants who need them rather than want them, so the only buyers are other cash-flow investors and there is little resale activity. Even selling at 10% more in ten years, about RM176,000, the surplus of roughly RM2,400 a year barely returns the down payment. In the worst case it cannot be sold, and repairs after bad tenants eat the surplus.

reasons.title: It spends a 90% loan slot
reasons.body: Malaysians get two 90% loans for residential property. With her own-stay unit, this would use the second, so any better deal later could only be financed at 70%. Paying cash would be worse still: EPF pays about 6% with less risk.

reasons.title: Better deals are out there
reasons.body: She has not compared it against 20 other properties. Sean finds deals from branded developers with higher returns and no upfront deposit, so an old, cheap unit like this would need a double-digit return, 10% to 15%, before he considered it.

actions: Visit at least 20 other properties in your price range, across new, subsale, auction and bulk purchase, before deciding.
Ask a bank for its valuation first, to see whether it would value the unit at the asking price.
Don't pay cash for a property like this; compare its return against EPF at about 6%.
Keep your remaining 90% loan slot for a deal with both cash flow and room to grow.
For an old, low-priced building, look for a double-digit return of 10% to 15% before considering it.
articles.caveat: Sean's no rests on having better deals within reach. Cheap units in old buildings can make sense at a double-digit yield, though he discourages investors from low-cost housing meant for those who need it most. Separately, he says buying her own-stay unit from a large developer gives her more certainty of completion while building costs rise.
articles.sourceNote: Summarised from Sean's full English captions for Asking Sean #311. The quoted answer is verbatim; everything else is paraphrased. Figures are as stated in May 2026. Sean buys through FAR Capital's bulk purchases as a client, not its owner.

video.title: ASKING SEAN #311 | THE GOAL IS NOT TO GET THE CHEAPEST

articles.title: When should you stop renting and buy a home?
articles.excerpt: A 34-year-old renter is tired of moving and wants a home of his own, but friends warn him off. Sean tests the decision with his 85% rule.

question.asker: From CY, a viewer who wrote in by email
question.context: CY is 34, single, earns about RM17,000 a month and lives frugally. He has RM180,000 in shares and cash and RM235,000 in EPF, and supports his mother. He rents a condo in Taman Desa for RM3,000 a month, and has had to move three times in six years when landlords took their units back. He is eyeing a RM850,000 project nearby with an instalment of about RM3,800, but friends say not to buy until he marries.
question.text: Should he buy a home in the area he already lives in, or keep renting and invest the money instead?

answer.quote: Go ahead bro, I really support that decision.
answer.summary: Buy it. He can afford it, he knows the area, and the unit would rent for most of its instalment if his plans ever change. That is what makes an own-stay purchase safe.

reasons.title: It passes the 85% rule
reasons.body: Sean's test for an own-stay home: local rent should cover about 85% of the instalment. In the early years most of each instalment is interest, so a tenant would cover that cost if you had to move out. Here, similar units rent for about RM3,000 against an instalment of about RM3,800, which Sean counts as meeting the rule.

reasons.title: He is buying where he already lives
reasons.body: The classic mistake is an emotional dream home far from work, such as a landed house in an outer suburb. The owner then faces hours of daily traffic or rents a second place in town. A home renovated for yourself is hard to let out, and a distant one is hard to sell. Taman Desa is central and CY has lived around it for six years.

reasons.title: His foundations are in place
reasons.body: Before buying a home, Sean wants three things settled: solid savings, a stable career and insurance protection. CY has all three, so the question becomes whether he wants to spend on housing, not whether he can afford to.

reasons.title: A home pays you in certainty
reasons.body: Some property is bought to make money; a home is bought to spend it. The instalment buys the security renting cannot: no landlord calling to reclaim the unit in your busiest month. Sean compares it to choosing a better car than the bare minimum, which is fine if you can afford it.

actions: Check what the unit would rent for, and aim for rent covering about 85% of your instalment.
Buy in an area you already know and that suits your daily commute, not a faraway dream location.
Confirm your savings, career and insurance are solid before committing.
Plan the exit now: if a better job comes up elsewhere, you can rent the unit out at market rate.
Treat renovation as spending on yourself. It makes the home yours but adds little to the resale price.
articles.caveat: If you want to build a property portfolio, Sean's own order is the reverse: buy investment units whose rent covers the instalment first, so your borrowing capacity stays intact, and buy your home later. His "just buy it" is for someone like CY, who invests elsewhere and wants a home for stability.
articles.sourceNote: Summarised from Sean's full English captions for Asking Sean #282. The quoted answer is verbatim; everything else is paraphrased. Prices and rents are as stated in the episode.

video.title: ASKING SEAN #282 | CONSIDERATIONS FOR OWN-STAY PROPERTY

articles.title: Can I complain if my new home isn't ready when I get the keys?
articles.excerpt: A friend collected his keys to find the facilities unfinished. Sean explains the protection homebuyers have under the Housing Development Act, and the tribunal where they can claim without a lawyer.

question.context: A friend of Sean's paid about RM800,000 for a new home, but at vacant possession the facilities weren't ready and buyers were angry. Many owners don't know what protection they have.
question.text: What can a buyer do when a new home or its facilities are not delivered as promised?

answer.quote: you need to claim back what is your right
answer.summary: Buyers of residential property are protected by the Housing Development Act, and a developer should hand over only when an architect certifies the facilities are ready. For serious failures you can file a claim at a tribunal without a lawyer, but claim what your SPA promises, not grievances like a cheaper later phase.

reasons.title: Homes have legal protection
reasons.body: The Housing Development Act protects buyers of residential property. Buyers of shop offices or factories are not covered by it.

reasons.title: Facilities should come with the keys
reasons.body: A home without a finished car park or access road can't be lived in, so a developer needs a professional architect's certification before handing over.

reasons.title: Claims don't need a lawyer
reasons.body: The tribunal Sean describes is meant for laymen, and lawyers can't act there. If a developer ignores a reported defect and you pay to fix it, you can claim the cost back.

actions: Read your SPA to know exactly what must be delivered at vacant possession.
Report defects to the developer in writing and keep records and photos.
If they don't respond, fix the defect, keep the bill and claim the cost.
File serious claims at the tribunal yourself rather than hiring a lawyer.
Don't expect a claim to succeed over a later phase being cheaper.
articles.caveat: Minor hairline cracks or patchy paint are not what the tribunal is for. Sean also notes that established developers usually make handover far smoother than small ones.
articles.sourceNote: Summarised from Sean's English captions for this November 2018 video. The tribunal's name, its filing fee and the deadline for developers to repair are unclear in the captions, so they are left out; check the current tribunal and procedure before filing. The quoted line is verbatim; everything else is paraphrased.

articles.title: A third of my condo is unsold. Will the developer cut prices on me?
articles.excerpt: A buyer's RM620,000 condo is about to be handed over with 270 of 770 units unsold, and rent nearby falls short of the instalment. Sean explains how developers clear stock, and why he would furnish, rent and hold.

question.asker: From CG, a viewer who wrote in by email
question.context: CG bought a 1,100 sq ft condo for RM620,000 four years ago, at 28, to live in, partly out of fear of missing out. Due for handover soon, it is low-density and far from public transport; 270 of its 770 units are still unsold, though the developer has raised the price twice. The instalment is about RM2,900, while smaller partly furnished units next door rent for RM2,500 to RM2,700. CG now wants to rent it out or sell.
question.text: Will the developer cut prices to clear unsold units, what does selling cost, and should CG rent below the instalment or sell at a loss?

answer.quote: entry price is everything
answer.summary: Don't sell at a loss. Fully furnish it at handover, rent it out to cover most of the instalment, and hold until the market recovers enough to sell without a loss. Developers rarely cut prices openly, but they do sell leftover units privately through bulk purchasers, which is the competition CG faces.

reasons.title: Price rises are not profit
reasons.body: Developers often raise prices to fund bigger discounts, because the marketing budget is a share of the price. A higher list price only means gains if units actually sell at it.

reasons.title: Leftovers are sold quietly
reasons.body: Cutting prices in public would anger existing buyers, so developers short of cash sell blocks of units under NDA to bulk purchasers. Those buyers get lower instalments and can rent for less than earlier owners.

reasons.title: Selling below the loan costs cash
reasons.body: Selling for less than you owe means paying the bank the difference, perhaps RM40,000 to RM50,000. Renting at a shortfall of about RM200 a month would take many years to cost as much.

reasons.title: A furnished unit stands out
reasons.body: Discouraged owners in a slow project tend not to furnish, so a well-furnished unit can win the tenants who like the area but cannot afford to buy, at a rent close to the instalment.

actions: Fully furnish the unit at handover and rent it out.
Compare your break-even rent, instalment plus maintenance, with what furnished units achieve.
Hold for two to three years and sell once a price covers your loan and costs.
Avoid paying down the loan with savings just to cut the interest, unless you have no better use for the cash.
For future purchases, compare the price with the area's median price per sq ft.
articles.caveat: Sean's expectation of a coming property upturn underpins the advice to hold. An own-stay buyer whose budget cannot carry the monthly shortfall may still need to sell.
articles.sourceNote: Summarised from Sean's full English captions for Asking Sean #273. The quoted line is verbatim; everything else is paraphrased. Figures are as stated in February 2025. Sean is a member of FAR Capital, a bulk-purchase club, not its owner, and says three of his last four purchases were stock-clearance deals of the kind described.

video.title: ASKING SEAN #273 | PROPERTY STOCK CLEARANCE

articles.title: Should we save to buy in cash, or take a long housing loan?
articles.excerpt: A self-employed couple with RM300,000 saved disagree: she wants little or no debt, he wants a normal loan and to invest. Sean suggests a middle ground that suits both.

question.asker: From W, a viewer who wrote in by email
question.context: W and his girlfriend plan to marry. Both are self-employed, earn about RM7,000 to RM8,000 a month each and have no debts. They have about RM300,000 saved and a budget of RM500,000 to RM600,000 for a first home in KL. She follows Dave Ramsey and wants a big down payment and a 15-year loan, or to save until they can pay cash; he wants a normal loan and to invest the rest.
question.text: How much should go into the down payment, should they minimise the loan or buy in cash, and is there a balance they can both live with?

answer.quote: My suggestion is to do both and have a medium ground.
answer.summary: Do both. Buy with the market-standard 10% down payment, keep the rest as reserves, and let each partner manage their own money: he takes the loan in his own name and invests, she keeps her savings in safe instruments.

reasons.title: Debt-free advice fits the US, not Malaysia
reasons.body: In the US a 30-year fixed mortgage is about 7.2% and property tax about 1% a year, so short loans make sense there. In Malaysia a good housing loan is about 3.7% to 4% and quit rent and assessment are tiny, so a long loan is cheap money.

reasons.title: Saving for cash can't catch up
reasons.body: A good property rises by around 3% to 5% a year, so savings chase a moving target. And if a property doesn't rise in five years, Sean asks why you would want to buy it at all.

reasons.title: Cash in a house is hard to get back
reasons.body: Put the RM300,000 into the house and you have a home, no savings and a monthly instalment. Selling takes about six to seven months for a freehold unit and longer for leasehold, so in an emergency you would be left with credit cards.

reasons.title: A joint loan wastes a loan slot
reasons.body: A joint 15-year loan costs about the same each month as one person's 35-year loan, and it uses up both people's housing loan slots. Buying in one name keeps the other partner's slots free for later.

actions: Agree how long you could keep your lifestyle if both incomes stopped; Sean keeps about a year of living costs, plus six months of instalments for each property.
For a RM500,000 subsale, budget about 10% down plus 8% for fees, roughly RM90,000, and keep the rest for renovation and reserves.
Buy in one partner's name with a long loan, and keep a shared account only for monthly household bills.
Let the more cautious partner keep their savings in fixed deposits and blue chips, and never borrow from them for investments.
Compare all the buying channels, including bulk purchase, before choosing between new and subsale.
articles.caveat: Sean stresses he is not a certified financial planner and that risk tolerance is personal. The older you are, the more conservative you should be, because there is less time to earn money back.
articles.sourceNote: Summarised from Sean's full English captions for Asking Sean #325. The quoted answer is verbatim; everything else is paraphrased. Figures are as Sean stated them in the episode; loan and deposit rates change. Sean points viewers to the bulk-purchase investment club linked in his video description, which he belongs to.

video.title: ASKING SEAN #325 | SAVE LONGER SO DON'T NEED TO TAKE LOAN

articles.title: Should I sell my Penang condo at a loss to free up a 90% loan?
articles.excerpt: A 38-year-old already sold a Cyberjaya unit at a loss and now wants to sell a Penang condo below cost to buy something better. Sean agrees with cutting losses, and explains room rental and getting past two loans.

question.asker: From R, a viewer who wrote in by email
question.context: R is 38 and lives in Perak. He and his wife bought two investment properties on hearsay. He sold the Cyberjaya unit after six years for RM210,000, about RM40,000 less than he paid. He bought a Penang condo five years ago for RM610,000; agents now value it at about RM560,000, and it is let for RM1,800. He wants to sell it to free up his 90% loan for a property with cashback and cash flow, possibly rented out room by room.
question.text: Is cutting his losses wise, is renting room by room better than a normal tenancy, and how can someone with both 90% loans used buy a third property?

answer.quote: I'm absolutely agreeable to cutting losses just to open up slots to get more.
answer.summary: Yes, sell, if the money and loan it frees can go into a clearly better property. A monthly drain hurts more than a one-off loss. Renting by the room works near offices and colleges but not in family areas. Beyond two 90% loans you need partners, refinancing outside CCRIS, or bulk-purchase discounts.

reasons.title: Opportunity cost outweighs a one-off loss
reasons.body: Sean sold his own semi-detached house at a loss because its large monthly instalments held him back more than the loss did. Cash flow matters more than paper losses.

reasons.title: Rent shows demand before prices do
reasons.body: Cyberjaya has jobs, universities, malls and good roads, yet high-rise rents and prices kept falling while its landed homes did well. Checking rents before buying would have shown the weak demand.

reasons.title: Room rental depends on the tenants nearby
reasons.body: Splitting a unit into rooms, and turning unused common areas into more rooms or a pantry, can raise income near offices and colleges. Large operators should clear it with the management body first, since it affects security and facilities.

reasons.title: Past the second loan takes more work
reasons.body: Options include buying with family or friends under a proper agreement, refinancing existing loans into a facility outside CCRIS at a somewhat higher rate, as Sean has done, or bulk purchases with larger discounts.

actions: Find out exactly what is owed on the Penang condo before selling.
Check the rents of any next property before committing to it.
Assess who rents near a unit before splitting it into rooms.
Check the advice of anyone recommending a property, especially if they earn commission on it.
Do your own due diligence even when a trusted person recommends a project.
articles.caveat: The old flipping stories no longer work, partly because of property gains tax on early sales. Selling only helps if the next deal is genuinely better, so line it up before cutting the loss.
articles.sourceNote: Summarised from Sean's full English captions for Asking Sean #192. The quoted line is verbatim; everything else is paraphrased. Figures are as the viewer stated them in November 2022. Sean shares the contact of a mortgage specialist who helped him refinance, and mentions bulk-purchase companies; loan and tax rules change, so check current ones.

video.title: ASKING SEAN #192 | CUTTING LOSSES

articles.title: What should you check when you get your keys?
articles.excerpt: Most buyers hunt for scratches and hollow tiles and miss what stops a home from working. Sean sets out what to check first in a defect inspection.

question.context: You have collected the keys to a new home, and the developer gives you a limited window to report defects. Most buyers walk in looking for stains and scratches, and miss the things that actually stop a home from working.
question.text: What should you check during a defect inspection, and in what order?

answer.quote: These are things that you cannot really live without.
answer.summary: Check function before looks. Test every power point, water point, door and window first, compare the unit against your sale agreement, then move on to cosmetic flaws, and report everything through the proper channel.

reasons.title: Utilities come first
reasons.body: Test every power point with a phone charger, plus the distribution board, doorbell and any water heater or appliances supplied. Doors and windows should open and close smoothly, and window seals should feel firm.

reasons.title: Water problems hide
reasons.body: Fill each sink and check the joints underneath. Pour water on bathroom floors, especially in the shower, to see that it runs to the drain. Look for stains on ceilings and around windows that point to leaks, particularly in landed homes.

reasons.title: Your sale agreement is the checklist
reasons.body: If the agreement promises laminated flooring in the bedrooms or full-height tiles in the kitchen, check that is what you got; a mismatch matters more than a stain. Some buyers even measure wall to wall, after stories of 900 sq ft units measuring 850.

reasons.title: Hollow tiles are more serious than they look
reasons.body: A hollow wall tile can eventually fall off; a hollow floor tile can crack under heavy furniture because there is no mortar beneath it. Straight walls and even floors are not a luxury at any price point.

actions: Bring a phone charger, your sale agreement and a measuring tape, and mark each defect with a sticker as you go.
Check the common facilities too: the building should have its certificate of completion, and the gym and pool should be working, not "under maintenance".
Submit defects through the developer's official channel; the staff follow process, so be thorough rather than confrontational.
Note the defect liability period, usually 24 months; leaks or cracks in that time are the developer's to fix. Structural renovation in a landed home can void claims for related cracks.
For a rental unit, prioritise whatever stops a tenant moving in; each round of repairs can cost two to three months of instalments.
articles.caveat: The quality of supplied furniture and finishes is usually not a claimable defect, because it cannot be measured. For a rental, cosmetic flaws rarely matter to tenants; for your own home, ones that bother you every day are worth pursuing.
articles.sourceNote: Summarised from Sean's English captions for this January 2020 walk-through. The quoted answer is verbatim; everything else is paraphrased. Parts of the older automatic captions are unclear, so only clearly stated points are included.

video.title: CHECK FOR DEFECTS IN YOUR PROPERTY

articles.title: After an earthquake and a gas fire, how protected is your property?
articles.excerpt: After the Myanmar earthquake, the Putra Heights gas pipeline fire and a market sell-off, viewers asked whether property is still safe. Sean goes through the protections every owner should have in place.

question.context: In one week, an earthquake damaged buildings in Myanmar and Bangkok, a gas pipeline fire destroyed homes in Putra Heights, Selangor, and new US tariffs hit share and crypto prices. Sean's inbox filled with questions about whether high-rises are safe and whether owning property is too risky.
question.text: What should a property owner have in place before disaster strikes, and do events like these change what to buy?

answer.quote: the key question for all of us to answer is, how covered are you?
answer.summary: Disasters cannot be predicted, but their damage to your finances can be limited. Keep an emergency fund, insure your life, your loans and the building, keep a cash buffer for each property, and check what is around a home before you buy it.

reasons.title: Heirs inherit the debt too
reasons.body: If an owner dies, their family must keep paying any outstanding housing loans. Without enough life insurance, MLTA or MRTA, which the bank offers with the loan, is the cheaper way to cover that. Sean warns against cancelling it to save money unless the property is worth well more than the loan.

reasons.title: Check what your fire policy covers
reasons.body: Some policies cover only the structure, others also cover belongings, and not all cover floods. Earthquake cover is unlikely to be available from Malaysian insurers at a sensible cost.

reasons.title: A buffer gives you time
reasons.body: Sean keeps enough cash to pay six months of instalments on every property, so a unit can stand empty for six months without affecting him. An emergency fund of three to six months' expenses can pay a rental deposit while an insurance claim is processed.

reasons.title: Know what is next to the house
reasons.body: Rivers, pylons and pipelines have setback zones. Township developments make sense because buyers can see what surrounds them. Sean expects high-rises with proper piling and shear walls to withstand tremors better than older landed houses.

actions: Build an emergency fund of three to six months' expenses before investing.
Get at least a medical card, and life cover or MLTA or MRTA for every property loan.
Read your fire policy to see whether it covers floods and contents as well as the structure.
Keep six months of instalments in cash for each property you own.
Check for pipelines, pylons and rivers near a home before you buy.
articles.caveat: Sean notes that the cause of the fire was still under investigation when he recorded this. He also sees sell-offs after such events as buying opportunities, which only suits investors who have done their own research.
articles.sourceNote: Summarised from Sean's full English captions for Asking Sean #279, recorded in the week after these events rather than in answer to a single viewer. The quoted line is verbatim; everything else is paraphrased. Sean mentions a recent purchase through FAR Capital, a bulk-purchase club he is a member of, not its owner, and that The Makeover Guys, a renovation company, furnishes his units; neither bears on the protections summarised here.

video.title: ASKING SEAN #279 | LESSONS FROM THE EARTHQUAKE, FIRE, AND TARIFFS

articles.title: I bought at a discount. Why am I still losing money?
articles.excerpt: A homeowner who bought "at a good rate" during COVID now struggles with the instalment and cannot find tenants. Sean explains why a discount is not a bargain, and how to decide whether to hold, rent or sell.

question.asker: From Mr A, a viewer who wrote in by email
question.context: Mr A bought a 1,500 sq ft condo at Subang Park Homes in SS19 during COVID, because the price looked like a good deal. He lives there with his wife and child, but the loan and maintenance now cost about RM4,000 a month, and similar units listed for rent at RM3,000 to RM3,500 find no takers.
question.text: Did he buy into a money-losing development, and what should he do now?

answer.quote: Is it cheaper? Yes. Is it still expensive? Yes.
answer.summary: A discount only helps if the price ends up below the area's median, not just below the project's old price. For a home already bought, the question now is whether to hold, rent or sell, and that depends on valuation, recent sales and the loan balance.

reasons.title: The discount was measured against the wrong number
reasons.body: "20% below market value" usually means below a bank valuation or the developer's old asking price. The real market price is what similar units actually sold for. If the area median is RM900 per sq ft and a project drops from RM1,300 to RM1,100, it is cheaper and still expensive.

reasons.title: A quiet address does not draw tenants
reasons.body: High rents come from temporary demand: jobs, universities and tourism. A hidden residential corner suits a family, but most renters will pay more to live near a train station or highway.

reasons.title: The 85% test was never done
reasons.body: For an own-stay home, Sean checks that local rent covers about 85% of the instalment, so you have an exit if plans change. On a RM3,500 instalment that means rent of about RM3,000. Checking demand first would have shown the risk.

reasons.title: Who loses depends on when they bought
reasons.body: The developer profited at launch, and early buyers likely gained, but later buyers at peak prices often have not. Across the market, people who bought at the 2015 to 2016 peak are still underwater, while those who bought in the 2019 to 2021 dip gained equity.

actions: Ask your bank for a current valuation; it sets what your buyer can borrow.
Check the latest transacted prices in your project. If the last sale was a year ago, demand is thin.
Compare your outstanding loan with a realistic sale price. If selling leaves you owing the bank, decide whether to pay the gap now or keep paying monthly.
If you rent it out, check the competition: unfurnished listings with no takers leave room to win; furnished ones with no takers signal real trouble.
Next time, decide own stay or investment first, and check local rent before you buy.
articles.caveat: As a family home, the property is doing its job, so it is not automatically a failure; the pain is the instalment. On smart-home features, which Mr A also asked about, Sean thinks they add little to rent or resale and suit owners furnishing a home for themselves.
articles.sourceNote: Summarised from Sean's full English captions for Asking Sean #309. The quoted answer is verbatim; everything else is paraphrased. Figures are as stated in April 2026.

video.title: ASKING SEAN #309 | BOUGHT AT DISCOUNT PRICE STILL LOSE MONEY

articles.title: A JB condo now sells 60% below launch price. Is it a bargain?
articles.excerpt: A 24-year-old in Singapore can buy a Danga Bay subsale launched at about RM1 million for RM380,000, with rent covering the loan. Sean calls it only an okay deal and suggests other options.

question.asker: From E, a viewer who wrote in by email
question.context: E is 24, works in Singapore and earns about S$7,000 a month. He prefers subsales because he can negotiate and calculate the yield. He has found an 881 sq ft two-bedroom unit in a Danga Bay high-rise, launched at about RM1 million and now valued around RM470,000, and negotiated it down to RM380,000. It is tenanted at about RM1,700 to RM1,800, a yield of about 5.6%, but the developer has a poor reputation online, many units remain unsold, and the township is on reclaimed land.
question.text: Is this a sensible buy, should he take a full loan and cash out the difference, and is this the right way to play the property game?

answer.quote: Great deals are crafted.
answer.summary: Among JB apartments it is an okay deal and he understands the risks, but Sean would look further. At 24, E could afford more risk: a landed home in JB, which still has room to appreciate, or a completed, sold-out project from another developer. He should also weigh keeping his savings in Singapore dollars.

reasons.title: Buying below launch price isn't the same as cheap
reasons.body: Buyers who paid RM1 million on a 90% loan may still owe RM700,000 to RM800,000 on units now worth RM380,000. That shows the risk of buying with no check of rents and surrounding prices; the launch price is no measure of value.

reasons.title: JB high-rise has little room to grow
reasons.body: With plenty of land and supply, even well-run JB condos see little capital gain. Many Malaysians working there would rather pay a bit more for a landed home than RM380,000 for an apartment.

reasons.title: Stigma and unsold stock affect resale
reasons.body: While the developer still has unsold units and a poor reputation, the market can't correct itself, and the next buyer's perception sets the selling price. Check who runs the mall and how the building is managed.

reasons.title: The currency is part of the return
reasons.body: Keeping money in Singapore dollars already gains against the ringgit. Advertised rents for small units or Airbnb are often marketing claims, so rely on the real long-term rents around the building.

actions: Compare this unit with completed, sold-out projects by other JB developers offering similar discounts.
Run the same rent-versus-instalment check on landed homes near the border, even if they cost about RM1,000 a month to hold.
Weigh the return in ringgit against keeping the capital in Singapore dollars.
If he buys, decide on the loan size by how much monthly shortfall he is comfortable with.
Look up complaints and the mall's management before committing.
articles.caveat: For an older, conservative investor who wants a unit that pays for itself with little risk, this deal makes more sense. Sean has no insight into the build quality or the reclaimed land, so E should check those himself.
articles.sourceNote: Summarised from Sean's full English captions for Asking Sean #199. The quoted line is verbatim; everything else is paraphrased. Figures are as the viewer stated them in February 2023; prices and exchange rates have changed since.

video.title: ASKING SEAN #199 | PRICES OF JB APARTMENTS DROPPED 70%

articles.title: I'm between jobs with savings. Should I buy my first property now?
articles.excerpt: A 27-year-old who left medicine for a master's degree has about RM380,000 saved and wants a RM400,000 investment unit in the Klang Valley, which he barely knows. Sean says research now, buy after six months in a new job.

question.asker: From Mr J, a viewer who wrote in by email
question.context: Mr J is 27 and lives in Melaka. He resigned as a government doctor to study a one-year master's in health tech, finishing in late 2026, and earns occasional income as a part-time property agent. Counting money market funds, cash, stocks and an insurance savings plan, he has about RM380,000, and he spends about RM2,000 a month. He is a client of a property investment club, can borrow RM600,000 to RM700,000, and wants a unit of about RM400,000 for cash flow, though he doesn't know KL or Selangor.
question.text: How should he choose between projects in unfamiliar areas, do view and floor level matter, and what should he do with his cash?

answer.quote: Don't buy any properties before 6 months income from your new job.
answer.summary: Wait. Without a payslip he can't qualify for a loan anyway, and a 35-year commitment needs a steady income first. Use the time to get to know the Klang Valley, then buy once he has six months of income from his new job.

reasons.title: Invest where people move for work
reasons.body: Sean always recommends main city centres such as KL, JB, Penang and Kuching, because fresh graduates head to the capital for jobs and rooms there are in short supply: about RM700 for a small room and RM1,200 for a master bedroom around Cheras. JB prices near the RTS link have already run up.

reasons.title: View matters only at the extremes
reasons.body: A KLCC or KL skyline view earns a premium for luxury and short-stay units, and a unit facing another tower 30 m away loses out. For a unit bought on rent versus instalment, view hardly matters, but floor level does in dense areas like Mont Kiara or Bangsar South, where low floors sit in the shadow of the next tower.

reasons.title: Completed units let you roll faster
reasons.body: A new launch can take four years before it earns rent you can show the bank. A completed or nearly completed unit can be let within months, and six months of declared rent helps you qualify for the next loan; developers also negotiate harder near completion.

reasons.title: His cash is well placed
reasons.body: Money market funds and savings keep him liquid while he has no steady income. With RM2,000 a month in spending, RM110,000 in the bank covers about four years, more than he needs as a buffer.

actions: Watch videos of KL and Selangor areas, then visit them: ride the LRT, walk the malls and get a feel for each address.
Join site tours if your investment club runs them, and view about 20 properties within your budget.
Stay within the RM400,000 range you are comfortable with, below the most you can borrow.
Plan who will manage the unit for you if you buy far from where you live.
Leave room in your savings for a wedding if marriage is likely in the next few years.
articles.caveat: Property investment beyond two or three units suits people who enjoy driving around, viewing buildings and dealing with strangers; if that drains you, stopping after using your two 90% loans is enough. Sean's thoughts on stocks in the episode are, in his words, not financial advice.
articles.sourceNote: Summarised from Sean's full English captions for Asking Sean #298. The quoted answer is verbatim; everything else is paraphrased. Figures are as stated in October 2025. Sean is a customer of FAR Capital, the club Mr J belongs to, not its owner.

video.title: ASKING SEAN #298 | DOCTOR TURNED AGENT HUSTLING FOR A KL PROPERTY

articles.title: We're doctors who may be posted anywhere. Should we buy a home in JB?
articles.excerpt: Two government doctors in JB with a baby on the way weigh a condo near the hospital against a strata landed home further out. Sean says rent close to work and buy a home only when you need it.

question.asker: From W, a viewer who wrote in by email
question.context: W, 35, and his wife, 33, are newly qualified medical specialists in government service in JB, on call at night and expecting a baby. They will stay in JB for at least two years, after which he may be posted elsewhere for three to four years of training, followed by a seven-year bond before private practice. They are weighing a condo 15 minutes from work against a RM700,000 to RM800,000 strata landed home in Mount Austin, 30 to 40 minutes away, while JB condo prices keep falling.
question.text: Should they buy a condo near the hospital now and upgrade to landed later, or buy the landed home?

answer.quote: I should get that particular home just in time when I need it.
answer.summary: Prioritise flexibility. Rent an apartment close to the hospital, which is cheap while JB condo prices are low, and don't tie themselves to a home they may have to leave. If they want property, buy it purely as an investment that generates cash flow, and buy the family home in their early 40s once their careers settle and their child needs space.

reasons.title: Postings make ownership a burden
reasons.body: If they are sent to another state soon after buying, they end up renting the house out, maintaining it from afar and topping up the instalment. A rented flat near work lets them get home quickly between calls.

reasons.title: Babies need convenience, not a big house
reasons.body: A single-level apartment makes it easier to feed, clean and work while the baby sleeps, and pools and playgrounds downstairs are what young children enjoy. Space and privacy matter later, around ages 10 to 12.

reasons.title: JB high-rise and landed behave differently
reasons.body: Condos were built largely for Singapore investors and have fallen in value, partly through oversupply, while landed homes stay expensive because many Malaysians working in Singapore buy them for their families.

reasons.title: A home bought early rarely makes money
reasons.body: Interest and instalments over 15 years account for much of a house's rise in value. A rental property that tenants pay for builds equity even without capital gains, and can be sold later to fund the family home.

actions: Rent an apartment within a short drive of the hospital.
If they invest, judge each JB project only on whether its rent covers the instalment.
Add a second rental property after two or three years if the first works.
Buy the long-term family home once private practice and their child's needs are clear.
As government employees, look into the LPPSA housing loan.
