articles.title: My father gave me cash and two houses. Should I buy my next property in cash or with a loan?
articles.excerpt: A 23-year-old earning RM3,500 has been given cash, shares and two houses, and wants a RM200,000 to RM300,000 apartment. The parents say pay cash; Sean says use the two 90% loans and keep the cash.

question.asker: From M, a viewer who wrote in by email
question.context: M is 23 and earns RM3,500 a month. M's father has given M RM800,000 in cash, RM500,000 in shares, RM130,000 in a unit trust and two houses worth about RM1.2 million; the family owns five other properties, mostly bought in cash. M wants to buy an apartment in Cheras for about RM200,000 to RM300,000 as an investment, with an instalment of about RM1,300, but M's parents would rather pay cash to save interest.
question.text: Is it better to buy with a loan or in cash, and can M take housing loans for two properties at once on this salary?

answer.quote: Your active income will be the limiting factor.
answer.summary: Use loans for the first two purchases, while the 90% margin is available, and leave the cash in fixed deposits; the tenant's rent pays the interest. Buy one at a time: after about six months of rent records the bank counts the rent as income for the next loan. Cash comes in later, for a third property at 70% and for furnishing.

reasons.title: Cheap loans favour leverage
reasons.body: M's parents bought when interest rates were around 10% to 12%, so paying cash made sense. With rates far lower, it's better to use the bank's money and keep the cash working.

reasons.title: Rent becomes income
reasons.body: If the rent is a little above the instalment, the surplus adds to M's income for the next loan once there is a tenancy agreement and six months of payments. Two loans at once won't pass on RM3,500 a month.

reasons.title: Cash has its turn later
reasons.body: The third housing loan is capped at 70%, so a RM500,000 unit needs about RM150,000 down; furnishing a RM300,000 subsale to let may cost RM30,000 to RM40,000. The gifted houses can also be refinanced, if M's income supports it.

reasons.title: Income is the real limit
reasons.body: Every loan and refinance depends on M's own income, so building skills and a career matters as much as the assets. Having more to lose also means more care: learn, take advice and run due diligence.

actions: Buy the first unit with a loan, but only if the rent covers the instalment.
Keep the cash in fixed deposits and leave the shares as they are while you learn.
Set a furnishing budget for each unit so it rents well from day one.
Wait about six months after letting the first unit before applying for the second loan.
Learn how rental and dividend income are declared and taxed, so they count towards future loans.
articles.caveat: Sean respects the parents' cash approach, which suited the high rates of their time. The plan depends on the rent covering each instalment; if it doesn't, paying more upfront is the safer route.
articles.sourceNote: Summarised from Sean's full English captions for Asking Sean #228. The quoted line is verbatim; everything else is paraphrased. Figures are as the viewer and Sean stated them in October 2023. The captions don't make clear whether the asker is a man or a woman, so the article uses 'M' throughout.

articles.title: Is a guaranteed rental return worth buying into?
articles.excerpt: A reader has booked a hotel unit with a guaranteed 7% return. Sean explains where the guarantee really comes from, and why the exit is the bigger problem.

question.asker: From JH, a viewer who wrote in by email
question.context: JH has booked a 360 sq ft unit for RM700,000 in a hotel-run project near Genting Highlands. The developer guarantees a 7% return for three years, enough to cover the instalment and management fees with about RM1,000 a month to spare. After that, investors share 70% of the hotel profit for six years, and the operator handles utilities, furnishing and a refurbishment every three years.
question.text: He worries about the narrow access road, the operator choosing not to renew after nine years, and another pandemic. Is this kind of investment worth it?

answer.quote: I'm not a huge fan of GRR investment property.
answer.summary: Stay away unless it is a third or fourth property you can afford to lose. The guaranteed return is your own borrowed money paid back to you, the price is inflated, and the hotel operator is your only way out.

reasons.title: The guarantee is built into the price
reasons.body: A guaranteed rental return (GRR) is usually loaded into the sale price. A unit worth RM500,000 might be sold at RM700,000; you borrow the extra RM200,000 from the bank, and the developer hands it back to you as "returns" over three to five years.

reasons.title: You are paying city-centre prices for Genting
reasons.body: RM700,000 for 360 sq ft is about RM1,944 per sq ft, around what KLCC and TRX projects cost and more than Bukit Bintang. For short-stay rentals, the city centre also draws far more visitors than a tourist spot.

reasons.title: There is only one way out
reasons.body: A good investment property can be let long-term to families, short-term to expats, room by room or on Airbnb. This one only works as a hotel. If the operator walks away, as several did during the pandemic, you cannot live in it, rent it to locals or easily sell it, because buyers only want it for income it no longer makes.

reasons.title: The real return is thinner than 7%
reasons.body: Take off about 4% loan interest and roughly 1% in operating costs, and the margin is closer to 2%. Hotel use wears a building fast, so maintenance only rises. The operator is on a service contract it can leave after five years while your loan runs for 35, and business terms outside the sale agreement are not government-regulated.

actions: Work out the price per sq ft and compare it with prime city projects before trusting a guaranteed yield.
Ask what you would do if the operator left: could you live in it, rent it to locals, or sell it?
If you fear not finding tenants, buy below your limit instead. Sean suggests that someone approved for RM600,000 buy around RM480,000, so six empty months are survivable.
Keep your first two properties conventional; treat a scheme like this only as a third or fourth you can afford to lose.
Compare it with simpler options: fixed deposits, an index fund, or KL rentals yielding 5 to 6%.
articles.caveat: Sean stresses this is his general view of guaranteed-return schemes, not a judgement on this operator, and having a licensed hotel operator is a point in its favour. For an experienced investor with four or five properties, it is a risk you can choose to take.
articles.sourceNote: Summarised from Sean's full English captions for Asking Sean #259. The quoted answer is verbatim; everything else is paraphrased. Scheme terms vary by developer, so read the actual agreement before relying on any guarantee.

articles.title: What does buying a property really cost beyond the 10%?
articles.excerpt: Most first-time buyers budget the deposit and nothing else. Sean lists the costs that kept surprising him on his first purchase.

question.context: Ask what you need to buy a property in Malaysia and most people say 10%. Sean had exactly that for his first purchase, and the bills he had not budgeted for kept arriving one after another.
question.text: What else do you actually have to pay when you buy a property?

answer.quote: It's never 10%.
answer.summary: Budget well beyond the deposit. Legal fees on both the purchase and the loan, transfer stamp duty, valuation, handover deposits, compulsory insurance and yearly taxes all fall on the buyer, and a subsale costs the most upfront.

reasons.title: Legal fees come with more than one agreement
reasons.body: Developers often advertise a "free SPA", but that covers only the sale agreement. You also pay legal fees on the loan agreement with your bank, and owners of older blocks later pay again when the strata title is issued.

reasons.title: The transfer duty is the big one
reasons.body: Stamp duty on the memorandum of transfer (MOT) is due when ownership passes to you. Sean puts it at up to about 2% of the price, around RM14,000 on a RM700,000 home, and says few developers cover it.

reasons.title: Handover comes with deposits
reasons.body: Before you get the keys, a strata property usually needs about three months of maintenance fees as deposit, plus deposits for water, electricity and telecoms. A subsale also needs an independent valuation, paid by the buyer, before the bank will lend.

reasons.title: Some costs never stop
reasons.body: Banks effectively require mortgage insurance (MRTA or MLTA) before lending, and many require fire insurance too. Every year you also pay quit rent to the state and assessment tax to the local council; in strata buildings these often appear as a jump in the January or February maintenance bill.

actions: Plan for upfront cash well above 10% of the price, and more for a subsale.
Ask the developer in writing exactly which legal fees, and whether the MOT duty, are covered.
Set aside handover money: about three months of maintenance plus utility deposits.
Add mortgage and fire insurance to your loan costs, and quit rent and assessment tax to your yearly budget.
Estimate the legal fees and stamp duty for your price with the purchase cost calculator on this site.
articles.caveat: This is a 2019 episode. Fee scales have been revised since, and first-home stamp duty exemptions come and go with each Budget, so use these costs as a checklist and get current figures from your lawyer.
articles.sourceNote: Summarised from Sean's English captions for this April 2019 episode. The quoted answer is verbatim; everything else is paraphrased. Fee levels are as Sean described them at the time and have since changed.

articles.title: I earn well but fear losing my savings. Should I invest in property?
articles.excerpt: A 30-year-old in Melaka earning RM24,000 a month, with RM450,000 in cash, fears one wrong move. Sean says buy a rental unit well within her means, and leave renovate-and-flip alone.

question.asker: From Miss J, a viewer who wrote in by email
question.context: Miss J is 30, lives in Melaka and works in sales, averaging about RM24,000 a month. She has about RM450,000 in cash, RM80,000 in stocks and a RM160,000 car loan, and spends about RM10,000 a month. Coming from an ordinary family with no backup, she worries that one failure would be hard to recover from, and wonders whether to flip a renovated landed house, buy for rental, keep her money in fixed deposits or start a business.
question.text: Is she ready to invest in property, what should she buy, and should she flip houses or start a business instead?

answer.quote: Don't even think about flipping.
answer.summary: Yes, she is ready, but should play well within her means: a rental unit of RM500,000 to RM1 million in a proven KL location, where the rent covers the instalment. Buying an old house to renovate and sell is where people without construction experience lose money.

reasons.title: A rental unit has few unknowns
reasons.body: In an established area you can see the selling prices, rents and neighbours before you buy, and work out the instalment and furnishing costs. If you can carry six months of vacancy, the worst case is lowering the rent a little until a tenant signs.

reasons.title: She can absorb a bad month
reasons.body: She could borrow RM2.5 million or more, but a RM1 million loan costs about RM4,500 a month, which her RM14,000 monthly surplus covers even if the unit sits empty. Sean prefers one RM1 million unit in a top KL location to two RM500,000 units elsewhere.

reasons.title: The contractor wins most flips
reasons.body: Without contacts or experience, contractors will exceed any budget: a RM200,000 gap between a run-down and a renovated terrace vanishes once wiring, pipes or the roof need replacing. Sean has never seen anyone outside the trade make money flipping.

reasons.title: Melaka's high-rise market is weak
reasons.body: Melaka has a population limit, abandoned projects and too many units built for short-term stays, which Penang and some building managements now restrict. Landed homes for own use still do well there, but for high-rise investment Sean points her to KL.

actions: Learn how each kind of loan charges interest, so you can tell a fair return from a scam.
Follow Sean's four steps: set your intent, check your loan eligibility, view 20 properties in your budget, then buy.
Start with a unit of RM500,000 to RM1 million whose market rent covers the instalment.
Have RM50,000 for furnishing plus six months of instalments ready at key collection, and skip auctions for a first purchase.
Keep your job; if you want a business, test the idea cheaply before putting savings into it.
articles.caveat: Buying a landed house in Melaka to renovate and live in for ten years or more is a different matter: bought at the median price, Sean is confident it wouldn't lose money. It is the quick two-year flip he disagrees with.
articles.sourceNote: Summarised from Sean's full English captions for Asking Sean #304. The quoted answer is verbatim; everything else is paraphrased. Figures are as stated in December 2025.

video.title: ASKING SEAN #304 | PROPERTY INVESTMENT NEED NOT TO BE RISKY

articles.title: Why hold a property for 35 years instead of selling it?
articles.excerpt: A first-time buyer plans to sell after five years for a RM100,000 gain and asks why anyone would hold for 35. Sean explains the long equity game and why cash loses to inflation.

question.asker: From Mr. C, a viewer who wrote in by email
question.context: Mr. C is planning his first purchase, a two-bedroom unit in a new Subang Jaya project with strong rent. His plan was to buy where rent covers the instalment and maintenance, then sell after about five years for a gain of perhaps RM100,000. He doubts the long game: older apartments decline, newer projects keep coming, and a RM500 to RM1,000 monthly surplus could turn negative during vacancies or repairs.
question.text: What is the point of holding several properties for 30 to 35 years if they may be hard to rent or sell by then?

answer.quote: Don't be too concerned of cash. Build the asset first.
answer.summary: Flipping is hard now because developers already price in the gains, so Sean holds properties whose rent covers the instalment on zero down payment and lets tenants pay them off. Cash from a sale loses value to inflation while the property keeps pace, though there is no rule that you must hold to the end.

reasons.title: Each RM500 surplus is about RM100,000 of value
reasons.body: A buyer can pay about RM100,000 more and still have rent cover the instalment. Sean's Mont Kiara unit, bought for about RM1 million three years ago with a RM4,000 instalment, should rent for RM5,500 to RM6,000, so he could sell at RM1.2 million to RM1.3 million, but would then have to find somewhere to put the cash.

reasons.title: Cash loses to inflation
reasons.body: Sean puts real inflation at around 10% to 12%, against about 6% from EPF, so cash shrinks every year. Property hedges inflation: rising building costs, higher wages and lower interest rates all lift the value of what existing owners hold.

reasons.title: Older units still rent
reasons.body: Older Mont Kiara units first sold at around RM380,000 to RM420,000 still yield about 5% to 5.5% at today's prices, because not everyone can afford new. Whether new beats old still comes down to location and management.

reasons.title: Tenants and the bank do the work
reasons.body: A break-even portfolio costs Sean about one and a half to two months of instalments a year in agent fees and repairs, roughly five years' worth over a 30-year loan. Five RM300,000 units renting at RM1,500 each would then pay him RM7,500 a month, for working on each unit once or twice a year.

actions: Buy only where rent covers the instalment and maintenance with zero down payment, Sean's strict rule.
Compare the price with the area's median so you never overpay.
Look at 20 different properties across the buying channels before settling on this one.
Use credit for property and put your own capital into other investments.
Judge any gain as a percentage of what you put in, not as a lump sum.
articles.caveat: The plan fails if the unit bleeds, with rent covering only half the instalment. Nor must you hold to the end: if life changes, such as moving overseas, Sean would sell. And if RM100,000 is large against your savings, taking the gain may be the right call for you.
articles.sourceNote: Summarised from Sean's full English captions for Asking Sean #303. The quoted answer is verbatim; everything else is paraphrased. Figures are as stated in December 2025.

articles.title: We're moving from Hong Kong to Kuala Lumpur. Should we buy now or rent first?
articles.excerpt: A Hong Kong couple with an MM2H visa and cash from selling their flat are being shown KL's priciest condos. Sean says rent for two years, think like a local, and buy for yield, not prestige.

question.asker: From W, a viewer who wrote in by email
question.context: W and her husband are moving from Hong Kong to Kuala Lumpur next year on a Malaysia My Second Home (MM2H) visa, with cash from selling their Hong Kong flat. They don't drive, want to be near the MRT and malls, and want to avoid buildings with short-stay guests; they have been shown high-end projects around Damansara Heights, TRX and KL Sentral. They also want to invest, perhaps in one unit of RM1.5 million to RM2 million in Mont Kiara or two RM1 million units near KLCC, and have been told to split units into two to raise the rent.
question.text: Should they buy now or rent first, which areas and units suit them, and is splitting a unit a good idea?

answer.quote: Don't compare with whatever projects you had back in your hometown.
answer.summary: Rent first, for about two years, keep the cash in fixed deposits or other stable investments, and explore the city like a local before buying. Prices that look cheap against Hong Kong are often the most expensive in Kuala Lumpur, and for investment buy whichever unit's rent covers its instalment, whether that is one unit or two.

reasons.title: Foreign buyers get shown the top tier
reasons.body: Agents and developers push the priciest projects to buyers converting stronger currencies. A street or two stations away, prices can halve: about RM2,000 per sq ft near TRX against RM700 to RM800 in Cheras, or about RM1,000 in Mont Kiara against RM600 to RM700 in Segambut.

reasons.title: Prices here rise slowly
reasons.body: Malaysian property has grown about 3% to 4% a year on average, with constant new launches, so renting for two years costs little in missed gains. Meanwhile they can compare Mont Kiara, Desa ParkCity, Cheras, Bangsar, Subang Jaya and Shah Alam firsthand.

reasons.title: Buy what Hong Kong can't offer
reasons.body: With a car, a gated landed home of 3,000 to 3,500 sq ft can cost about RM2 million in the Klang Valley, above the foreign-ownership minimum, and renting a landed home costs far less than a city condo with the same rent.

reasons.title: Splitting units has risks
reasons.body: Dual-key units designed by the developer are fine. Adding partitions yourself can break Kuala Lumpur's new partition rules, fail renovation approval, upset the management and leave fire insurance void.

actions: Rent in an area you like for about two years and spend weekends viewing other neighbourhoods.
Keep the sale proceeds in fixed deposits or other stable investments while you look.
For an investment unit, compare prices from developers, subsales, auctions and bulk purchase groups, and check transacted prices nearby.
Choose the unit whose rent covers its instalment, rather than buying more units that each lose money.
Check the foreign-ownership minimum price and whether short-stay letting is allowed before buying in any building.
articles.caveat: Sean wasn't sure whether foreigners can buy non-strata landed homes, so check the state's rules first. If they are moving for a job in the city centre, paying for a prime location may be worth it.
articles.sourceNote: Summarised from Sean's full English captions for Asking Sean #231. The quoted line is verbatim; everything else is paraphrased. Figures are as Sean stated them in November 2023; MM2H and foreign-ownership rules change, so check the current ones. Sean mentions a mortgage specialist who works for a property investment company he uses; the article leaves out her details.

articles.title: Our hotel-scheme unit has paid nothing and won't sell. What now?
articles.excerpt: Two siblings bought a serviced apartment leased back to a hotel operator with a guaranteed return. It completed four years late and has paid nothing since. Sean lists the red flags and their few ways out.

question.asker: From Mr K, a viewer who wrote in by email
question.context: Mr K and his sister jointly bought a serviced apartment as an investment, leased back to a hotel operator under a guaranteed rental return. It completed more than four years late; they sued for late delivery and won. The operator, which shared an office with the developer, never paid them; they won judgment against it, but it is a RM2 company. There is still no strata title and no AGM, and unknown companies bill them for utilities and maintenance. They could not find a buyer even at RM210,000 below their purchase price.
question.text: What can they do with a unit that pays nothing and cannot be sold?

answer.quote: not all properties make money
answer.summary: There is no good way out. They can sell at a deeper loss and pay the bank the difference now, or keep paying the loan and wait on a rescue by a bigger developer that may never come. The real lessons are for buyers who have not yet signed for a scheme like this.

reasons.title: Guaranteed returns are priced in
reasons.body: A guaranteed 6% for five years is usually added to the price up front, so a unit worth RM500,000 is sold at about RM650,000 with a large discount. It only works if the operator and developer stay solvent and honest.

reasons.title: If it's so good, why share it?
reasons.body: A developer with a profitable hotel would run it or partner with another developer. Selling rooms to hundreds of buyers is a way to raise cash from people who want an investment with no effort.

reasons.title: You may not control your own unit
reasons.body: In a hotel-run building the key cards are held centrally, so owners often cannot rent their unit out themselves.

reasons.title: Selling below the loan costs cash
reasons.body: If the loan is about RM800,000 and the unit sells for less, the owners must pay the bank the difference in cash. The alternative is to keep paying for years while the unit earns nothing.

actions: Before buying, check that current rents nearby already cover the instalment you will pay at completion.
Avoid guaranteed-rental-return and hotel-leaseback schemes.
Avoid buying jointly with a relative unless each of you can carry the loss alone.
If stuck, work out whether you can afford to sell below the loan before cutting your losses.
Take complaints about a missing joint management body or strata title to the Commissioner of Buildings, and keep legal advice on disputed bills.
articles.caveat: Sean notes the worst case is the developer winding up altogether; while it is still operating, a takeover by a bigger developer remains a slim chance. For other buyers, distressed sellers in such buildings can be an opportunity if the price falls below replacement cost.
articles.sourceNote: Summarised from Sean's full English captions for Asking Sean #275. The quoted line is verbatim; everything else is paraphrased. Figures are as stated in February 2025. The developer and project are not named here. The episode is sponsored by The Makeover Guys, a renovation company.

articles.title: Can I make money flipping old houses in Malaysia?
articles.excerpt: A 24-year-old bank employee wants to buy dated houses below market value, renovate them and resell within months. Sean explains why flipping only pays for contractors, and suggests selling property instead.

question.asker: From F, a viewer who wrote in on Instagram
question.context: F is 24, has worked at a bank for a year and a half, lives with his parents and has low expenses. He enjoys interior design and wants to buy abandoned or dated houses below market value, renovate them and sell at market price within about six months, rather than hold rentals for years. He hopes his job gives him better loan rates.
question.text: Is house flipping a viable way to make money in Malaysia, and can he take a long loan for a short flip?

answer.quote: Property investment was supposed to be slow.
answer.summary: For him, no. Flipping pays mainly for renovation contractors and interior designers who profit from the building work itself, while an outsider takes all the risk. Sean suggests he sell property as an agent instead: little risk, he learns the market, and his income depends on his own effort.

reasons.title: The numbers only work at the bank's valuation
reasons.body: If a house sells for RM800,000 but the bank values it at RM1 million, a buyer who qualifies for a RM900,000 loan has room for renovation. But a newcomer often doesn't know what a kitchen, roof, water tank or auto gate costs, and each one eats into the margin.

reasons.title: Tax on a quick sale removes much of the gain
reasons.body: Property gains tax is highest in the first years after the SPA, so on a RM100,000 gain perhaps RM30,000 goes in tax. The third and later loans also can't get 90% financing, which limits repeat flips.

reasons.title: The deals and the work are hard to find
reasons.body: Neighbours snap up genuinely cheap houses first. Contractors can abandon jobs, and coordinating cabinet makers, ceiling installers and electricians takes far more hours than people expect, while the instalment keeps running.

reasons.title: Contractors profit regardless
reasons.body: A builder or interior design firm prices the works at cost and knows from past projects what a house will fetch. An outside buyer pays their margin and still has to find a buyer after tax.

actions: Learn the difference between bank valuation and the price buyers actually pay nearby.
Check current property gains tax rates on sales in the first few years.
Consider working as a property agent part-time to learn the market with little risk.
If you still want to flip, partner with an experienced contractor rather than going alone.
articles.caveat: A refurbished house in a good location can still sell above neighbouring prices, because buyers will pay to skip the hassle. Flipping isn't impossible, just poorly suited to a newcomer financing it alone.
articles.sourceNote: Summarised from Sean's full English captions for Asking Sean #191. The quoted line is verbatim; everything else is paraphrased. Figures are as Sean stated them in November 2022; property gains tax rates and loan limits change, so check current ones. Sean refers to his work at The Makeover Guys, a furnishing company.

articles.title: Can I buy a terrace house and run my tuition class in it?
articles.excerpt: A teacher in Kuantan wants a RM440,000 double-storey house to hold tuition classes downstairs and rent out the rooms upstairs. Sean says check first whether it can legally host a business.

question.asker: From Mr TG, a viewer who wrote in by email
question.context: TG is 35, a government secondary school teacher recently transferred to Kuantan, where he now lives with his wife. He earns about RM6,000 a month, has no debts, RM130,000 in savings and RM30,000 in ETFs and stocks. His wife's own house, due in late 2026, is too small for classes, so he is eyeing the last unsold intermediate double-storey house in a completed Bukit Setongkol project for RM440,000, with the developer paying the SPA legal fees and stamp duty. He would hold it for about 20 years, then retire to Selangor.
question.text: Should he buy the house to run his tuition class downstairs and rent out the rooms upstairs?

answer.quote: I want to make money the right way, the legal way.
answer.summary: Only once he knows he can legally run a tuition centre there. Many do it in houses, but a residential title isn't meant for it, and neighbours, safety and licensing can end the plan. Without the business, the house has to stand as an investment, and its rent won't cover the instalment.

reasons.title: A home is not a licensed premises
reasons.body: A proper tuition centre usually rents a shop office, registers a business and meets fire and space requirements. Running one in a house saves on rent, utilities and licences, which is why it is common, but it lasts only until someone is hurt, something goes wrong or a neighbour complains.

reasons.title: Neighbours bear the cost
reasons.body: Classes of 30 to 100 students bring cars dropping off and picking up every evening, noise at night and heavy use of toilets and water. Some older KL houses on busy roads have been rezoned for business, but they still register as businesses and cost more to maintain.

reasons.title: Landed rent rarely covers the loan
reasons.body: At RM440,000 the instalment would be about RM2,000 a month, while local rents point to about RM1,500 to RM1,600, so the tenant would pay the interest and he the principal. In small towns people buy as soon as they can afford to, so rents stay low; landed homes earn mainly through price growth of about 3% to 5% a year.

reasons.title: Rooms for transferred staff can pay
reasons.body: In smaller towns, teachers, doctors and nurses on transfer struggle to find rooms quickly and will pay 20% to 30% more for immediate availability. His network of transferred teachers could fill the house room by room.

actions: Ask the local council whether you can get a licence to run a tuition centre in that house before buying.
Check rents for double-storey houses in the area; Sean would buy if it could rent for about RM2,000 a month.
Use your LPPSA housing loan if you go ahead.
Compare it with a unit of about RM400,000 to RM440,000 in KL whose rent covers the instalment.
When researching any home, find out what causes the area's traffic jams, such as schools, markets or highway bottlenecks.
articles.caveat: If he simply wants a family home near his wife's relatives to hold for 20 years, buying is reasonable, and the house number 4, which the agent offered to change, doesn't bother Sean. As a teacher on transfer, renting may also be the cheaper choice in a small town.
articles.sourceNote: Summarised from Sean's full English captions for Asking Sean #300. The quoted answer is verbatim; everything else is paraphrased. The rental data Sean checked was for single-storey houses, so the rents are an estimate. Figures are as stated in October 2025. The episode's sponsor, a retirement fund provider, is unrelated to this advice.

articles.title: How much housing loan can I actually get?
articles.excerpt: Banks decide with one number, your debt service ratio. Rena Choong shows how to estimate your own loan eligibility before visiting a sales gallery, and what CCRIS and CTOS reveal.

question.context: Sean's second step for every buyer is to find out how much they can borrow, yet many people avoid checking. In the second episode of his mortgage series, he asks Rena Choong, FAR Capital's head of mortgage, how banks work it out.
question.text: How do banks decide how much housing loan you can get, and how can you work it out yourself before you start looking?

by.name: Rena Choong
by.role: head of mortgage at FAR Capital

answer.quote: You should at least go and calculate your loan eligibility.
answer.summary: Banks use your debt service ratio: all your loan repayments, existing and new, divided by your net income. Work out your own figure first, so you only look at properties you can finance and don't collect rejections.

reasons.title: The DSR limit rises with income
reasons.body: Banks cap repayments at about 60% of net income for those earning under RM3,000 gross, 70% to 75% at RM3,000 to RM5,000, 75% to 80% above RM5,000, and up to 85% or 90% at some banks above RM10,000. Only debts in CCRIS count, such as housing, car, personal and PTPTN loans, credit cards and ASB financing; living costs and insurance don't.

reasons.title: A quick formula gives your limit
reasons.body: Take 80% of gross income as net, apply the bank's DSR limit, subtract existing repayments, then multiply by 250 for a 35-year loan. On RM6,000 gross, RM4,800 at 75% is RM3,600; less RM500 of debts leaves RM3,100, or about RM775,000. The multiplier falls with age, to about 230, 220 and 210, because loans end at around 70.

reasons.title: Your repayment record sets your rate
reasons.body: CCRIS shows the last 12 months, and each digit is the number of months in arrears; twos appearing more than once can sink an application. A weaker bank credit score still gets a loan, but at a higher rate, for example 3.4% or 3.5% instead of 3.3%.

reasons.title: Card balances count, not card limits
reasons.body: Banks count 5% of your outstanding credit card balance as a monthly commitment, and instalment plans count in full, so a big purchase just before applying can tip your DSR. Rena advises keeping card use below 30% of the limit.

actions: Get your free CCRIS report from Bank Negara (you register in person once), and consider a CTOS report, which also shows legal and trade records.
Calculate your DSR and loan eligibility before visiting sales galleries, and shortlist only properties within it.
Keep every repayment on time for at least the 12 months before you apply.
If your CCRIS is empty, take a credit card, spend a little and pay it off in full for about six months to build a record.
If you are self-employed or own over about 20% of a company, file and pay tax: banks will use your last two years of tax returns, not your payslip.
articles.caveat: Limits vary between banks and with Bank Negara rules; these are 2022 figures. A borderline DSR can sometimes still pass if you pledge a fixed deposit, while a poor repayment record can fail you even with eligibility to spare.
articles.sourceNote: Summarised from Sean's full English captions for episode 2 of his mortgage series with Rena Choong, FAR Capital's head of mortgage (August 2022). The quoted answer is Rena's own words; everything else is paraphrased. DSR limits and rates are as stated in 2022 and differ between banks. Sean is a customer of FAR Capital, not its owner.

video.title: HOW TO CALCULATE YOUR LOAN ELIGIBILITY (EP 2)

articles.title: Flexi, semi-flexi or fixed: how does housing loan interest work?
articles.excerpt: Most buyers compare loans only by the monthly instalment. Rena Choong explains how housing loans charge interest, why a lump sum belongs there, and when full flexi is worth its fee.

question.context: Sean admits he rarely talks about the loan side of buying, even though rules on eligibility change often. In the first episode of his mortgage series, he asks Rena Choong, FAR Capital's head of mortgage and his own investment coach, how different loans charge interest.
question.text: How does a housing loan charge interest compared with a personal or car loan, and which type should you take if you want to pay it down faster?

by.name: Rena Choong
by.role: head of mortgage at FAR Capital

answer.quote: What you should do right now is actually first take a full flexi loan.
answer.summary: A housing loan charges interest only on what you still owe, so a lump-sum prepayment cuts the interest and can shorten the loan, while personal and car loans fix the interest up front. If you will prepay or draw money back often, take a full flexi loan; on a semi-flexi loan you must ask the bank to apply any extra payment to the principal.

reasons.title: Flat-rate loans charge all interest up front
reasons.body: A RM100,000 personal loan at 6% over 10 years adds RM60,000 of interest at the start, so you repay RM160,000, about RM1,333 a month. Paying it off early saves nothing unless you settle the whole amount.

reasons.title: Housing loan interest falls as you pay
reasons.body: On RM500,000 at 3.3% over 35 years, the instalment is about RM2,000, and early on roughly 70% of it, about RM1,300, is interest. Prepay RM100,000 and interest is charged on RM400,000 instead, so more of each instalment goes to principal and the term could shrink to 20 or 25 years.

reasons.title: Extra money in semi-flexi just sits there
reasons.body: Pay RM2,500 instead of RM2,000 on a semi-flexi loan and the bank still takes RM2,000; the rest is carried to next month without cutting interest. You have to register a prepayment by form, phone or email, and withdrawals need an application and a fee. Sean found his own surplus rent had been sitting idle this way.

reasons.title: Full flexi works like a cheaper overdraft
reasons.body: A full flexi loan lets you prepay and withdraw online at any time for a monthly fee of about RM10 to RM15. It suits business owners and the self-employed with uneven cash, and costs far less than an overdraft at 5% to 6%.

actions: Check whether each loan you hold is flat-rate or balance-reducing before deciding which to pay down.
Put spare lump sums against a balance-reducing loan's principal, not into a flat-rate loan you can't settle in full.
On a semi-flexi loan, save extra money into a lump sum and tell the bank in writing to apply it as a prepayment.
Choose full flexi if your income is irregular or you may need to draw the money back out.
Clear credit card debt first: it costs about 18% a year, against under 3% on Sean's latest housing loan in 2022.
articles.caveat: A fixed-rate housing loan protects you if the OPR rises but costs more if it falls, and banks offer it as a promotion rather than at your choosing. Rates, fees and prepayment terms differ between banks and have changed since 2022.
articles.sourceNote: Summarised from Sean's full English captions for episode 1 of his mortgage series with Rena Choong, FAR Capital's head of mortgage (August 2022). The quoted answer is Rena's own words; everything else is paraphrased. Rates are as stated in 2022, so check current ones. Sean is a customer of FAR Capital, not its owner.

video.title: THINGS TO KNOW BEFORE APPLYING FOR HOUSING LOAN (EP 1)

articles.title: Why was my housing loan rejected?
articles.excerpt: A rejected loan stays on record and makes the next bank wary. Rena Choong goes through the most common reasons banks say no, and what to fix before you apply again.

question.context: A rejection doesn't only cost you the property; it stays on record and makes the next bank cautious. In the third episode of his mortgage series, Sean asks Rena Choong which problems most often get a housing loan turned down.
question.text: What are the most common reasons banks reject a housing loan, and how do you avoid them?

by.name: Rena Choong
by.role: head of mortgage at FAR Capital

answer.quote: Please don't submit, wait until you fully settle it.
answer.summary: Most rejections are predictable: a DSR over the limit, recent arrears in CCRIS, a restructured loan, or a legal or AKPK record. Fix what you can and wait for a clean record before applying, because each rejection is visible to the next bank.

reasons.title: Recent arrears mean an upfront no
reasons.body: One month late is usually acceptable, but two or three months of arrears in CCRIS is treated as an upfront rejection. Settle in full and wait until the latest six months show zeros; late credit card payments are easier to explain than housing loan arrears.

reasons.title: Restructuring is worse than refinancing
reasons.body: Restructuring or rescheduling, stretching a loan because you can't keep up, signals distress and often leads to rejection. Refinancing to draw cash from a property's built-up equity is different, and a government-backed moratorium doesn't mark CCRIS, though applying to the same bank that granted it is awkward.

reasons.title: Legal records block even eligible buyers
reasons.body: Summonses and court cases, including against a company you direct, trade references such as unpaid phone or instalment bills above about RM300, AKPK and bankruptcy lead to rejection however good your income. A PTPTN arrears flag is lighter: settle the overdue amount, get the settlement letter, and you can apply within a month or two.

reasons.title: Every application leaves a mark
reasons.body: CCRIS shows pending applications, and banks notice when others have turned you down, so submitting to five or six banks at once looks bad. Rena suggests two or three at most.

actions: Check your DSR, loan eligibility and CCRIS before you apply.
Clear any arrears and wait for clean months before submitting.
Apply to two or three banks, not every panel bank at once.
If your DSR is borderline, pay down credit card balances, which count at 5% of what you owe, before applying.
If you have little credit history, use one credit card lightly and pay it in full each month, rather than collecting several cards.
articles.caveat: Banks weigh these things differently, so a case one bank rejects may suit another, and these are 2022 practices. With AKPK or bankruptcy on record, Sean's view is that buying property shouldn't be the priority for now.
articles.sourceNote: Summarised from Sean's full English captions for episode 3 of his mortgage series with Rena Choong, FAR Capital's head of mortgage (September 2022). The quoted answer is Rena's own words; everything else is paraphrased. Bank practices are as described in 2022 and change over time. Sean is a customer of FAR Capital, not its owner.

video.title: COMMON REASONS FOR LOAN REJECTIONS (EP 3)

articles.title: Is a rent-to-own scheme like HouzKEY worth it?
articles.excerpt: When lockdown halved how banks assessed his income, Sean bought his Bukit Jalil home through Maybank Islamic's HouzKEY rent-to-own scheme. Collecting the keys four years later, he weighs what worked and what to watch.

question.context: During the COVID lockdown, banks counted only half of Sean's income, so he could not qualify for a normal home loan for the new launch he wanted. A salesperson suggested Maybank Islamic's HouzKEY, a rent-to-own scheme in which the bank buys the unit and you rent it from the bank, with the option to convert to financing later.
question.text: How does a rent-to-own scheme like HouzKEY work, and is it a good way to buy?

answer.quote: it would make a lot of sense to convert back into a home financing
answer.summary: For Sean it was the right choice: it let him secure the unit before prices rose, at rent well below the market and below a normal instalment. Because conversion is at the original SPA price, it pays off if values rise; if they don't, you can keep renting and walk away after five years.

reasons.title: It opens the door when income looks weak
reasons.body: The scheme suits young couples, or anyone whose finances look thin at the time of buying, who expect to be able to afford a loan later.

reasons.title: Conversion is at the original price
reasons.body: You can convert to normal financing from year two to five at the SPA price. Sean's first tower sold at a little over RM700 per sq ft; the last tower at over RM900, so converting locks in that gain.

reasons.title: Rent eases you in
reasons.body: The rent is set in a schedule, lowest in year one. Sean pays far less than the RM2,700 he paid for a rented home nearby, and less than similar furnished units fetch.

reasons.title: There are extra steps
reasons.body: Because the bank was the owner under his version, Sean collected his keys months after other buyers. The scheme has been revised several times, and some later versions make the buyer the owner.

actions: Ask the bank which version of the scheme applies, and who is the legal owner.
Check the rent schedule for each year and the conversion terms.
Research the project's prospects, since the benefit comes from converting at the old price.
Keep your finances in order while renting, so you still qualify to convert.
Compare with subsale prices before converting; if values fell, buying subsale may be cheaper.
articles.caveat: Some applicants could not convert because they took on other debts, such as a new car, and no longer qualified. If the property doesn't appreciate, the scheme works out as an ordinary five-year tenancy.
articles.sourceNote: Summarised from Sean's full English captions for this October 2024 video, part of a series on buying his own home. The quoted line is verbatim; everything else is paraphrased. Sean mentions that The Makeover Guys, a renovation company he works with, is fitting out the unit. The rent he pays under the scheme was unclear in the captions and is left out.

video.title: WAS HOUZKEY WORTH IT?? | EP 06

articles.title: What tricks do developers use to make me buy?
articles.excerpt: With supply outstripping demand, developers pull every lever. Sean walks through the four Ps of their marketing, from lavish sales galleries to rebates and schemes, and reminds buyers who pays for them.

question.context: Decades ago, buyers queued and even paid under the table for new launches. With more supply than demand, developers now compete with show villages, facility lists, discounts and ownership schemes.
question.text: How do developers persuade buyers, and how should I respond?

answer.quote: the decision needs to come from your own judgment
answer.summary: Recognise the four Ps, place, product, price and packaging, as emotional triggers, and remember that every freebie is built into the price. Be patient, shop around, and buy only what you could afford even without a tenant.

reasons.title: Place: galleries built to hold you
reasons.body: From the landscaped entrance to the guard who opens the door, galleries and show villages work like a fish trap: easy to enter, hard to leave. Free food and family events bring you in.

reasons.title: Product: always something new
reasons.body: Mixed developments, transit-oriented projects, townships of thousands of acres, semi-Ds that look like bungalows, dual keys, dozens of facilities and smart homes give the brochure something to print.

reasons.title: Price and packaging: you pay for it all
reasons.body: Roads, security, landscaping and brand are priced in, and so are discounts, loyalty and referral rebates, free legal fees, furnishing and guaranteed returns of 6% for three to five years.

actions: Treat every promotion as part of the price, and compare the net price.
Ignore deadlines: campaigns are often extended.
Shop around and compare with similar projects before deciding.
Buy only if you can afford the instalment even without a tenant.
articles.caveat: Not every scheme is bad; Sean's point is to decide with a clear head. If you are buying to live in and can afford it, go ahead.
articles.sourceNote: Summarised from Sean's English captions for this July 2019 video. Some scheme names in the captions are unclear and are left out. The quoted line is verbatim; everything else is paraphrased.

video.title: THINGS DEVELOPERS DO TO MAKE YOU BUY THEIR PROPERTY

articles.title: How do I calculate the return on a rental property?
articles.excerpt: A 4% or 5% return on property can look poor next to 10% from shares. Sean shows how rental ROI is worked out, and why leverage changes the comparison.

question.context: Developers and agents quote property returns of 4%, 5% or 6%, while friends boast of 10% a year from shares. A viewer asked how return on investment is calculated and how to compare the two.
question.text: How is return on investment calculated for a rental property, and what counts as a good return?

answer.quote: your profit versus your initial amount
answer.summary: ROI is yearly return divided by the amount invested. For property, divide a year's rent by the price. A return above fixed deposit rates is already decent, and one above your loan interest rate is very good, because the bank funds most of the purchase.

reasons.title: The basic sum
reasons.body: A RM500,000 property rented at RM2,000 a month earns RM24,000 a year, or 4.8% of the price.

reasons.title: Leverage changes the picture
reasons.body: RM50,000 in shares at 10% returns RM5,000 a year. The same RM50,000 as a down payment can control a RM400,000 property renting at RM1,500, or RM18,000 a year. The 4.5% is on the whole price, but you put in only about 10%.

reasons.title: Few assets come with a loan
reasons.body: Banks will lend ordinary buyers around 90% to buy property, but will not lend them money to buy shares.

actions: Work out yearly rent divided by price for any unit you consider.
Compare the result with fixed deposit rates and your loan interest rate.
Remember the return is earned on the full price, not just your down payment.
Keep some savings in cash, shares and insurance rather than everything in property.
articles.caveat: Sean's benchmarks of a 3% fixed deposit and a 4.5% loan rate date from 2019. Higher returns come with higher risk, and he stresses doing your homework rather than assuming property always wins.
articles.sourceNote: Summarised from Sean's full English captions for this January 2019 video, made in answer to a viewer's question. The quoted line is verbatim; everything else is paraphrased. The 4.8% is worked from his own figures.

video.title: How to calculate Return On Investment?

articles.title: My mother gave me her old house. Should I sell it?
articles.excerpt: A 53-year-old was gifted the Penang semi-D his mother bought 40 years ago. It barely rents, but he is attached to it. Sean says to find its true value first, then decide what the money is for.

question.asker: From Mr L, a viewer who wrote in by email
question.context: Mr L is 53 and lives elsewhere in Penang. His mother has gifted him an old semi-detached house near Green Lane that she bought about 40 years ago. Since a business tenant left, it has been hard to let; a friend rented it for about RM1,300 a month for a year. Similar houses nearby are listed at around RM1.9 million, several are for sale on his road, and he has about RM200,000 in stocks and savings and no commitments besides his child's school fees.
question.text: Should he sell the house, given its low rent, or keep it for its sentimental value and as his only landed property?

answer.quote: Property is a tool for us to achieve what we want to achieve.
answer.summary: Either is defensible, because he has no urgent need for the money. First find out what the house is really worth. If a buyer offers above market value, Sean would sell, clear any housing loan and set up his child's education fund; otherwise holding it is fine.

reasons.title: Rent is the wrong yardstick
reasons.body: RM1,300 a month is about RM15,600 a year, under 1% of a RM1.75 million house, so a fixed deposit looks better. But landed homes earn through scarcity and price growth: at a conservative 3% a year, the same house gains about RM52,500, which should be added to the rent before comparing.

reasons.title: Sentiment has a cost
reasons.body: Unless you live in it, Sean sees a house as a tool, and this one has done its job of giving the next generation a head start. Keeping it for sentiment means paying to maintain an old house, and the question becomes real the day a large sum is needed.

reasons.title: Sell when you don't need the money
reasons.body: The best prices come when you aren't forced to sell. Need half a million urgently and the first low offer wins, which is how investors find their deals.

reasons.title: Without a goal, nothing moves
reasons.body: With no retirement plan, education fund or other target, there is no reason to act, so the status quo wins. Sean suggests setting goals with a timeline, such as funding his child's university, alongside valuing the house.

actions: Get a bank valuation on the house, then ask local agents what it would sell for.
Check past transaction prices for similar houses nearby, so you don't sell for less than it's worth.
Work out your retirement plan and an education fund for your child, with the sums and dates they need.
If you sell, sell only above market value, then clear any housing loan and set aside the education fund.
Discuss the decision with your spouse.
articles.caveat: Sean was unsure whether Mr L's income was RM2,500 or RM25,000 a month, and his advice to consider selling assumes the lower figure. If Mr L plans to move into the house, or simply doesn't need the money, keeping it is also a sound choice; property is a good hedge against inflation.
articles.sourceNote: Summarised from Sean's full English captions for Asking Sean #305. The quoted answer is verbatim; everything else is paraphrased. The RM1.75 million value is Sean's working assumption, not a valuation. Figures are as stated in January 2026.

video.title: ASKING SEAN #305 | WHAT TO DO WITH AN INHERITED PROPERTY?

articles.title: Dad left us a neglected shop lot. Should we sell it, renovate it or rent it out?
articles.excerpt: A family inherited a paid-off shop lot bought above market in 2005, empty for years with RM50,000 in unpaid taxes. Sean says get three numbers, then sell unless they still believe in the area.

question.asker: From Mr L, a viewer who wrote in by email
question.context: Mr L, 30, lost his father just before Chinese New Year. His father's will left his mother a fully paid double-storey shop lot in Bukit Beruntung, bought in 2005 well above market price and left vacant and unattended; an agent suggests about RM1,000 a month in rent. It carries about RM50,000 in unpaid quit rent and assessment, and the family's only other fund is a RM100,000 life insurance payout meant to support his mother, who turns 60 this year.
question.text: Should the family sell it as it is, renovate and sell, or renovate and rent it out for his mother's income?

answer.quote: Do you still believe in this location?
answer.summary: Find three numbers first: the renovation cost, the price as it stands and the price once made good. Unless the family still believes in the area, selling is the obvious choice: a sale of around RM500,000 kept in fixed deposit would beat RM1,000 a month in rent, and what their father paid no longer matters.

reasons.title: His purchase price isn't their loss
reasons.body: The loan is fully paid, so whatever it sells for is money in the family's hands. Recent listings nearby averaged about RM600,000, so Sean assumes about RM500,000 given its condition.

reasons.title: RM80,000 for RM1,000 a month doesn't add up
reasons.body: Clearing the RM50,000 in arrears and perhaps RM20,000 to RM30,000 of work, to earn RM1,000 a month, isn't justified for a family already stretched. Rents quoted nearby ranged from RM900 to RM5,000, so check with several agents.

reasons.title: Shop lots need little work
reasons.body: A commercial unit only has to be restored to its original state: grilles, shutters, windows, wiring, water and a sound roof. Tenants fit it out for their business, so a cheaper or even DIY job may be enough.

reasons.title: Refinancing needs a qualifying borrower
reasons.body: Keeping it and refinancing to fund the work only works if the new owner has enough income for the bank's debt service ratio. A paid-off property alone won't get a loan.

actions: Get quotes for restoring the unit to working order, and consider doing simple work yourselves.
Ask several agents for the price as it is and the price once made good, and compare rents from more than one source.
If renovating to sell gains much more than it costs and you can fund it, do it; if not, sell as it is and expect buyers to negotiate.
Keep the unit only if the family still believes the area will develop, and check who would qualify for any refinancing.
If you invest in property yourself, keep three to six months' emergency fund and enough MRTA, MLTA or life cover that loans never pass to your family as debts.
articles.caveat: Sean couldn't judge the damage or renovation cost from the email, so the figures are rough. If the family believes the area will take off again, holding on can be reasonable, but only with the arrears cleared and someone able to manage the unit.
articles.sourceNote: Summarised from Sean's full English captions for Asking Sean #243. The quoted line is verbatim; everything else is paraphrased. Market prices and rents are rough figures Sean read from listings during the episode in March 2024. The episode was sponsored by The Makeover Guys, a renovation company Sean works with.

video.title: ASKING SEAN #243 | INHERIT MY DAD'S MISTAKE

articles.title: I inherited three paid-off properties at 23. How do I build on them?
articles.excerpt: A 23-year-old nurse in Singapore inherited three fully paid properties and wants ten rentals one day. Sean says settle the brother's care first, then learn before borrowing against anything.

question.asker: From MK, a viewer who wrote in by email
question.context: MK, 23, is a Malaysian with Singapore PR working as a nurse in Singapore, earning about RM100,000 a year. MK's mother recently passed away, leaving three fully paid properties: a two-storey terrace house rented out for RM3,600, a two-storey office lot previously rented for RM5,000, and a single-storey terrace house in Batu Pahat, plus RM150,000 in cash. MK also looks after an elder brother with special needs, whose care costs about RM2,000 a month.
question.text: How can MK use refinancing, collateral and the rental income to build a lifetime portfolio of ten rental properties?

answer.quote: Start building from now, assuming you have nothing.
answer.summary: Not yet. First decide how the brother will be cared for, because that decides where MK works and so what income the banks will see. Then treat the inheritance as untouchable for the next five to eight years, keep the cash safe, and spend that time learning how property investing works before borrowing against anything.

reasons.title: Refinancing still needs an income
reasons.body: Paid-off properties can't simply be pushed to a bank for cash: the bank must see enough income to service the new loan. Staying in Singapore or coming home to give care changes that income completely.

reasons.title: The rent already covers the care
reasons.body: About RM8,600 a month in rent from fully paid properties can pay for professional care, even at RM5,000 to RM6,000 a month, while MK keeps the Singapore career. The mother has already done the heavy lifting.

reasons.title: A young heir attracts sales pitches
reasons.body: People close to MK know about the inheritance and may push mutual funds, policies or ventures. Whether these are right depends on knowledge MK doesn't have yet, so stay discreet and sign nothing in a hurry.

reasons.title: The income is already ahead
reasons.body: At 23, MK earns what many in Kuala Lumpur only reach as managers in their late twenties, and Malaysian banks assess Singapore income like a local's. That is a strong base to build on with MK's own credit.

actions: Decide on your brother's care first: yourself, a home helper or a professional facility.
Keep the RM150,000 in fixed deposit until you know what you want to do with it.
Work through Sean's four basic steps: set your intent, find your loan eligibility, view properties, then decide.
Learn how to manage tenants, declare rental income so it counts for future loans, and check that rent covers the instalment.
When you do borrow, take enough mortgage insurance (MRTA or MLTA) so your loans never pass to your family as debts.
articles.caveat: MK's plans may change within a few years, such as settling in Singapore, where buying an HDB flat would affect how they invest in Malaysia. Sean leaves what and where to buy until MK understands the rules.
articles.sourceNote: Summarised from Sean's full English captions for Asking Sean #246. The quoted line is verbatim; everything else is paraphrased. Figures are as the viewer and Sean stated them in April 2024. Sean recommends FAR Capital, a property investment club he says he is a member of, not an owner, and earns from what it sells; the article leaves out that recommendation.

video.title: ASKING SEAN #246 | INHERITANCE PASSED DOWN BY MOM

articles.title: Should I buy an investment condo now, or save 12 years for my dream landed home?
articles.excerpt: A 33-year-old father earning RM10,000 wonders whether to buy an investment condo or save until his late 40s for a corner terrace. Sean says prices will outrun his savings, so buy a unit the rent can carry.

question.asker: From Mr N, a viewer who wrote in by email
question.context: Mr N, 33, takes home about RM10,000 a month, has two young children and lives with his parents. After insurance, a car loan, a RM2,700 housing loan, food, his mother's allowance and other costs he has about RM2,500 left each month, plus about RM75,000 in crypto. He is weighing a studio or two-room condo of up to RM700,000 as an investment in 2024 against saving for 12 years to buy a corner terrace house in Kwasa Land or Elmina in his late 40s.
question.text: Should he buy an investment property now despite his budget, or keep saving for his dream landed home?

answer.quote: I think the proposition here is to own the apartment first.
answer.summary: Buy an investment unit first, but a smaller one than RM700,000: an instalment of about RM2,000 to RM2,500, on a unit where current rents already cover it. Let it build equity for 10 to 12 years, then sell it for the down payment on the terrace house, instead of chasing prices with savings alone.

reasons.title: Savings rarely catch property prices
reasons.body: Elmina Green homes launched at about RM600,000 to RM700,000, and later phases cost about RM1.2 million. A friend of Sean's saved for years for a Shah Alam terrace as its price kept moving out of reach.

reasons.title: A RM4,000 instalment is too much stress
reasons.body: His income could get a loan of about RM1 million, but a RM4,000 instalment with two children leaves no room if the unit sits empty or his job changes. About RM2,000 to RM2,500 a month is his sweet spot, roughly a RM500,000 to RM600,000 unit.

reasons.title: Build in a safety factor
reasons.body: Choose a unit where rents nearby already cover the instalment, so it still works if rents fall 10% by completion. And budget about RM50,000 for furnishing so it can be let as soon as the keys arrive.

reasons.title: Crypto isn't a plan
reasons.body: Money in crypto should be money he can afford to lose overnight, not the foundation for a home.

actions: Set your instalment limit at about RM2,000 to RM2,500 a month and search for units at that price.
Check current rents for each shortlisted unit, and make sure a 10% drop still covers the instalment.
Save bonuses towards a furnishing budget of about RM50,000 for handover.
With little time for research, consider paying for professional deal sourcing and data.
Plan to sell the unit in 10 to 12 years to fund the down payment on your terrace house.
articles.caveat: This depends on his job staying secure; if it doesn't, a smaller unit or waiting is safer. Sean points to a bulk purchase club he is a VIP member of and buys from, which he says he doesn't run.
articles.sourceNote: Summarised from Sean's full English captions for Asking Sean #219. The quoted line is verbatim; everything else is paraphrased. Figures are as the viewer and Sean stated them in August 2023. Sean recommends a property investment club he is a VIP member of and buys from.

video.title: ASKING SEAN #219 | SALARY CANNOT CATCH UP WITH PROPERTY PRICE

articles.title: I'm 45 and my home is paid off. Should I start investing in property, in Penang or the Klang Valley?
articles.excerpt: A 45-year-old Penang mother with a paid-off home asks whether to start investing, and where. Sean says it depends on her ambition and appetite for risk, and that units with several ways to let are safest.

question.asker: From Q, a viewer who wrote in by email
question.context: Q, 45, lives in Penang, is married with two children, has no loans and her home is fully paid; she is in the top 20% income group and already has fixed deposits, shares, unit trusts and ETFs. Agents have pitched her units under RM600,000 in Kuala Lumpur, including a 300 sq ft studio near KLCC aimed at short stays. The Klang Valley seems to offer better yields and more choice, but she doesn't know the area and worries about managing a property from afar.
question.text: Should she buy investment property at her age rather than other investments, and is the Klang Valley or Penang the better choice?

answer.quote: The more options I have for a particular property, the more confidence I have.
answer.summary: Only if she wants to grow more for her family and can stomach the risk; if she is already comfortable, she doesn't need to. At 45 her loans will be shorter, so rent rarely covers the instalment and she should expect to put more cash down. The Klang Valley offers more, but only if she is willing to travel and manage it, and she should favour units that can be let in several ways.

reasons.title: Shorter loans change the maths
reasons.body: Banks lend until about 65 to 70, so she would get around 20 years rather than 35, and residential rents rarely cover such instalments. Many older investors simply borrow 30% to 50% and pay the rest in cash.

reasons.title: Her paid-off home is a safety net
reasons.body: It can be refinanced in an emergency, which lets her take a little more risk. The questions are her ambition, how much loss she could bear, and whether she enjoys property enough to research it.

reasons.title: Rents follow jobs
reasons.body: Penang homes are expensive and mostly owner-occupied, so rents are low, except in Batu Kawan, where new factories have drawn workers. The Klang Valley still draws graduates from across Malaysia, keeping rents higher.

reasons.title: Several ways to let protect you
reasons.body: A unit that suits families, working couples, short stays and room-by-room letting has fallbacks if one market fails. A 300 sq ft studio at about RM2,000 per sq ft relies on short stays, and its long-term rent and resale are harder.

actions: Decide whether you need more wealth or are content, and how much of a price fall you could live with.
If you buy, plan to put down enough cash that the shorter loan stays comfortable.
View about 20 properties, including subsales in person, before choosing.
Prefer units that can be let long-term, furnished for medium stays, short-term or by the room.
Furnish the unit well; few owners in a building do, and it widens your choice of tenants.
articles.caveat: If travelling to manage a Klang Valley unit would be a burden, Sean suggests other investments, or studying Batu Kawan closer to home. He mentions a project he booked through FAR Capital, a property investment club he is a VIP member of.
articles.sourceNote: Summarised from Sean's full English captions for Asking Sean #209. The quoted line is verbatim; everything else is paraphrased. Figures are as the viewer and Sean stated them in April 2023. The episode was sponsored by Dreame, an unrelated vacuum cleaner brand; Sean also points viewers to FAR Capital, a property investment club he is a VIP member of.

articles.title: I'm over 60. Should I still invest in property?
articles.excerpt: A reader over 60 is being offered short-stay units promising 9% returns. Sean explains why property loses its main advantage at that age, and what to consider instead.

question.asker: From Bernadette, a viewer who wrote in by email
question.context: Bernadette is over 60. People keep telling her fixed deposits are pointless and EPF returns may disappoint, and she has been shown developer-run short-stay projects in Bukit Bintang and KLCC advertised at 9.2% to 9.6% returns.
question.text: Should she invest in property at her age? Should she pay cash or borrow, buy new or subsale, and are these short-stay projects worth it?

answer.quote: A bit too late for real estate? Personally, I think so.
answer.summary: Probably not as a main plan. Property's big advantage is decades of cheap borrowing that tenants help repay, and at 60 that is mostly gone. Low-risk options paying a similar return, without the hassle or locked-up money, suit her better.

reasons.title: The leverage advantage is mostly gone
reasons.body: Banks usually cap loans around age 70, so the tenure is short. A RM500,000 loan at 4% costs about RM5,000 a month over 10 years against about RM2,200 over 35. Almost no RM500,000 unit rents for RM5,000.

reasons.title: Property locks your money up
reasons.body: Selling takes about four to five months for freehold and seven to eight for leasehold, which needs state consent. That is a problem if you suddenly need money for health or an emergency.

reasons.title: Other assets pay similar returns more easily
reasons.body: RM500,000 in fixed deposits at about 3% pays roughly RM1,250 a month; a property yielding 6% pays about RM2,500 but needs tenants, agents and upkeep. EPF has paid around 6%, and some Malaysian dividend stocks have paid more, with the freedom to sell part at any time.

reasons.title: Advertised short-stay returns rarely last
reasons.body: High returns usually hold only for the first years. Once a building proves profitable, more owners convert and a price war follows: in one Bukit Bintang project, nightly rates fell from about RM300 to RM120. Only investors buy such units, and authorities can ban short stays, as Singapore and Penang have.

actions: First decide whether this money is spare or what you will live on. If you depend on it, keep it liquid.
Compare any property yield with fixed deposits, EPF and dividend income before buying.
If you still earn and do buy for investment, Sean would borrow rather than pay cash, keeping cash for medical costs, with mortgage insurance so no debt passes to your family.
If you already own a short-stay unit, plan to sell while it is still profitable, typically within five years.
Be wary of returns quoted by the people selling the unit; get independent advice.
articles.caveat: For someone over 60 with spare capital, experience and other income, property can still work; Sean knows seasoned investors buying offices and land in cash at that age. For younger readers the lesson runs the other way: two or three paid-off properties by 60 can fund a comfortable retirement.
articles.sourceNote: Summarised from Sean's full English captions for Asking Sean #289. The quoted answer is verbatim; everything else is paraphrased. Rates and returns are as stated in July 2025 and will have changed.

articles.title: How is buying property in the UK different from Malaysia?
articles.excerpt: Many Malaysians and Singaporeans buy in UK cities for their children's education and to diversify. After a study trip to Manchester, Sean compares supply, certainty, building design, planning and loans.

question.context: Malaysian and Singaporean investors increasingly look at UK cities such as Manchester, drawn by a shared language and common-law system and, for Singaporeans, by strict rules at home. Sean recorded this after a study trip to Manchester.
question.text: What are the main differences between investing in UK property and Malaysian property?

answer.quote: make informed decisions and take calculated risk
answer.summary: The UK has a housing shortage, so tenants compete for units, and announcements and data are reliable. Malaysia has an oversupply, policies can change overnight, and buyers must verify everything themselves. UK loans are also approved closer to completion and weigh the property's rent, not just the buyer's income.

reasons.title: Shortage against oversupply
reasons.body: A Malaysian who bought in Manchester asked for £1,200 a month and, after tenants bid against each other, got about £1,400. In Bukit Jalil alone, about seven new projects launched in one month.

reasons.title: Plans happen there
reasons.body: UK marketing claims must cite sources, and announced stations and regeneration projects are delivered. In Malaysia, announcements such as changes to foreign-buyer thresholds have been reversed before taking effect, so check sites yourself.

reasons.title: Design follows pedestrians, not cars
reasons.body: Malaysian high-rises are designed around car access and standard facilities set by the housing ministry. UK projects are designed pedestrian-first, with parking sold separately and facilities such as co-working spaces offered as selling points.

reasons.title: Zoning and loans work differently
reasons.body: UK cities are divided into clear zones, which makes price comparison easy. Loans are applied for six to nine months before completion, and the expected rent helps qualify the loan.

actions: Compare a project's price with others in the same city zone.
Check that announced infrastructure is funded and scheduled.
Prepare for the UK loan process early, ideally with a partner on the ground.
Budget for parking separately in UK projects.
Treat a sponsor's projections as marketing until you verify them.
articles.caveat: This video was sponsored by a UK developer marketing a Manchester project; its projected yield and growth figures are left out here. Singapore's tight rules make it unsuitable for most investors, in Sean's view.
articles.sourceNote: Summarised from Sean's full English captions for this August 2023 video, which was sponsored by Select Property, a UK developer, and opens with an advertisement for its Manchester project. The general comparison is kept and the project pitch is left out. The quoted line is verbatim; everything else is paraphrased.

articles.title: First investment: a co-living unit near Johor's RTS, or a KL condo?
articles.excerpt: A 35-year-old in Johor Bahru with a RM1.1 million budget weighs a seven-room co-living unit near the RTS against a Mont Kiara condo. Sean warns about Johor's hype, and explains why he would buy a completed unit first.

question.asker: From Peter, a viewer who wrote in by email
question.context: Peter is 35, married and lives and works in Johor Bahru; his wife earns Singapore dollars. He has no loans and some shares but little cash, after past financial setbacks that are now settled. With a budget of up to RM1.1 million for his first property, he is weighing a unit near the RTS Link at about RM700 per sq ft, partitioned into seven rooms and earning about RM5,500 gross, against a resale unit in a Mont Kiara condo at about RM920 per sq ft, and two projects offered through a bulk-purchase club.
question.text: Which should he buy, and how should a unit in a prime area be priced to rent well without undercutting himself?

answer.quote: entry price is the most important
answer.summary: Be wary of Johor's current hype and of any unit that only works partitioned into rooms. Sean would buy a completed unit with proven rents first, compare its yield and upfront cash with the Mont Kiara unit, and buy an under-construction one only once the first is rented.

reasons.title: Johor buyers are paying a premium
reasons.body: Over the past two years almost no resale transactions in Johor exceeded about RM800 per sq ft, yet new launches near the RTS sell at about RM1,300. Buying at the top of the last boom left owners bleeding for eight to twelve years.

reasons.title: One rental strategy is a risk
reasons.body: Kuala Lumpur banned splitting units into more rooms, and Penang restricted Airbnb; if Johor did the same, a seven-room co-living unit would lose its rent. Sean prefers units that can rent long-term, short-term or by room.

reasons.title: Completed units build a portfolio faster
reasons.body: A completed unit can be rented within months; six months of rent with a stamped tenancy and SPA counts as income for the next loan. A new launch ties up that loan slot for three or four years.

reasons.title: Furnishing wins top rents
reasons.body: Sean gets above-average rent in Mont Kiara by furnishing fully, spreading the cost over many tenancies rather than expecting one lease to repay it.

actions: Check the area's median transacted price per sq ft before paying a launch premium.
Prefer a completed unit with existing rental data for your first purchase.
Compare yield, upfront cash and growth potential side by side for each option.
Invest where you can manage the unit, or budget for a property manager.
Keep four to six months of rent in reserve for each property.
articles.caveat: Sean sees Iskandar Puteri (Medini) projects with high yields at current prices, so Johor is not ruled out; the warning is against paying launch prices driven by the RTS story.
articles.sourceNote: Summarised from Sean's full English captions for Asking Sean #262. The quoted line is verbatim; everything else is paraphrased. Figures are as stated in September 2024. Sean is a client of FAR Capital, not its owner, and appears in its Battle Royale research series; he says he is part of the team at The Makeover Guys, a renovation company, and his units are managed by its arm Cozy Homes. He also endorses financing at a higher SPA price than the asking price, which is left out here.
