articles.title: My ex and I own a house together. Should we sell or rent it out?
articles.excerpt: A couple bought a Puncak Alam home in joint names, then broke up badly. Selling now costs him about RM16,000; she wants to rent it out for five years. Sean says take the loss and move on.

question.asker: From Mr G, a viewer who wrote in by email
question.context: Mr G and his then-girlfriend bought a home in Puncak Alam in joint names for own stay, with an SPA price of about RM738,000 after discounts. They have since broken up on bad terms. The unit is now worth about RM650,000 against a loan balance of about RM656,000, so selling means covering a RM6,000 shortfall and about RM10,000 in legal fees. She wants to rent it out unfurnished for about RM1,500 to RM1,700 and sell in five years; he wants to sell now and is considering legal action to exit.
question.text: From an investment point of view, is selling now the right choice?

answer.quote: Own it. Own the mistake and move on.
answer.summary: Sell. Holding might work out better on paper, but not for him: two people who can't talk will fight over tenants and costs for years. About RM16,000 is a fair price for a clean slate, even if he pays her share as a farewell gift.

reasons.title: Numbers won't settle a feud
reasons.body: Both are accountants, but a spreadsheet won't persuade an ex who wants him out of her life. Each will expect the other to deal with tenants while the rent is split equally, and every conversation will start with blame.

reasons.title: He made the choices
reasons.body: They paid above nearby prices because it was a dream home, and the slow-growing location was there from the start. Accepting that the property and the partner were his choices is the quickest way out of the trouble.

reasons.title: Discounts were money from the future
reasons.body: A heavy discount lets you buy without the 18% in cash a subsale needs, but it means paying more than the market's price. Making that back over three to five years, as his friend in an earlier phase has, is a normal result, not a failure.

reasons.title: Unfurnished units rent cheaply
reasons.body: An empty unit only attracts tenants with very low rent. Owners who plan from the start to spend RM70,000 to RM80,000 furnishing it can rent for more, and the furnishing serves tenant after tenant, but that has to be planned before the keys, not after.

actions: Get quotes from lawyers for the sale costs and budget the shortfall to the bank.
Sell, even if you end up covering the full RM16,000 yourself.
Never buy a home in joint names with a boyfriend or girlfriend; if you must buy together, put it in one name.
If a couple can't afford a home in one name, rent, and each buy a unit of RM400,000 to RM500,000 whose rent covers the instalment.
If you buy to rent out, plan and save for furnishing before key collection.
articles.caveat: There is no RPGT to pay when selling below the SPA price. And to investors, Sean notes, sellers in this position are where good deals come from, which is why he always knows how much he can borrow.
articles.sourceNote: Summarised from Sean's full English captions for Asking Sean #297. The quoted answer is verbatim; everything else is paraphrased. Figures are as stated in September 2025. Sean mentions he works with The Makeover Guys, a furnishing company, on his own unit.

articles.title: Beyond the facade: how do I judge a building's design before buying?
articles.excerpt: Buyers judge a building by its facade and its pool, but Sean, trained as an architect, looks at access, density, corridors and what is next door. He explains what each says about a project.

question.context: Developers market projects through their facade, sky pools and fancy facilities. Sean, who trained in architecture, argues that the design that matters to residents runs from town planning down to the corridor outside their door.
question.text: Which aspects of a building's design should affect a buying decision?

answer.quote: it's way more than just facade
answer.summary: Look beyond the facade and facilities, which are mostly marketing. Compare how you actually reach the building, the density, the lift-to-unit ratio, the corridor width and layout, and what sits on the plot next door. Unit layouts in a price range are similar because they follow the same efficiency formula.

reasons.title: Being next to a big road isn't access
reasons.body: Traffic flows from highways to primary, secondary and local roads, so a project beside a major road may be reached only after several junctions. A rail line matters only if the station is near.

reasons.title: Rules shape what gets built
reasons.body: Density limits based on unit numbers push developers to build bigger units, which is one reason condos gave way to serviced apartments in mixed developments.

reasons.title: Corridors reveal the budget
reasons.body: Developers can't sell corridors, so they squeeze them. Some are about 1.2 metres; luxury projects allow about 2.25 metres, wide enough for two wheelchairs. Double-loaded corridors, with units on both sides, are more efficient but busier.

reasons.title: Facilities cost money to carry
reasons.body: A rooftop pool adds structural cost; one on the car park podium is cheaper. Ask whether a feature shaped like an 8 or a Jacuzzi would actually change your decision. The share of glass on a facade is a better sign of how premium a project is.

actions: Trace the route from the main road to the project entrance.
Compare unit size, lift-to-unit ratio, units per floor and total units between projects.
Measure corridor widths and check whether they are single- or double-loaded.
Ask what is planned for the next plot: a cemetery, substation or water tank won't be mentioned.
Check how the residential entrance is separated from shops and offices in mixed developments.
articles.caveat: Sean notes that striking architecture does not guarantee resale value: some award-winning towers have not done well on the subsale market.
articles.sourceNote: Summarised from Sean's full English captions for this November 2019 video. Sean trained as an architect. The quoted line is verbatim; everything else is paraphrased.

articles.title: Should I buy a RM1 million landed house for my parents to live in?
articles.excerpt: A Malaysian working in Singapore wants to buy her renting parents a landed home in Cheras. Sean explains why landed rents are so low, how to judge a renovated house, and a cheaper option first.

question.asker: From Miss R, a viewer who wrote in by email
question.context: Miss R is in her mid-30s and works in Singapore. Her parents rent a house in the Cheras area and didn't like the condos they viewed, so she raised her budget for a landed house from RM800,000 to about RM1 million. Renovated houses ask around RM1 million while unrenovated ones nearby sell for RM800,000 to RM900,000, and similar houses rent for only about RM2,000 a month, less than half her expected instalment.
question.text: Is such a low rent normal for landed homes, and should she pay a premium for a renovated house, renovate an old one herself, or keep looking?

answer.quote: I don't think that renting is all that bad.
answer.summary: Yes, it is normal: a RM1 million landed house on a 90% loan costs about RM4,000 a month, while it rents for about RM2,000. Sean would first try to secure her parents' current rental with the landlord. If she still buys, choose between renovated and unrenovated by the bank's valuation and the cash she has left for works.

reasons.title: Landed homes rarely pay for themselves
reasons.body: Rent on a landed house is often barely half the instalment, which is why Sean favours high-rise units whose rent covers the loan. His one exception is a house near Johor's Second Link, where rent from cross-border workers almost covers the instalment.

reasons.title: Renting's only real risk can be managed
reasons.body: The setback of renting is the owner selling and asking the tenants to leave, so older people lose their neighbours and routines. A longer lease, and a written promise that the landlord offers them the house first if he sells, deals with most of that.

reasons.title: Banks value the house, not your renovation
reasons.body: A renovated house is worth the premium only if the bank values it near the asking price, so the loan covers it. Valuers count only legal structural extensions, usually for about three years. If a RM800,000 house values at RM850,000, the extra room helps pay for her own works.

reasons.title: Count the full cash before the keys
reasons.body: On a RM1 million house, about 18% up front for the down payment, stamp duty and legal fees, plus about RM200,000 of renovation, comes to roughly RM380,000. Renovating an old landed house from Singapore can also take three to six months.

actions: Ask her parents' landlord for a longer lease, a slightly lower rent, and first refusal in writing if the house is sold.
Use the money she saves to buy an investment unit whose rent covers its instalment.
If she buys, ask the agent for the bank's valuation of each house before deciding.
Budget the renovation separately from the loan she qualifies for.
Decide what will happen to the house later, including whether she may want to settle in Singapore.
articles.caveat: Landed houses are one of a kind, so if her parents fall in love with one house and she has the capital, paying for it can still make sense. Sean also notes that many older people don't want to move, which argues for keeping them where they are.
articles.sourceNote: Summarised from Sean's full English captions for Asking Sean #207. The quoted line is verbatim; everything else is paraphrased. Figures are as the viewer and Sean stated them in March 2023. Sean mentions he owns a landed house near Johor's Second Link whose rent almost covers its instalment.

articles.title: We're in our 50s. Should we sell our house and buy a new landed home for semi-retirement?
articles.excerpt: A couple in their early 50s want a double-storey home outside KL for semi-retirement and their parents, but fear new projects after one was abandoned. Sean backs the plan and says time your readiness, not the market.

question.asker: From Mrs I, a viewer who wrote in by email
question.context: Mrs I and her husband are in their early 50s, both work for multinationals and save about RM5,000 a month after expenses. They own a condo in Desa Petaling and a single-storey house in Kuala Lumpur, both paid off; their first property, 20 years ago, was abandoned for nine years before another developer finished it. In three years, once the children finish school, they plan to sell the single-storey house and buy a double-storey home of RM750,000 to RM880,000 in areas such as Semenyih, Salak Tinggi or Cyberjaya, also housing his parents.
question.text: Is this a sensible semi-retirement plan, are new projects safe, and should they buy new now or subsale later, given a friend says it's a bad time to buy?

answer.quote: Any time is the right time to buy.
answer.summary: Yes, if they can afford it: their 40s and 50s are when most people can finally choose a home for themselves rather than for work or school. Since they know the area, a subsale lets them see the exact house and negotiate; for new projects, today's laws make abandonment rarer. Don't wait for the right market, buy below the area's median price when you are ready.

reasons.title: A dream home fits this stage of life
reasons.body: Earlier, where you live is set by work and the children's schools. With the children nearly grown, they know what lifestyle they want and can afford, and selling a small single-storey house to fund a larger home elsewhere is a sensible trade.

reasons.title: Age shortens the loan
reasons.body: Banks lend until 65 or 70, so an RM800,000 house on a shorter loan may cost about RM3,000 a month. Make sure they are comfortable with that, plus renovation, before committing.

reasons.title: Abandoned projects are rarer, but costly
reasons.body: Since the Housing Development Act was strengthened, abandoned projects are less common. If it happens, buyers still repay the loan and interest on money the bank already released, so listed developers offer more certainty, at higher prices.

reasons.title: Timing the market is a guess
reasons.body: Ask whether the person saying it's a bad time owns property themselves. Every area has a median price; buying below it is good timing, buying far above it, as many did in Iskandar Malaysia, is the real risk.

actions: Stay in each shortlisted area a few times, for example in a homestay, before choosing.
Compare subsale houses in the same estates; you see the exact unit and can negotiate.
Check the area's median price per square foot and avoid paying well above it.
If a landed strata project limits changes to the façade, make sure that suits your renovation plans.
Decide whether this is purely a home or partly an investment, since that changes what you compare.
articles.caveat: Whether the area suits them for daily life is something only they can judge. Sean also suggests they consider their hometown, which may give more value and keep them closer to family.
articles.sourceNote: Summarised from Sean's full English captions for Asking Sean #215. The quoted line is verbatim; everything else is paraphrased. Figures are as the viewer and Sean stated them in July 2023. The captions garble the shortlisted project names, so they are left out.

articles.title: Zero-lot bungalow, link semi-D, guarded estate: what am I buying?
articles.excerpt: Developers' names for landed homes can blur what you're getting. Sean explains zero-lot bungalows and link semi-Ds, what you can and can't do on individual title, and how strata estates are run.

question.context: After a first video on landed home types, viewers asked Sean what terms like zero-lot bungalow and link semi-D actually mean, and how individual-title and strata landed homes differ in daily life.
question.text: What do common landed home labels mean, and how do individual-title and strata estates differ in practice?

answer.quote: these are just languages of developers
answer.summary: A zero-lot bungalow is a semi-D with the pair pulled apart, and a link semi-D is a terrace house shaped to look like a semi-D. On individual title you own the land but can't close public roads, and renovations need council approval; on strata, a management body runs the estate and can enforce maintenance fees.

reasons.title: Names can oversell
reasons.body: A zero-lot bungalow has one side built on the boundary with no windows or doors, so only three sides open. A link semi-D is a link house with staggered fronts and small gaps that make it look semi-detached.

reasons.title: Individual title has public roads
reasons.body: The council maintains roads, lamps and drains, so residents can't simply gate them. They can register a residents' association, apply for a guarding licence, and collect fees, though some neighbours never pay.

reasons.title: Renovations still need approval
reasons.body: Building by-laws limit how far you extend to the front and back for fire safety. The council can fine owners, or order an unapproved extension torn down.

reasons.title: Strata estates are run by owners
reasons.body: A joint management body with the developer hands over to an owners' management committee. Under the Strata Management Act, owners who don't pay maintenance fees can face legal action.

actions: Ask exactly how many sides of a 'bungalow' have openings.
Check whether an estate's guarding is by a residents' association or a strata body.
Get council approval before extending an individual-title home.
For strata, confirm the development is registered as strata and use a licensed managing agent.
Join the management committee or attend its meetings.
articles.caveat: Sean says foreigners can't buy individual-title landed homes, but rules for foreign buyers vary by state and price threshold; check the current ones.
articles.sourceNote: Summarised from Sean's English captions for this May 2018 follow-up to his first landed typology video. The quoted line is verbatim; everything else is paraphrased.

articles.title: We swapped landed living for a 2,200 sq ft condo. Is a big apartment a better family home?
articles.excerpt: A mother who left multi-storey landed homes for a five-room condo near Sungai Long is delighted. Sean compares large apartments with terrace houses, and explains how to read price per sq ft.

question.asker: From W, a viewer who wrote in by email
question.context: W lived in landed homes in Cheras for 40 years, first her parents' three-storey house and then her in-laws' two-storey one, which were hot under the roof and kept her children upstairs and apart. In 2020 she bought a 2,200 sq ft condo at about RM335 per sq ft, with five rooms, five bathrooms and an extended terrace facing a golf course near Sungai Long. She is delighted with the space, the breeze and having no stairs.
question.text: How does a large apartment compare with a landed house as a family home?

answer.quote: What we want is daylight; what we don't want is sunlight.
answer.summary: For many families a large apartment lives better than a terrace house: one level, no stairs, cooler rooms and facilities for the children, at a price close to a comparable terrace in the city. Landed homes still win on parking right at the door, freedom to renovate and, so far, capital growth.

reasons.title: Compare price per square foot like for like
reasons.body: Bigger units always have a lower price per square foot, which is why developers quote the largest unit's figure. Compare new with new and similar sizes, such as 2,000 to 2,500 sq ft units with each other, before judging a price.

reasons.title: One level suits young children and ageing knees
reasons.body: In a three-storey house the staircase takes about 18% to 20% of the built-up area, and families end up split between floors. A single level makes night feeds, keeping an eye on children and getting older much easier.

reasons.title: Orientation decides how hot it gets
reasons.body: Walls facing the evening sun soak up heat and release it at night. Sean wants daylight, not direct sun, so he prefers east over west when those are the only choices; terrace houses with roofs fully exposed are usually hotter than flats.

reasons.title: Renovation and growth differ
reasons.body: Condos can't be structurally changed, so a renovation budget goes further. Landed houses still lead capital growth in NAPIC data, though large units in Kuala Lumpur rent well; Sean says a large Mont Kiara unit furnished by The Makeover Guys rents for RM13,000 to RM15,000.

actions: Compare a unit's price per square foot only with units of similar size and age nearby.
Picture daily routines, such as groceries, children and older parents, in both a condo and a landed home before choosing.
Check which way the main rooms and balcony face; avoid units that take the full evening sun.
Budget for the condo's higher maintenance fee against a landed home's irregular upkeep, such as painting and gates.
Plan ahead: a large condo can be rented out when the children leave and you downsize.
articles.caveat: Landed living is easier when you go to and from the car often, and remains Sean's pick for capital growth. His view that large apartments may become the better investment is a hypothesis he hasn't proven.
articles.sourceNote: Summarised from Sean's full English captions for Asking Sean #245. The quoted line is verbatim; everything else is paraphrased. Prices are as Sean stated them in March 2024. The episode was sponsored by The Makeover Guys, a renovation company Sean works with; he says he also rents one of their furnished units.

articles.title: My developer delivered late. What can I claim, and from when?
articles.excerpt: A court case ruled that late-delivery damages run from the booking date, not the SPA date. Sean explains how LAD works, how buyers can claim, and what ending booking fees could mean for buyers and developers.

question.context: A buyer disputed how a developer calculated late-delivery damages, took it to the tribunal and then to court, and won: the delay was counted from the date of booking rather than the date the SPA was signed. Reports also said booking fees would be prohibited altogether.
question.text: What are liquidated damages for late delivery, how can a buyer claim them, and what changes if booking fees go?

answer.quote: you must definitely read through that document
answer.summary: If a developer hands over late, the standard SPA for new homes entitles you to liquidated ascertained damages calculated daily, and the homebuyer tribunal is open to any buyer without a lawyer. Sean sympathises with the buyer, but warns that banning booking fees could raise the cash needed to buy and squeeze out smaller developers.

reasons.title: Delivery periods are set in the SPA
reasons.body: Individual-title houses typically have 24 months to complete, and strata properties usually 36 months or longer as approved. A delay costs the buyer rent and loan interest at the same time, which is what the damages compensate.

reasons.title: The tribunal needs evidence, not taste
reasons.body: Any buyer can file a claim, but complaints about quality must be backed by a registered contractor or professional, not personal preference. New-home SPAs are standardised; subsale agreements differ, so read yours.

reasons.title: Booking fees let buyers in with little cash
reasons.body: Without bookings, every buyer would need a 3% deposit and the rest of 10% within about 21 days, as in a subsale. Banks may also lend only on the price net of discounts, adding to the cash needed.

reasons.title: Investors prefer well-sold projects
reasons.body: Developers gauge interest through bookings before launching. A project that sells out has its construction funded by buyers' loans and leaves no unsold stock competing with owners for tenants and buyers.

actions: Read your SPA's delivery date and damages clause before signing.
Keep your booking receipt and dates, which may count towards a delay.
If the developer refuses a fair claim, file with the homebuyer tribunal.
Get a registered professional's report for any quality complaint.
Favour projects that have sold well when buying to invest.
articles.caveat: This reflects the ruling and reports as Sean understood them in January 2021; rules on booking fees and how damages are counted should be checked with a lawyer today.
articles.sourceNote: Summarised from Sean's full English captions for this January 2021 video, recorded after a court decision on how late delivery is counted. The quoted line is verbatim; everything else is paraphrased.

articles.title: With RM70,000 at 25, should I start a business or buy property first?
articles.excerpt: A 25-year-old with RM70,000 saved wants to escape the rat race, either with a self-service laundry or rental properties. Sean says start the business first: property keeps you rich rather than making you rich.

question.asker: From C, a viewer who wrote in by email
question.context: C is 25, lives with his parents, earns a little over RM3,000 a month and has about RM70,000 in savings. He wants to escape the rat race, either by opening a self-service laundry or by building rental properties, and hopes to reach RM5,000 to RM6,000 a month from rent. He fears a failed business would send him back to a job, while buying property would leave no money for the business.
question.text: Should he start the business or the property investment first, and how many rental units would it take to live off rent?

answer.quote: Real estate don't really make you rich, real estate keeps you rich.
answer.summary: Start the business first, carefully and if possible while keeping his job. At 25 with no commitments he can afford to fail, and running a business teaches him far more than a salary does. Once the business makes money, buy properties whose rent covers the instalment, and use them to store that wealth.

reasons.title: Living off rent takes many units and years
reasons.body: A unit with a surplus of RM500 a month after its instalment is already a good one, so RM5,000 to RM6,000 would take about ten such units bought years ago, with the risk that some sit empty.

reasons.title: Positive cash flow comes from time or crafted deals
reasons.body: Sean's Puchong apartment, bought for about RM300,000, only broke even for its first three to five years before rents rose. Otherwise, the deals come from motivated sellers known through specialist agents, or from buying in bulk for a developer discount.

reasons.title: A business teaches what a job can't
reasons.body: Customers, capital and operating costs, hiring, company registration, accounts and the rent versus footfall of a location are all lessons for later wealth. If it fails at 25, he can simply go back to work.

reasons.title: Property compounds quietly
reasons.body: After ten years his tenants had paid his Puchong loan below RM300,000 while the unit was worth about RM400,000, so he could refinance and buy again. Repeating that builds two or three paid-off units by about 60.

actions: Plan the laundry business carefully, with costs, location and footfall, and don't spend all RM70,000 at once.
Keep his job while the business is starting, if he can.
Once the business earns money, buy properties whose current rent covers the instalment.
Expect each unit to give a modest surplus, and let tenants build the equity over time.
Read up on the cash flow quadrant idea of employees, self-employed, business owners and investors.
articles.caveat: Rents rarely jump, so a unit's surplus stays modest unless it is improved. Sean chose a corporate career and property in his early 20s himself, so the right order depends on the path you want.
articles.sourceNote: Summarised from Sean's full English captions for Asking Sean #193. The quoted line is verbatim; everything else is paraphrased. Figures are as the viewer and Sean stated them in December 2022.

articles.title: Is a leasehold condo with 60-odd years left too risky to buy?
articles.excerpt: A couple love a leasehold condo but worry it will be hard to sell with 60 to 70 years left on the lease. Sean says the lease is the smaller risk; buying together unmarried is the bigger one.

question.asker: From K, a viewer who wrote in by email
question.context: K and their girlfriend are from Penang, work in Selangor and earn RM15,000 a month between them, with only a RM700 car loan. They rent for RM1,280 a month and love a leasehold condo in Damansara Damai, built in 2006, for its space, quiet and reasonable price. They may move back to Penang or upgrade around 2036, when the lease would have roughly 60 to 70 years left.
question.text: Will a condo with 60 to 70 years left on its lease be hard to sell, even at the price they paid?

answer.quote: My concern is you buying with her as boyfriend, girlfriend.
answer.summary: The lease isn't the real risk. If the rent covers the instalment, they can always rent the unit out and wait, so they can buy if they like it. What worries Sean is buying jointly without an agreement.

reasons.title: Lease renewals can lift prices
reasons.body: Sean cites a Penang condo near Queensbay whose lease, with 30-odd years left, was renewed to 99 years for a fee of about RM1,000 to RM2,000 per owner; a local property expert told him prices nearly doubled. He sees little reason for a state to refuse to renew land under people's homes.

reasons.title: Freehold isn't absolute either
reasons.body: The government can compulsorily acquire any land, freehold included, for public works, and pays compensation based on market value. Freehold is now rare enough to sell at a premium, and this condo is reasonably priced partly because it is leasehold.

reasons.title: The real exit risk is financing
reasons.body: Once around 60 years are left, Sean says banks may not lend to the next buyer, which shrinks the pool you can sell to. That is why the rental market matters more than the title.

reasons.title: Here the rent covers the loan
reasons.body: Four-bedroom units were listed at about RM450,000 to RM460,000. A RM400,000 loan over 35 years at 4% costs about RM1,800 a month, and similar units rent for around RM2,000. If they need to leave, they can rent it out rather than sell.

actions: Check the rent for the same unit type: if it covers the instalment, your exit is settled even if selling becomes hard.
If you will need the sale money to upgrade, plan to sell sooner, around ten years in, rather than waiting until the lease is shorter.
If you buy as an unmarried couple, agree in writing first who can cash out and whether a buy-over is at market or SPA price.
Consider buying in one name: each of you keeps two 90% loan slots, while a joint purchase leaves you three between you.
Visit a few units before committing.
articles.caveat: If freehold is available at the same price, Sean would still choose it. His answer also relies on the rent covering the instalment; where it doesn't, the leasehold exit problem is real.
articles.sourceNote: Summarised from Sean's full English captions for Asking Sean #234. The quoted answer is verbatim; everything else is paraphrased. Prices and rents are as Sean checked them in December 2023. Parts of the automatic captions are unclear, so only clearly stated figures are included.

articles.title: What can I learn from Sean's worst property deal?
articles.excerpt: Sean bought a semi-D in Johor Bahru when everyone seemed to be making money there, and was still paying for it a year after handover. He sums up the four mistakes he made.

question.context: About three years before this video, when everyone seemed to be making money in Johor Bahru, Sean booked a semi-D there. A year after vacant possession he was still holding it and paying the instalments, and young viewers were asking him whether to stretch for property beyond their means.
question.text: What went wrong in Sean's worst deal, and how can a buyer avoid the same mistakes?

answer.quote: not all real estate deals you make money
answer.summary: Sean names four mistakes: buying on emotion when the numbers didn't work, overcommitting until instalments took about 94% to 95% of his income, assuming the developer's name didn't matter, and letting the bad deal weigh on him instead of looking for solutions.

reasons.title: Emotion over figures
reasons.body: The design and renderings were beautiful and the market was hot, so he bought although his calculations didn't make sense.

reasons.title: Overcommitting
reasons.body: With instalments taking about 94% to 95% of his income, he was financially crippled for a time. That only works if you can live on very little.

reasons.title: The developer matters
reasons.body: Established developers tend to stand behind their projects and their after-sales service; the one he bought from did not serve him well after the purchase.

reasons.title: Dwelling on it doesn't help
reasons.body: He let the mistake drag on him for a while before realising the only way out is to look for solutions rather than at the problem.

actions: Run the numbers, and walk away if they don't work, however much you like the design.
Keep the instalment well within your income, with room to live.
Check the developer's track record and after-sales service.
Calculate the downside before buying in a hot market.
If a deal goes wrong, focus on solutions, such as selling or renting, rather than the loss.
articles.caveat: Sean shares this to encourage young buyers rather than scare them: he says the worst outcome wasn't as frightening as he feared, and the lessons made him a better investor.
articles.sourceNote: Summarised from Sean's English captions for this October 2017 video about a semi-D he bought in Johor Bahru. The quoted line is verbatim; everything else is paraphrased.

articles.title: I just got my keys. How do I let out the unit?
articles.excerpt: After the keys come four decisions: how long to let for, what rent to ask, how far to furnish, and who will manage tenants. Sean's checklist for new landlords.

question.context: New investors often struggle after handover: finding and filtering tenants, setting rent and managing turnovers, while the instalment keeps coming every month and the unit sits empty.
question.text: What should a new owner decide before letting out a unit?

answer.quote: there's no such thing as passive income
answer.summary: Settle four things: the tenancy length, the rent the market will bear, how much to furnish, and who will market and manage the unit. Spend a little to stand out, because a new project hands over hundreds of units at once, all chasing the same tenants.

reasons.title: Short or long stays
reasons.body: Short stays usually earn more, but checking guests in and out and cleaning between them is like running a hotel. Long tenancies can be set as 2+1, two years at a fixed rent with an option for one more.

reasons.title: The market sets the rent
reasons.body: Find out what similar units actually rent for from agents and the property portals before deciding what to ask.

reasons.title: Furnish to stand out
reasons.body: Letting a bare unit cheaply or furnishing well both have a cost. The aim is the minimum spend that makes tenants consider your unit first.

reasons.title: Someone has to manage it
reasons.body: Between tenants, someone must clean, inspect and check that utility bills are paid. Agents handle long lets; short-stay operators can run a unit for a share of the profit.

actions: Decide on short stays or a long tenancy, and the length, such as 2+1.
Check the going rent for similar units before you list.
Furnish just enough to rank among the first units tenants consider.
Choose who lists and manages the unit: yourself, an agent or an operator.
Arrange cleaning and a utilities check for each change of tenant.
articles.caveat: Short-stay letting may be restricted by your building's rules or local regulations; check before choosing it.
articles.sourceNote: Summarised from Sean's English captions for this January 2018 vlog, his first sponsored video, made with a company that lets units to corporate clients and filmed in one of its units. The quoted line is verbatim; everything else is paraphrased.

video.title: 4 Things to Know to Let Out Your Unit | Vlog 006

articles.title: Why do strata buildings run down, and what can owners do about it?
articles.excerpt: Most of us will end up living in strata property, yet few owners understand how a building is run. Sean talks to David Foo, whose firm serves about 500 neighbourhoods, about fees, committees and upkeep.

question.context: More and more Malaysians live in strata property, or in landed areas run by residents' associations, where a joint management body or management corporation collects fees and maintains common areas. Committees are volunteers with little training, and many buildings decline as fees fall short. Sean's guest, David Foo, co-founded a company providing management apps and accounting to about 500 neighbourhoods.
question.text: What makes some strata buildings well kept while others run down, and what can owners and committees do?

by.name: David Foo
by.role: co-founder of Jaga Solution, a company that provides management software to residential communities

answer.quote: it's like a marriage you need to manage
answer.summary: A strata building is run like a company: owners are shareholders, the committee is the board and the building manager is the chief executive. Buildings decline when collection lags behind rising costs and committees try to save rather than maintain. Pay on time, attend AGMs, and expect the committee to set targets and use numbers.

reasons.title: Collection can never exceed 100%
reasons.body: Guards, cleaners and managers cost more every year, but fees collected can't exceed what is billed. When committees settle for 85%, they end up cutting guards and cleaners until the building visibly declines.

reasons.title: Low fees at launch store up trouble
reasons.body: Developers set low maintenance fees to sell units while adding costly features such as fountains. After handover, committees must raise fees or remove features, and owners resist both.

reasons.title: Maintain, don't hoard
reasons.body: A management body is not meant to make a profit; money collected should be spent keeping the building in shape, with preventive maintenance rather than fixing things only once they break.

reasons.title: People make the difference
reasons.body: Price level matters less than residents who treat the place as home. One well-run building in Bangsar keeps spare tiles in the same colour to replace any that crack.

actions: Pay maintenance fees in full and on time.
Attend AGMs, or at least read the accounts and proposals.
If you serve on a committee, set targets for the building manager and supervise rather than do the work yourself.
Compare your building's costs and staffing with similar buildings before cutting services.
Budget for upkeep on an individual-title house too, since nobody else will fix the roof.
articles.caveat: David notes that buyers in managed buildings still need to understand basics, such as who should fix a leak from the unit above, which nobody is taught.
articles.sourceNote: Summarised from the full English captions of this October 2021 episode of Sean's My First Property podcast. The views and quoted line are those of the guest, David Foo, whose company sells management software to residential communities; Sean says a cousin of his works there. Everything except the quote is paraphrased.

articles.title: Salaried, on commission or self-employed: what trips up a loan?
articles.excerpt: Banks judge your income by how you earn it. Rena Choong explains where employees, commission earners and business owners go wrong, and which records to prepare months ahead.

question.context: Banks look at income differently depending on how you earn it. In the fourth episode of his mortgage series, Sean asks Rena Choong where salaried employees, commission earners and business owners most often go wrong when they apply.
question.text: What mistakes get housing loans rejected for employees, commission earners and the self-employed, and how should each prepare?

by.name: Rena Choong
by.role: head of mortgage at FAR Capital

answer.quote: First of all, know which one is your income segment.
answer.summary: Know which income group you are in, because each is judged on different records: payslips and EPF for employees, commission statements and tax returns for agents, and company accounts and bank statements for business owners. Prepare them months before you buy, and never dress your income up.

reasons.title: Employees: the documents must match
reasons.body: The salary credited to your account should match your payslip, EPF should be paid, and you should be past probation; contracts shorter than six months are hard to finance. A sudden pay rise of around 50% needs a letter explaining it, and banks may call or email HR to check your job.

reasons.title: Bonuses count for less than basic pay
reasons.body: Some banks ignore performance bonuses or count about half, often only from multinationals and only after two years of history. A higher basic salary helps a loan more than a large bonus.

reasons.title: Commission earners need tax returns
reasons.body: Banks want six months of commission statements plus your latest tax return, so new agents who haven't filed one struggle. If income swings by more than about 30% from month to month, some banks count only half of the six-month average.

reasons.title: Business owners are judged by the company
reasons.body: Most banks want the company registered for at least two years, a busy bank account, month-end balances that aren't too low (Rena treats under RM50,000 as low), and invoices for large one-off credits. Declaring losses to cut tax shows up in CTOS and works against you.

actions: Keep a monthly file of payslips, bank statements and tax returns, so you can apply when a good deal appears.
If you are employed, wait until you are confirmed, and get a letter from HR for any big salary increase.
If you earn commission or run a business, file and pay tax on your full income for at least the last year or two.
If your income is complicated, ask a mortgage adviser who knows which banks favour your profile.
Never use arranged employment or inflated payslips to qualify; Rena and Sean call it fraud.
articles.caveat: Bank policies vary widely, especially for side income and mixed earnings, and these are 2022 practices. Income from investments or trading counts only once it is declared for tax, so declare it before you apply.
articles.sourceNote: Summarised from Sean's full English captions for episode 4 of his mortgage series with Rena Choong, FAR Capital's head of mortgage (October 2022). The quoted answer is Rena's own words; everything else is paraphrased. Bank practices are as described in 2022. Sean is a customer of FAR Capital, which offers mortgage advice, not its owner.

video.title: COMMON MISTAKES MADE DURING LOAN APPLICATION (EP4)

articles.title: Should I use tricks to qualify for a bigger housing loan?
articles.excerpt: Young buyers write to Sean bleeding thousands a month on units they qualified for with fake payslips or recycled rent. He explains the tricks, why a rejection is a warning, and how the loss can follow you after selling.

question.context: Sean received many emails from buyers in their early 30s who cannot keep up with instalments. Some had qualified for loans through so-called loan restructurers: employers issuing payslips for higher salaries, owners withdrawing their own money and paying it back in as fake rent, or turning card debt into instalment plans to lower their monthly commitments.
question.text: Is it worth using these tricks to get a housing loan approved?

answer.quote: there's a difference between investment and taking a risk like gambling
answer.summary: No. A rejection means your income cannot carry the commitment for 30 to 35 years. Everyone in the sale earns their cut once you sign, but if the rent doesn't cover the loan, you alone carry the shortfall, and selling may still leave you owing the bank.

reasons.title: The bank's rule exists for a reason
reasons.body: Roughly a third of net income is treated as affordable for a housing loan, because you still need to live, eat and drive. On RM6,000 net, that is about RM2,000 a month, enough for a property of around RM400,000.

reasons.title: Everyone else is paid at signing
reasons.body: Agents, developers and loan arrangers earn when the SPA is signed. If you later can't pay, none of them is obliged to help; nobody forced you to sign.

reasons.title: Selling may not clear the loan
reasons.body: Discounts and rebates mean the SPA price, and your loan, can be well above what the unit fetches after handover. If you must sell below what you owe, you have to find the difference in cash.

reasons.title: Holidays on instalments add up
reasons.body: Car loans, student loans and card debt converted to monthly plans all reduce what you can borrow, and should be cleared honestly rather than hidden.

actions: Treat a loan rejection as a sign to cut debts or raise income, not to find a workaround.
Never submit inflated payslips or manufactured rental deposits.
Check that rent will cover the instalment before you buy to invest.
Work out what you would still owe if you had to sell at today's market price.
Ask yourself whether you need the property now, or only want to be seen owning one.
articles.caveat: Restructuring debts to qualify is not wrong in itself if you genuinely can afford the property; the danger is borrowing beyond what your real income supports.
articles.sourceNote: Summarised from Sean's full English captions for this April 2020 video. The quoted line is verbatim; everything else is paraphrased. Some figures in his worked example were unclear in the captions and are left out.

video.title: DON'T CHEAT FOR A BANK LOAN YOU CANNOT AFFORD TO PAY BACK

articles.title: Is "location, location, location" still the rule?
articles.excerpt: A young investor has shortlisted Bangsar South by its rental demand. Sean argues that location is not what makes you money; the price you pay against the area median is.

question.asker: From An anonymous viewer who wrote in by email
question.context: The reader is 26, works for a multinational in Johor and takes home about RM9,500 a month. He already owns a PJ serviced apartment whose RM2,200 rent nearly covers its RM2,300 instalment, plus RM150,000 in US stocks and RM50,000 in spare cash. He has shortlisted Bangsar South for its rental demand and compared units on tenure, age, size, furnishing, distance to the LRT and price per square foot.
question.text: Is "location, location, location" still the rule? Should he pay more for a newer project or buy an older subsale, and could he fund it with a 36-month interest-free credit card plan?

answer.quote: That's just a very cool way to say things in a lazy manner.
answer.summary: Location matters less than people think. Most KL areas will end up with the same amenities, so your profit is decided by your entry price: buy below the area's median price.

reasons.title: Entry price decides profit, not the postcode
reasons.body: In time, every KL location gets a mall, schools, a hospital and parks. What separates a good buy is paying below the local median. Sean would rather buy in Rawang at RM480 per sq ft where the median is RM600 than in KL Sentral at RM800 where the median is RM700.

reasons.title: High rent follows temporary demand
reasons.body: Strong rents come from people posted somewhere for two or three years, so job hubs such as Mont Kiara, KL Sentral, KLCC and Bangsar South do well, with Cheras, Subang and Bukit Jalil rising. In purely residential areas, long-term residents would rather buy than pay rent above an instalment, so yields are lower.

reasons.title: New costs more but ages better
reasons.body: Malaysian building and strata rules mean an old apartment's layout cannot be changed. Newer projects have brighter rooms, better ventilation and corridors, so they tend to appreciate more, while older ones usually yield more. Decide which you are buying for.

reasons.title: A subsale starts earning sooner
reasons.body: With cash on hand, a completed subsale lets you negotiate on price and collect rent within about nine months of signing. A new launch ties up one of your loan slots for three to four years before it earns anything.

actions: Check every shortlisted unit's price per sq ft against the area median, and only buy below it.
Decide whether you want rental yield or capital growth before choosing between an older subsale and a newer project.
Skip the interest-free credit card plan if you can pay cash. Sean would take the safe route rather than leave no room for error.
Visit the buildings in person; a spreadsheet cannot show you what a project is really like.
Avoid low-cost flats bought purely for yield. Sean will not buy social housing meant for people in need.
articles.caveat: Sean holds any unit whose rent covers its instalment for the full 30 years, while others prefer to sell after seven or eight years, once yields fall from about 7% to 5.5%. Both can work. Sean also mentions buying through FAR Capital, a deal-sourcing service he pays to use, for readers short on research time.
articles.sourceNote: Summarised from Sean's full English captions for Asking Sean #239. The quoted answer is verbatim; everything else is paraphrased. Prices per square foot are Sean's illustrations from February 2024. Sean is a paying member of FAR Capital, not its owner.

video.title: ASKING SEAN #239 | "LOCATION LOCATION LOCATION" STILL VALID?

articles.title: My first property lost value and I hate living there. Should I buy another?
articles.excerpt: A buyer whose Setapak condo fell in value, with a short-stay unit also bought, is shortlisting a third project. Sean says stop buying, rent out the condo and fix how you choose properties first.

question.asker: From KF, a viewer who wrote in by email
question.context: KF bought a subsale condo in Setapak for RM510,000, using most of his savings, and it is now worth about RM400,000 to RM450,000; the rent wouldn't cover the loan without partitions. Last year he also bought into a project near KLCC meant for short-stay rentals. Construction noise from a new development opposite drove him out of the Setapak condo to a family member's home, and he is now choosing between three new projects near train lines.
question.text: Which new project should he buy, should he stay with family or move out, and should he rent out or sell the Setapak unit?

answer.quote: Buying the property is not the solution.
answer.summary: Stop buying for now. Rent out the Setapak unit so the tenant pays much of the instalment, stay with family or rent elsewhere, and decide whether to sell once the project opposite is finished and priced. Before any third purchase, fix the way he picks properties: check median prices and real rents first, and settle on one clear intent.

reasons.title: Property doesn't always make money
reasons.body: Even a subsale bought at the wrong price can lose value. Not buying only means missing a chance to make money, while buying wrongly can wipe out years of savings.

reasons.title: Check the numbers before, not after
reasons.body: Compare the price with the area's median price per square foot, and look up what tenants actually pay nearby before buying, not after. Sean is happy if rent covers about 90% of an investment's instalment, or 85% for a home you may later rent out.

reasons.title: Wanting everything means no clear intent
reasons.body: Near a train line, easy to rent, good for short stays and good to live in: that list is every goal at once. A third residential loan is also capped at 70%, so the next purchase needs a much larger down payment.

reasons.title: Short-stay buildings need an exit plan
reasons.body: Sean prefers units that can be let several ways. Short-stay rules can change, as in Penang, hotel-style buildings have lost money before, and the only buyer later is another investor.

actions: Rent out the Setapak unit rather than leaving it empty, and furnish it well enough to attract tenants.
If you stay with family, pay them a fair rent or share the bills, or rent a place of your own.
Wait until the project opposite is finished, compare its prices with yours, then decide whether to sell.
Before buying again, check each project's median price per square foot and real rents nearby.
Decide whether your next home is to live in or to invest, and judge projects against that one intent.
articles.caveat: Construction noise is part of development and is usually limited to permitted hours, so Sean doesn't blame the developer. If the project opposite sells for more than his unit, holding on may be the better choice.
articles.sourceNote: Summarised from Sean's full English captions for Asking Sean #253. The quoted line is verbatim; everything else is paraphrased. Figures are as the viewer stated them in June 2024. The episode was sponsored by PropertyGuru's Brickz home report, a paid transaction report Sean says he uses; median prices can also be checked free on its website.

video.title: ASKING SEAN #253 | GET OUT OF THAT VICTIM MINDSET

articles.title: I'm a civil servant. How should I use my LPPSA housing loan?
articles.excerpt: Civil servants can borrow from LPPSA on top of the usual bank loans. Rena Choong explains why the order you use them in matters, and the catches in LPPSA's terms.

question.context: Civil servants can borrow from LPPSA, the government's housing loan scheme for public-sector staff, on top of the bank loans everyone else uses. In the fifth episode of his mortgage series, Sean asks Rena Choong how it works and when to use it.
question.text: How does an LPPSA loan differ from a bank loan, and when should a civil servant use it?

by.name: Rena Choong
by.role: head of mortgage at FAR Capital

answer.quote: Please don't use it for your first and second.
answer.summary: Use your two 90% bank loans first and keep LPPSA, which can finance 100%, for the third property. LPPSA repayments come off your payslip, so using it first lowers the net income banks see and leaves your next bank loan at 70%.

reasons.title: The order changes your margins
reasons.body: LPPSA doesn't appear in CCRIS, but its deduction shows on your payslip, and banks count it. Banks give 90% on your first two residential loans; use LPPSA first and your third property needs a 70% bank loan, whereas two bank loans first leave LPPSA's 100% for the third.

reasons.title: A fixed 4% over a very long term
reasons.body: LPPSA charges a fixed 4%, close to banks' best rates of 3.7% to 3.8% at the time, and for those on the pension scheme it can run to age 90, against 70 or 75 at banks. But takaful cover is compulsory for the whole term, which becomes expensive if you borrow after about 45.

reasons.title: Full instalments start after two years
reasons.body: On a property under construction, LPPSA deductions begin about 24 months after you borrow, and from then you pay the full instalment even if the building isn't finished. A bank charges only progressive interest on what it has released, so a long or delayed project costs more under LPPSA.

reasons.title: LPPSA has its own limits
reasons.body: The maximum LPPSA loan is RM750,000 including takaful, and valuations by the government valuer tend to be conservative. If you leave government service, you must refinance with a commercial bank, and banks often don't recognise a civil servant's side income.

actions: Check how much you can borrow with LPPSA's own online calculator, which works from a fixed table by gross income.
Take your first two residential properties with bank loans, and save LPPSA for the third.
Prefer completed properties or short builds when using LPPSA, since full instalments start after 24 months.
Apply online and submit the physical documents yourself, or pay a runner to handle them.
Send loan documents only through a company's official channels, never to a personal email address, and guard your IC number.
articles.caveat: This only suits civil servants whose income comfortably covers several loans and whose properties earn rent; Sean warns against borrowing more just because the facility exists. Rates and limits are as stated in November 2022.
articles.sourceNote: Summarised from Sean's full English captions for episode 5 of his mortgage series with Rena Choong, FAR Capital's head of mortgage (November 2022). The quoted answer is Rena's own words; everything else is paraphrased. LPPSA rates and limits are as stated in 2022, so check LPPSA's current terms. Sean is a customer of FAR Capital, not its owner.

articles.title: We're getting married and planning kids. How do we keep building our property portfolio?
articles.excerpt: An engaged couple with three properties between them want three each. Sean says use the one 90% loan slot left, then pause and budget for the wedding, the birth and childcare.

question.asker: From Mr K, a viewer who wrote in by email
question.context: Mr K, 32, earns RM6,000 a month and has bought a RM500,000 home near PJ for his own use, due in early 2026, with a RM2,000 instalment. He also owns a unit worth about RM150,000, rented at RM700 against a RM300 instalment. His fiancée, 31, earns RM9,000 and has a RM380,000 unit due in mid 2025 that she plans to rent out. They have saved about RM150,000, plan a small wedding this year and hope for one or two children.
question.text: What would Sean do in their shoes, starting a family while wanting three properties each?

answer.quote: Focus on your wife's second 90% slot first, then call it a day.
answer.summary: They are already well placed with three properties. Use her remaining 90% loan slot, consider selling the RM150,000 unit that ties up one of his, and then pause buying for three to five years while they budget for the wedding, the birth and childcare and invest in their health, knowledge and insurance.

reasons.title: Three properties, one every decade
reasons.body: Sean's goal for every Malaysian is three properties by retirement: one to live in, one to sell for living costs and one for emergencies or a child's education. Buying one around 30, 40 and 50 is enough, and the first is usually paid off by 60.

reasons.title: A cheap unit wastes a 90% slot
reasons.body: Each person gets only two loans at a 90% margin. Holding a RM150,000 unit on one of them blocks a larger purchase his income could support, though there's no rush to sell.

reasons.title: A baby costs more than you expect
reasons.body: Sean's son's delivery in a private hospital cost about RM15,000 to RM18,000, confinement centres charge about RM13,000 to RM15,000 a month and premium ones RM20,000 or more, and daycare costs him about RM1,800 a month.

reasons.title: Small monthly savings rebuild a down payment
reasons.body: Putting aside RM1,000 a month builds RM48,000 in four years, enough for a down payment. Their portfolio can run on its own while the children are young, and they can buy again once they are at school.

actions: Budget RM30,000 to RM40,000 for her unit's handover fees and renovation, and check whether the MOT is included in the sales package.
Agree a wedding budget early; Sean suggests a simple wedding and more travel before the baby arrives.
Budget for the birth, confinement and childcare at the higher end first; cheaper options are a choice you can make later.
Use her second 90% loan slot carefully, then pause buying for three to five years.
Save a fixed sum each month, and invest in your health, your knowledge and enough insurance for both breadwinners.
articles.caveat: These are Sean's own family's costs and choices, and parents or in-laws who can help with childcare cut the budget a lot. Whether the RM150,000 unit should go depends on what they would buy with the freed slot.
articles.sourceNote: Summarised from Sean's full English captions for Asking Sean #238. The quoted line is verbatim; everything else is paraphrased. Figures are as the viewer and Sean stated them in January 2024, and the baby costs are Sean's own experience. Sean works with The Makeover Guys, the renovation company the viewer mentions.

articles.title: My unit has no strata title yet. Does it matter?
articles.excerpt: A high-rise unit still under the master title can be harder to sell and finance. Sean explains what a strata title proves, and what to ask about parcels and share units.

question.asker: From a viewer hunting for his first property
question.context: He found a high-rise unit whose strata title had yet to be issued, so it was still under the master title. Each plot of land has one title; when a developer builds, say, 300 units on it, each unit should later get its own strata title.
question.text: What does it mean when a unit is still under the master title, and can it still be sold?

answer.quote: Yes, but you need the consent of the land owner.
answer.summary: It means you can't yet prove ownership of your own unit. You can still sell it, but only with the consent of the land owner, usually the developer, which adds a hurdle for buyers and banks. A strata title removes it.

reasons.title: The title is the unit's birth certificate
reasons.body: A strata title proves which unit in which block is yours. Without it, banks find it harder to establish the owner, which complicates financing and sales. Sean expects units with strata titles to fetch slightly higher prices because the paperwork is easier.

reasons.title: A missing title may be delay or bad news
reasons.body: It may simply be in progress, since issuing titles takes time and newer strata rules push developers to issue them soon after handover. But it can also mean the developer won't follow through or has gone bankrupt.

reasons.title: Ownership gives you a vote
reasons.body: Strata owners take part in the joint management body or management corporation, which sets maintenance fees and may not make a profit. Votes are weighted by share units, increasingly used instead of floor area.

reasons.title: Parcels decide what you pay for
reasons.body: A strata unit has a main parcel, the unit itself, and accessory parcels such as a car park or air-conditioner ledge. Common property like the pool serves everyone, while mixed developments may have limited common property for offices or residents only. All of this shapes maintenance fees.

actions: Before buying a completed high-rise unit, ask whether its strata title has been issued.
If not, ask why and how long the developer expects it to take, and how it gives consent for a sale.
Ask what your accessory parcels include, such as car parks and air-conditioner ledges.
Ask how share units are calculated, since they set your voting weight and maintenance share.
articles.caveat: This applies to high-rise and other stratified developments; a landed house on its own individual title is a different case. A unit still waiting for its strata title soon after completion is normal; the concern is when it never arrives.
articles.sourceNote: Summarised from Sean's full English captions for this July 2018 episode. The quoted answer is verbatim; everything else is paraphrased. The captions are unclear in places, so only clearly stated points are included. Strata rules have changed since 2018, so check the current position with your lawyer.

articles.title: Between jobs at 27, should I move into my parents' empty apartment?
articles.excerpt: A 27-year-old quit his job to retrain for tech and wants to live alone in his parents' empty Puchong apartment. Sean supports the move, with rent and a deadline, and explains why having no loan gave him this freedom.

question.asker: From Sam, a viewer who wrote in by email
question.context: Sam is 27 and left a sales job in the motor industry paying RM5,500 plus commission to retrain for the tech industry. He lives with his parents in USJ and gives them RM1,500 a month. The family also owns a 960 sq ft, three-plus-one-bedroom apartment in Puchong, empty since a dispute with a tenant who damaged it; similar bare units rent for about RM1,300.
question.text: Is it wise to move into the Puchong apartment, furnish it on a budget while he looks for a remote job, and rent it out later once he is settled?

answer.quote: I am supportive of you moving in
answer.summary: Yes, move in, but agree it with his parents as a tenancy: treat his RM1,500 as rent, pay the maintenance and bills himself, furnish it on a budget, and set a deadline of one year plus one to land a job in tech. Sean would not have quit his job to retrain, though.

reasons.title: Living alone teaches the real costs
reasons.body: Paying for electricity, water, sewerage, maintenance and groceries yourself shows how much the family home was covering, and adds the urgency that living at home lacks.

reasons.title: Retrain while still employed
reasons.body: Sean would have studied on evenings, weekends and public holidays while keeping the salary, or moved into sales at a tech company first. Quitting is a luxury that living with family makes possible.

reasons.title: No commitments is a freedom
reasons.body: Without a loan to service, Sam can take a pay cut to change careers. That is why Sean tells young people not to rush into property: an instalment runs for up to 35 years, rain or shine, and property keeps you rich rather than making you rich.

reasons.title: Do the renovation yourself
reasons.body: Sean's own furnishing service, The Makeover Guys, suits people with no time or design sense. With time on his hands, Sam can source furniture online and manage the trades himself, and might find a side business in it.

actions: Propose to your parents that your monthly contribution becomes rent, with a one-year-plus-one tenancy.
Pay the maintenance fees, utilities and furnishing costs yourself.
Set a date to go back to your old industry if you have not found a job in the new one.
Look for an entry-level role at a tech company rather than studying full-time.
Before buying any property, have a six-month emergency fund, insurance and a clear career.
articles.caveat: This works because the apartment is already paid for and the family does not need the rent. If they rely on rental income, or the unit has a loan, the arrangement needs a real market rent.
articles.sourceNote: Summarised from Sean's full English captions for Asking Sean #277. The quoted answer is verbatim; everything else is paraphrased. Figures are as stated in March 2025. Sean mentions The Makeover Guys, a renovation company he works with, and recommends a cheaper route for this viewer.

articles.title: The rent won't cover the instalment by RM600 a month. Should I still buy?
articles.excerpt: A Malaysian working in New Zealand is weighing a resale unit near an MRT station that needs a RM500 to RM600 monthly top-up, and family tips on gold. Sean says move on and look further.

question.asker: From K, a viewer who wrote in by email
question.context: K works in New Zealand, where mortgage rates are 7% to 8%, and takes home about RM12,000 a month. A condo in Taman Desa is rented out and covers its repayment, and K plans to settle its remaining RM69,000 loan within months. K is considering a resale unit of about RM467,000 near an MRT station in Kuala Lumpur, with a 10% rebate, but nearby rents suggest a RM500 to RM600 monthly top-up. Family members say gold is the better buy right now.
question.text: Should K buy gold instead, take the resale unit, or look at high-density projects around Sunway Velocity?

answer.quote: Why must you settle for a project that cannot make money?
answer.summary: Don't commit to a unit you already know will cost you RM500 to RM600 a month; keep looking until you find one where the rent covers the instalment. As for gold, check whether the people recommending it have the results you want, and invest in what you understand.

reasons.title: Judge the advice by the adviser
reasons.body: Tips from relatives are often second-hand, from a short video or a sales commission. Sean puts his money in property because he knows it well, and sees the asset you understand best as the safest one.

reasons.title: There are always other projects
reasons.body: Buyers often fix on one development, then blame the developer or the market when it doesn't pay. Sean says view 20 projects of different types, ages and areas and move on from any that can't make money.

reasons.title: Developers sell at the recommended retail price
reasons.body: Investors try to buy below it: through subsale, where the owner's urgency gives room to negotiate; auctions, which can carry caveats, title problems or unpaid maintenance; or bulk purchase deals.

reasons.title: Settling a covered loan may waste cash
reasons.body: The Taman Desa rent already covers its instalment, so paying off the last RM69,000 may not be the best use of the money; it could fund another unit where the rent covers the loan. Sean couldn't judge this fully without knowing K's age.

actions: Ask whoever recommends gold or any other investment whether they have invested in it themselves and got the results you want.
Drop any unit whose rent won't cover the instalment, however close it is to a station.
View around 20 projects of different types and locations before choosing.
Compare subsale, auction and bulk purchase prices against the developer's price.
Before settling a loan the rent already covers, compare that with using the cash as a down payment elsewhere.
articles.caveat: Sean sees no legal problem with a unit resold after the first buyer's SPA was cancelled. Auctions are harder to manage from overseas, so he wouldn't suggest them for K.
articles.sourceNote: Summarised from Sean's full English captions for Asking Sean #233. The quoted line is verbatim; everything else is paraphrased. Figures are as the viewer stated them in December 2023; rates vary between countries and over time.

articles.title: A baby is coming. Move in, or rent out our first home?
articles.excerpt: A couple bought a new condo as their first home, but their first child arrives as it is handed over. Sean explains why he would rent it out and stay with family for now.

question.asker: From JC, a viewer who wrote in by email
question.context: JC, 32, and his wife are expecting their first child in May 2027. They take home about RM15,000 a month, have more than six months of emergency funds and around RM100,000 invested. In 2023 they bought a River Park unit in Bangsar South for about RM700,000, roughly RM900 per sq ft, at RM3,000 a month, as their first home. Handover has slipped into 2027, and they live with his parents in Kepong.
question.text: With a baby coming, should they stay with his parents, rent the unit out and live elsewhere, or move in as planned despite the renovation noise from 1,300 new neighbours?

answer.quote: Just keep it as an investment unit.
answer.summary: Stay with family for the first year or two and rent River Park out from handover. Treat it as an investment, and move somewhere that suits the baby later, renting if you need to.

reasons.title: A newborn needs hands more than space
reasons.body: The first six months mean broken sleep. Grandparents nearby give parents a few hours' break and can step in for daycare pickups. Sean moved out of his in-laws' home only when his son was about a year old.

reasons.title: The unit works better as a rental
reasons.body: To Sean, River Park looks more like an investment property than a family home. With the entry price on the high side, it needs rent of about RM3,300 (the RM3,000 instalment plus about RM300 maintenance) to break even, and the coming MRT3 station could lift rents.

reasons.title: 1,300 new units is less of a threat than it looks
reasons.body: Some 8,000 to 10,000 units are coming to the surrounding areas over five years. The way to compete is to be the best unit: Sean estimates only about 5% of owners spend RM50,000 to RM60,000 furnishing a rental properly.

reasons.title: Moving in now means a year of drilling
reasons.body: In a new block, most owners renovate in the first year, so the corridor noise is constant. That is a hard start for a newborn.

actions: Count the completion date from your sale agreement, not the agent's promises; delay compensation runs from your own signing date.
Furnish the unit well enough to stand out and attract the best-paying tenant.
Keep about six months of instalments in reserve for this unit.
Sort out life insurance and mortgage insurance now; Sean finds MRTA the simplest if you might lose track of separate policies.
Do not rush the next purchase; Sean would not buy again in the first three years of parenthood.
articles.caveat: If living with parents strains things once the baby arrives, renting a place near work or daycare is a reasonable next step while the unit stays rented. When you eventually sell, check the gains tax rules for that year; Sean notes residential property held over five years from signing generally pays none, but rules change with each Budget.
articles.sourceNote: Summarised from Sean's full English captions for Asking Sean #322. The quoted answer is verbatim; everything else is paraphrased. Figures are as stated in September 2026.

articles.title: My Rumawip home has left me drowning in debt. Rent it or go to AKPK?
articles.excerpt: A buyer's Rumawip unit has been handed over just as credit card and personal loan debts outrun his income, and he has no money to furnish it. Sean sets out three steps to stay out of bankruptcy.

question.asker: From Mr Lee, a viewer who wrote in by email
question.context: Mr Lee has a permanent job, but his credit card, personal loan and housing loan payments now exceed his income. His Rumawip unit in Kuala Lumpur has just been handed over, partly furnished with no furniture, and he cannot afford to fit it out or move in. His CCRIS record is still clean, but he expects to start missing payments within months.
question.text: Should he rent the unit out, or put all his debts through AKPK, the debt management agency, to avoid bankruptcy?

answer.quote: the only cure for anxiety is action
answer.summary: Rent the unit out and stay where he lived before. Use what credit he has left, or a friendly loan from his parents, to furnish it just enough to let. Go to AKPK only if he cannot keep up, and cut spending and add income straight away, because the cause is overspending, not the property.

reasons.title: Owning a home has three costs
reasons.body: The down payment, the monthly instalment and the cost of furnishing. Buyers of new launches often forget the third, and that raises in the years before handover rarely keep up with living costs.

reasons.title: Rent can carry the unit
reasons.body: Sean expects a Rumawip unit like this to rent for at least its instalment, roughly RM1,800 against RM2,000. A tenant's two-plus-one months' deposit also buys a few months' breathing room.

reasons.title: Debt for income is different
reasons.body: Borrowing on a zero-interest instalment plan to furnish a unit that then earns rent is not the same as borrowing for gadgets or clothes. If furnishing everything is too much, he can rent out the bigger rooms and live in the smallest.

reasons.title: AKPK is not bankruptcy
reasons.body: AKPK consolidates card and personal loan debts into one repayment and stops new credit. Missing payments instead leads to warnings, notices and, within about six months to a year, auction; bankruptcy can even cost a job, since you cannot hold a bank account.

actions: Move back to your previous home and put the unit up for rent.
Furnish only what a tenant needs, using zero-interest instalments, second-hand pieces or a loan from your parents.
Sell belongings you haven't used in three months, and downsize spending everywhere you can.
Take on part-time work at weekends and holidays to raise income quickly.
Before buying a home, set aside the would-be instalment each month to test whether you can carry it.
articles.caveat: Sean is not a licensed financial planner and had no figures for the debts, so the steps are general. Rumawip units carry a five-year moratorium on resale, which is why selling is not an option here.
articles.sourceNote: Summarised from Sean's full English captions for Asking Sean #274. The quoted line is verbatim; everything else is paraphrased. Figures are as stated in February 2025. The episode is sponsored by The Makeover Guys, a renovation company Sean mentions as offering instalment plans.

articles.title: Should you buy new from a developer or a subsale?
articles.excerpt: A new launch and a subsale unit can cost the same on paper but ask for very different cash, time and risk. Sean explains who each one suits.

question.context: A new launch from a developer and a subsale unit from an existing owner can carry similar prices, yet they demand very different amounts of cash, waiting time and risk. Many buyers choose on price alone.
question.text: Should you buy new from a developer, or a subsale unit?

answer.quote: I can immediately start renting out.
answer.summary: It depends on your cash and experience. Investors with capital should favour a subsale, where you can see the real condition and rent from day one. First-time buyers short on cash are better served by a new launch.

reasons.title: A new launch needs far less cash upfront
reasons.body: Developer packages and rebates can let you in with 1 to 2% in cash: about RM8,000 on an RM800,000 unit. Sean estimates a RM600,000 subsale needs around RM80,000, covering a 10% deposit plus your own lawyer, valuer, stamp duty and transfer costs.

reasons.title: Developers handle the paperwork
reasons.body: A developer lines up the bankers, lawyers, valuers and approvals for you. For a first-time buyer unfamiliar with the process, that convenience matters; a subsale means coordinating it all yourself.

reasons.title: With a subsale, what you see is what you get
reasons.body: You can see the actual condition, the neighbours, the schools and the train station that already exists. A new launch is sold on plans, and facilities marked "proposed" may arrive late or not at all.

reasons.title: A subsale earns rent straight away
reasons.body: New launches take about two years to complete for landed homes and three to five for large high-rises. A big project can also hand over thousands of units at once, all competing for the same tenants.

actions: Start from your intent and your cash: limited cash and a first purchase point to a new launch; capital and experience point to a subsale.
With a new launch, separate what is approved from what is only "proposed" in the brochure.
With a subsale, check current rents and condition, and budget about 10% plus fees in cash.
If you need somewhere to live soon, choose a completed unit; a new launch may take years.
In a large new project, consider how many units will hit the rental market at handover.
articles.caveat: This is a 2017 episode, so treat the cash figures as illustrations: developer packages vary, so get what is offered in writing. If you already own a home and can wait, a new launch can still suit an investor willing to hold through construction.
articles.sourceNote: Summarised from Sean's English captions for this August 2017 episode. The quoted answer is verbatim; everything else is paraphrased. Parts of the older automatic captions are unclear, so only clearly stated points are included.
