articles.title: Is a student-rental unit near Sunway a good investment?
articles.excerpt: A 30-year-old is eyeing a USJ 1 project built for room-by-room student rentals, linked by BRT to the Sunway universities. Sean thinks it can work, but warns that only another investor will ever buy it from you.

question.asker: From J, a viewer who wrote in by email
question.context: J is 30, married, earns RM7,000 a month and owns his own home in PJ, with only a RM700 car loan. He is looking at a new project in USJ 1, due in late 2028, designed for students reaching the Sunway-area universities by BRT. A 689 sq ft two-bedroom-plus-study unit of about RM480,000 to RM516,000, split into four rooms, is projected to rent for about RM4,800 a month against an instalment of about RM2,200.
question.text: Are student investment properties around Sunway sound, what are the risks, does furnishing matter, and should he pay a company to manage the rooms?

answer.quote: In conclusion, I think this is fine.
answer.summary: It can work. Sunway's universities and schools aren't likely to move, which removes the biggest risk, and the agent's figures aren't unrealistic. The real risk is the exit: a unit built only for students can be sold only to investors, and only while its numbers still add up.

reasons.title: A campus moving out is the main risk
reasons.body: Student areas suffer when a college relocates, as happened around one Cheras campus and to some extent SS15. In Bandar Sunway the university, schools and Taylor's lakeside campus are fixtures, and rents depend on how wealthy the students are, so results differ from one university town to another.

reasons.title: Only investors will buy it from you
reasons.body: Own-stay areas rise because people pay more to live there. A student or short-stay unit is bought only on its rent, so once wear and tear drags rents below the instalment, nobody will pay you more for it. The first five years feel great; by year seven, decide whether to exit.

reasons.title: Students wear buildings out
reasons.body: Young tenants use the lifts and facilities hard and care less than owners. Sean expects maintenance to slip after the first few years unless owners stay active in the joint management body or management corporation.

reasons.title: Furnishing is expected, and costs more
reasons.body: Students won't buy their own beds or fridges, so each room needs a bed, wardrobe, desk, curtains, air-conditioning and its own lock. Four bedroom sets cost more than a normal layout; furnishing a unit now costs RM38,000 to RM50,000, so freebies like air-conditioners and a kitchen cabinet are worth RM12,000 to RM15,000.

actions: Check the agent's projected room rents yourself on co-living and rental sites.
Visit nearby student areas to see how such buildings look after a few years.
Weigh the furnishing package in the sale, since it is covered by the loan.
Pay a management company 5% to 10% of the rent if your time is worth more than handling repairs and tenants yourself.
Plan when to exit while the rent still clearly covers the instalment.
articles.caveat: Sean once said he would only invest in a unit he would live in himself, but he has dropped that rule: data on what tenants actually pay matters more than his own taste. Tighter student visa policies abroad and at home could still change demand.
articles.sourceNote: Summarised from Sean's full English captions for Asking Sean #294. The quoted answer is verbatim; everything else is paraphrased. Rents and prices are the agent's projections as Sean read them in August 2025. Sean works with The Makeover Guys, a furnishing company he mentions in the episode, and says he is not selling this project.

articles.title: I'm 20 and earn RM3,500. How should I prepare for property?
articles.excerpt: A 20-year-old accounting student running his own social media agency wants to start investing after graduating. Sean says to hold off and build the business first.

question.asker: From V, a viewer who wrote in by email
question.context: V is 20, a full-time second-year accounting student who runs a social media agency and does freelance videography, earning about RM3,500 a month. He has been learning about property since school. By graduating in mid-2027 he aims to earn RM5,000 a month from the agency and have at least RM10,000 in savings to start with.
question.text: What should he do over the next few years to prepare for his first property?

answer.quote: I would suggest to not prioritize property investment first.
answer.summary: Don't make property the priority yet. While the business is young, flexibility and active income come first; property keeps you rich rather than makes you rich, so scale the agency and diversify once it earns well.

reasons.title: The business will out-earn any investment
reasons.body: Sean expects a media business to make more over the next ten years than any investment. Once V pays himself about RM5,000 a month and the company makes RM50,000 to RM100,000 a year, he can start diversifying.

reasons.title: Property ties up money
reasons.body: Property cannot be sold quickly when you need cash, the opposite of the flexibility a young business owner needs.

reasons.title: RM10,000 is not enough
reasons.body: Sean's test is to have, when you collect the keys, RM50,000 to furnish the unit plus six months of instalments, about RM63,500 for a RM500,000 unit, besides a six-month emergency fund, a medical card and a clear career path. At 22 he put all RM30,000 of his savings into a down payment, then found a subsale purchase needs about 17% to 18% in cash.

reasons.title: Expecting fast money is the classic mistake
reasons.body: Audit anyone giving advice by whether they live the life you want. Fake gurus work on ignorance and greed, and genuine investors rarely broadcast their wins, so physical community events are the place to meet them.

actions: Put your energy into scaling the agency: decide between sole proprietorship and Sdn Bhd, plan your hiring and use AI.
Keep your lifestyle well below your income as it grows.
Build savings towards a six-month emergency fund, then RM50,000 plus six months of instalments for your first unit.
Get medical insurance so you never become a burden on your family.
Join physical investor events to find a community, and judge advisers by the lives they lead.
articles.caveat: Sean bought young because his corporate career was in property development, where it fitted his path. Once the business is established and pays V a stable income, property becomes the natural next step.
articles.sourceNote: Summarised from Sean's full English captions for Asking Sean #302. The quoted answer is verbatim; everything else is paraphrased. Figures are as stated in November 2025.

video.title: ASKING SEAN #302 | PROPERTY INVESTMENT SHOULDN’T BE YOUR PRIORITY

articles.title: Is a partitioned student rental near a university a good first investment?
articles.excerpt: A 23-year-old freelancer wants a RM590,000 subsale let room by room to students, then a home. Sean likes the 7% yield, warns about partitions and exit, and says buy a second investment before a home.

question.asker: From A, a viewer who wrote in by email
question.context: A is 23, earns about RM20,000 a month freelancing and has RM200,000 saved. A plans to buy a RM590,000 subsale unit within walking distance of a university, already partitioned and let to students, expecting about RM3,500 a month in rent against a RM2,450 instalment plus about RM1,000 for maintenance, Wi-Fi and utilities. A also wants a RM500,000 to RM800,000 home in Ara Damansara or Kota Damansara within the same year.
question.text: Is the student unit a good investment, and is buying a second property for own use in the same year too fast?

answer.quote: I think you are on the right track, bro.
answer.summary: Yes: about RM42,000 a year in rent on RM590,000 is a 7.1% yield, well above fixed deposits and the loan rate. But budget about 18% of the price upfront, understand the partition and exit risks, and use the second 90% loan on another investment rather than a home while young and mobile.

reasons.title: The yield is unusually high
reasons.body: With loan rates around 3.85% to 4%, a yield of about 4% covers the interest and 5% is already good. Over 7% is usually only found near universities, in busy expatriate areas or in holiday spots, each with their own risks.

reasons.title: Partitions bring legal and insurance risk
reasons.body: Kuala Lumpur City Hall has moved to ban partitioned living rooms, and partitions built without approval can void the fire insurance. Rent that depends on them may not last.

reasons.title: Student units sell only to investors
reasons.body: Families rarely want to live among student tenants, so the buyer later is another investor who prices by rent. If rents rise, the value rises with them, but if a nearby campus moves, demand can go too.

reasons.title: A home can wait
reasons.body: At 23 and working freelance, renting in a cheaper suburb such as Cyberjaya keeps costs low and options open. With this income, a second investment can be financed without waiting for the first unit's rent records.

actions: Budget about 18% of the price for down payment, stamp duty and fees, about RM106,000 here, before any renovation.
Check whether the existing partitions were approved, and what rent the unit would earn without them.
Check that the university nearby is a main campus that is unlikely to move, not a branch run from shop lots.
Declare your full income for tax: it costs a little more but helps the bank approve larger loans.
Keep six months of expenses and insurance in place, and learn other assets with small regular amounts.
articles.caveat: If you want to live in a property later, the 85% rule applies instead: rent should cover at least 85% of the instalment so you can rent it out when you move. Sean assumed the income is steady; freelance income that varies changes the picture.
articles.sourceNote: Summarised from Sean's full English captions for Asking Sean #230. The quoted line is verbatim; everything else is paraphrased. Figures are as the viewer and Sean stated them in November 2023, when loan rates were about 3.85% to 4%.

video.title: ASKING SEAN #230 | RISK OF INVESTING IN STUDENT ACCOMMODATION

articles.title: The seller's unit is pledged to his business loan. Should I still buy?
articles.excerpt: A 28-year-old found her ideal RM300,000 subsale near work in PJ, then learnt it was charged to the seller's business loan, with only a master title. Sean says walk away while the deposit is refundable.

question.asker: From Miss V, a viewer who wrote in by email
question.context: Miss V is 28 and has commuted an hour each way for almost ten years. She found a two-room, 800 sq ft apartment in PJ near her work for about RM300,000, and her loan was approved quickly. After she signed the booking form, the agent said the seller had pledged the unit for a business loan and might not get the original documents back from his bank. The building has only a master title, and she can still withdraw and get her deposit back.
question.text: Should she sign the SPA and accept the risk that her bank won't release the loan, or give up the unit?

answer.quote: The greatest risk is not losing money, the greatest risk is losing ownership.
answer.summary: Walk away. If the documents can't be cleared, the bank may refuse to release her loan after she has already paid legal fees, and her ownership would stay uncertain. Better deals will come; she was lucky to find out before signing the SPA.

reasons.title: Ownership is what the paperwork protects
reasons.body: Malaysia's land system records exactly who owns each property, which is why a subsale transfer must be documented properly. A unit pledged to someone else's loan breaks that chain until the seller's bank releases it.

reasons.title: A master title adds a second risk
reasons.body: Many older apartments still sit on one master title, so transfers need the developer's or landowner's power of attorney. Where no landowner remains, banks often refuse to finance at all.

reasons.title: New launches are more standardised
reasons.body: Residential projects under the Housing Development Act use a standard SPA and billing schedule. Commercial titles, including SOHOs and serviced suites, are not standardised in the same way.

reasons.title: Paying for a deal that may collapse wastes money
reasons.body: If the bank won't release her loan, the sale falls through, the legal fees are gone, and she would struggle to move on to the next unit.

actions: Withdraw now while the deposit is still refundable.
Ask the agent to find other units in the same building, above or below, or nearby within the budget.
Before booking any subsale, ask whether the unit is charged to a bank and what title it has.
For new launches, check whether the project is under the Housing Development Act.
articles.caveat: If the seller's bank fully discharges the unit and clean documents are in hand before she signs, the risk largely disappears. Units bought for cash at auction are a different case.
articles.sourceNote: Summarised from Sean's full English captions for Asking Sean #200. The quoted line is verbatim; everything else is paraphrased. Figures are as the viewer stated them in February 2023. This is general information, not legal advice; ask a lawyer about a specific title.

video.title: ASKING SEAN #200 | NOT WORTH THE RISK

articles.title: I rent a room in Melaka for work. Subsale or new launch home?
articles.excerpt: A single first-time buyer posted to Melaka wants to stop renting and is torn between a subsale and a new project. Sean asks why buy a home there at all, and suggests an investment unit first.

question.asker: From C, a viewer who wrote in by email
question.context: C works in Melaka but isn't from there, and rents a room. C is a first-time buyer, single, and wants a place of their own soon. Subsales seem to involve more paperwork, a slower loan and an older house, while the new project C likes won't be ready until June 2024.
question.text: Should a first-time buyer pick a subsale or a new project, and what are the pros and cons of each?

answer.quote: Build cash flow vehicles first before seeking for comfort.
answer.summary: First ask why C needs a home in Melaka now. Unless C's career or partner means settling there, Sean would rent on and buy an investment unit in KL whose rent covers the instalment. A home to live in can come later, when life is settled.

reasons.title: Renting fits a temporary posting
reasons.body: Rent pays for space you need for a few uncertain years. If C may be transferred, owning a home there loses flexibility, and buyers who move often end up paying for an empty house and a rental elsewhere.

reasons.title: Subsale and new launch differ in cash and time
reasons.body: A freehold subsale takes about three to six months to transfer, and leasehold three or four months more for state consent, which varies by state. It needs about 18% up front in cash, while a new launch is a one-stop deal with financing but is often priced higher for the wait.

reasons.title: An own-stay home rarely makes money
reasons.body: Over 35 years the interest roughly doubles what you pay, so a RM500,000 home sold for RM1 million later barely breaks even. What you get is certainty and a form of forced saving.

reasons.title: Let tenants build your equity
reasons.body: A unit renting at about 4.5% to 5% of its price can cover its own instalment, so tenants pay it off while the value grows. Sean found several KL projects that would roughly break even at current rents.

actions: Decide first whether you are settling in Melaka for career or family.
If not, keep renting there and look for an investment unit in KL with a 4.5% to 5% rental yield.
If buying a subsale, budget about 18% of the price in cash and allow extra months for a leasehold title.
If buying a new launch, check the handover date against how long you will keep renting.
Keep the bigger own-stay or landed home for when your family and career are settled.
articles.caveat: If C has settled in Melaka to build a career or family, buying a home to live in there makes sense, and the subsale versus new launch choice then comes down to cash and timing.
articles.sourceNote: Summarised from Sean's full English captions for Asking Sean #201. The quoted line is verbatim; everything else is paraphrased. Figures are as Sean stated them in February 2023. Transfer times and state consent rules differ by state and change over time.

video.title: ASKING SEAN #201 | LANDED HOME IS ONLY A TEMPORARY NEED

articles.title: I support my parents and want my own space. Should I buy at auction?
articles.excerpt: A single man earning RM15,000 on contract pays for a semi-D his parents live in and wants to buy an auction unit for himself. Sean steers him away from auctions and suggests moving out first.

question.asker: From Dean, a viewer who wrote in by email
question.context: Dean is single and works in KL city centre on a contract paying about RM15,000 a month. He owns a RM500,000 semi-detached house in the Klang Valley with an instalment of about RM2,300, but his parents and grandmother live there and he has only a small room. He spends about RM4,000 a month on them, including the instalment, their insurance, car and utilities, and has saved RM200,000.
question.text: He plans to buy an auction unit of about RM500,000 near public transport next year to live in or rent out. Is that the right move?

answer.quote: Treat the house as the last obligation of love.
answer.summary: Keep supporting the house, but don't make an auction unit your next step. Either talk openly with his parents about a smaller home, or simply move out to a rented place near the city, keep the RM200,000 as a safety net, and buy an investment through a lower-capital channel.

reasons.title: Auctions often close at market price
reasons.body: Listings start about 30% below valuation, but a few eager bidders push the final price to around or above market. You can't view the unit, and outstanding maintenance, private caveats or a poor as-is condition can surface after you have paid the deposit.

reasons.title: A deadline can burn the deposit
reasons.body: If you can't sign the final agreement within the set period, about 30 days, the deposit is forfeited. Sean, who has bought new, subsale and through investment clubs, still avoids auctions.

reasons.title: His risk is higher than most
reasons.body: If a wrong investment coincides with losing his contract job, his parents and grandmother could lose their home. He needs income of about three times the instalment, roughly RM8,000, just to keep the house safe.

reasons.title: Two or three properties are enough
reasons.body: Sean's aim for viewers is two to three properties in a lifetime, about one every ten years. Bought at RM400,000 to RM600,000 and paid off by 77, they are worth about RM1.5 million in today's money, so you don't become a burden on your own children.

actions: If your family can talk about money, discuss your parents moving to a smaller rented terrace while you keep giving the same monthly sum.
Otherwise rent a room or small unit nearer the city for privacy and career, and visit your parents every week or two.
Keep the RM200,000 split between an emergency fund for your parents, your wedding and renovation, rather than spending it on a purchase.
Compare all four buying channels; a subsale needs about 17% to 18% of the price upfront, about RM90,000 for a RM500,000 unit.
Consider an investment unit under construction bought through a bulk-purchase club, which needs less capital and gives you two to three years before handover.
articles.caveat: Auctions can suit an experienced investor on a third or fourth property who knows the traps. Sean's advice on moving out depends on the family: in many Asian households asking parents to move is a sensitive step.
articles.sourceNote: Summarised from Sean's full English captions for Asking Sean #255, sponsored by PropertyGuru's Brickz transaction reports. The quoted answer is verbatim; everything else is paraphrased. Figures are as Sean stated them in June 2024. Sean says his last three purchases came through the bulk-purchase investment club linked in his video description.

video.title: ASKING SEAN #255 | AGING PARENTS BECAME A BURDEN

articles.title: I own two properties at 25. How do I reach RM10 million?
articles.excerpt: A 25-year-old second-generation business owner holds two KL properties bought below market and wants RM10 million in property within ten years. Sean says to pause and grow elsewhere.

question.asker: From JT, a viewer who wrote in by email
question.context: JT is 25, married to a foreign wife, lives with his parents and works in his family's business. He bought a 1,098 sq ft Bangsar unit at auction for RM870,000, now rented with positive cash flow and about RM500,000 below the median value, and an 800 sq ft Damansara Heights unit for about RM1.1 million, 20% below market, still awaiting keys. His loan margins are used up.
question.text: How should he grow towards RM10 million in property in ten years: commercial property, a purchase using his wife's foreigner quota, or more residential?

answer.quote: The critical path is your income journey.
answer.summary: For now, don't grow it. He already has the two or three properties Sean encourages over a lifetime, so the next step is to settle the second unit, put his own money into other, uncorrelated assets, and grow his income and business knowledge, because property keeps you rich rather than makes you rich.

reasons.title: A third property is expensive
reasons.body: Beyond two 90% loans, financing drops to 70%, so a RM1 million unit needs about RM300,000 down, or RM350,000 to RM380,000 with legal fees. Sean asks whether that money would do more in other assets than in a property growing marginally each year.

reasons.title: Commercial property is playing with fire
reasons.body: The successful commercial investors Sean knows buy subsale shop lots that already rent at 5% to 6%, rather than new launches that can take eight to 12 years to come alive. Businesses often buy commercial and industrial property mainly to hedge against inflation.

reasons.title: Diversify into uncorrelated assets
reasons.body: Sean uses his credit for Malaysian property, the game he understands, and his own money for other assets. Property cannot be dollar-cost averaged, so one bad purchase at the top of a cycle can ruin your credit and your confidence; he made that mistake himself after three successful deals.

reasons.title: Judge success by cash flow, not asset value
reasons.body: RM10 million can be reached with a single penthouse, so the number means little. Sean's first level of success is a portfolio that breaks even; the second is a surplus that also pays for your own home.

actions: Settle, furnish and rent out the second unit before looking for another.
Put your own savings into other assets, such as Malaysian or US stocks, and learn how they work.
If you buy commercial, choose a subsale unit that already rents at 5% to 6%.
If you use a foreign spouse's quota, buy a family home where RM1 million is the area's normal price, with a larger down payment, rather than an investment.
Before any purchase, run Sean's four basic steps: intent, affordability, 20 properties compared, then an informed decision.
articles.caveat: This is advice for someone already well ahead at 25, with family backing. Sean's worry is the opposite of most viewers': that the backing tempts him into risks beyond his means. For most buyers, his usual aim of two or three properties over a lifetime still applies.
articles.sourceNote: Summarised from Sean's full English captions for Asking Sean #307. The quoted answer is verbatim; everything else is paraphrased. Figures are as stated in February 2026. Sean buys through FAR Capital's bulk purchases as a member, not its owner.

video.title: ASKING SEAN #307 | PROPERTY INVESTMENT SHOULD BE PASSIVE

articles.title: I want 10 properties in 10 years on RM5,500 a month. Too aggressive?
articles.excerpt: A 29-year-old with RM50,000 saved wants positive cash flow and ten properties within 15 years. Sean explains cash back against cash flow, how rent drives a high-rise's value, and why to go slowly.

question.asker: From YK, a viewer who wrote in by email
question.context: YK is 29, works in a helping profession and earns about RM5,500 a month, with a six-month emergency fund, RM50,000 in savings and comprehensive insurance, and recently joined a bulk-purchase club. YK wants positive cash flow and early retirement, and is weighing a completed unit with high cash back but a monthly shortfall, then two more units soon after.
question.text: Should YK take high cash back with negative cash flow, how is capital growth judged, is buying three units in quick succession overcommitting, and should spare cash go into a flexi loan?

answer.quote: So, my suggestion is to go slow.
answer.summary: Take positive cash flow over cash back where possible, buy one unit at a time and get each one rented before the next, and build up salary first. Ten properties in ten years on RM5,500 a month is a target nobody else has set.

reasons.title: Cash back is borrowed money
reasons.body: It suits someone using it to clear credit card debt at about 18% or a personal loan at about 8%, or a business owner using a flexi loan as cheap working capital. Without that need, a smaller loan with rent above the instalment is better; buyers who spent their cash back are the ones who ended up in auctions.

reasons.title: Rent sets a high-rise's value
reasons.body: Each RM450 a month of surplus rent supports about RM100,000 more loan over 35 years at 4%. Sean's Mont Kiara unit, bought for about RM950,000, rents for about RM1,500 above its instalment, so the next investor could pay about RM1.25 million and still break even. That surplus mostly happens in tier one locations.

reasons.title: Studios suit only expensive land
reasons.body: Studios work where land is too costly for bigger units, such as Mont Kiara, Bangsar South and KLCC. In outlying areas they are a mismatch, however cheap they look.

reasons.title: Active income drives the portfolio
reasons.body: Investors who build portfolios fast usually earn RM30,000 or more. On RM5,500, a RM20,000 repair can hurt. Property keeps you rich; growing income is what makes you rich, and rental income replacing a salary is a goal for 55 or 60, not 35.

actions: Choose a lower loan with positive cash flow over cash back you don't need.
Rent each unit out before committing to the next.
Pick one route, subsale, auction or bulk purchase, and execute it rather than joining several courses.
Put spare cash in a flexi loan unless you can reliably earn more than the loan's 3.8% to 4%.
Set a goal by monthly cash flow or total value, not a number of units by a deadline.
articles.caveat: For someone with expensive debts to clear, a high cash back unit with a small monthly shortfall can make sense, provided the cash back is kept as a buffer and not spent.
articles.sourceNote: Summarised from Sean's full English captions for Asking Sean #284. The quoted answer is verbatim; everything else is paraphrased. Figures are as stated in May 2025. Sean is a client of FAR Capital, the bulk-purchase club YK has joined, not its owner; he says he bought his last four properties through it at members' prices. He leaves the specific project YK is considering to the club's advisers.

video.title: ASKING SEAN #284 | 10 PROPERTIES IN 10 YEARS

articles.title: My tenant has stopped paying rent. What can I legally do?
articles.excerpt: A tenant who stops paying but won't leave is every landlord's nightmare. Lawyer Tea explains the legal route Sean's viewers can take: a letter of demand, then a court distress order.

question.context: Sean counts a tenant who stops paying but won't leave among a landlord's two worst cases. Many owners don't know the legal steps, so they wait months or even years, or try cutting off the water or changing the locks. Sean puts the problem to Lawyer Tea, who handles distress proceedings for landlords.
question.text: When a tenant stops paying rent and won't leave, what is the legal way to get your money and your property back?

by.name: Lawyer Tea
by.role: a lawyer who acts for landlords against non-paying tenants

answer.quote: So yeah, the best way I would say it will be the distress orders.
answer.summary: Act on the first missed month: send a letter of demand, and if the tenant hasn't paid within 14 days, apply to court for a distress order. The order lets you seize and auction the tenant's belongings and take the unit back, in two to three months at best.

reasons.title: Start while the deposit still covers you
reasons.body: Landlords usually hold two months' deposit. Sending the letter of demand after the first missed month means the court order can be ready by about the third month, before the losses run far beyond the deposit.

reasons.title: A distress order moves quickly
reasons.body: The landlord applies alone, without the tenant appearing in court, which is why it can take as little as two to three months. The tenant is normally given 14 days to leave, and anything left in the unit is presumed theirs and sold at a court auction.

reasons.title: Doing it yourself can backfire
reasons.body: A tenancy agreement normally promises the tenant quiet enjoyment of the unit. Cutting off water or electricity, or locking them out, can let them sue you for their losses or for belongings they say went missing.

reasons.title: Paperwork decides what you recover
reasons.body: An agreement has to be stamped to be admissible in court, which costs only a few hundred ringgit, and an expired agreement still counts. Without one you can apply for a writ of possession to get the unit back, but recovering money is hard; rent paid by bank transfer, not cash, helps prove the tenancy.

actions: Use a proper, stamped tenancy agreement that sets out each side's rights and what happens if rent isn't paid, not an agent's copied template.
Collect rent by bank transfer, and put the electricity account in the tenant's name.
Run a CTOS check on prospective tenants. Sean also treats an offer of a year's rent in cash, or a rush to move in the next day, as warning signs.
Send a letter of demand after the first missed month, and apply for a distress order if 14 days pass without payment.
Budget about RM10,000 in legal fees for the letter and the order, and let the court bailiff and the police carry out the eviction.
articles.caveat: Against squatters, or with no agreement or payment record, you can usually recover only the property, not the rent. If you suspect illegal activity in the unit, report it to the police at once; an owner who knew and said nothing can be held responsible.
articles.sourceNote: Summarised from Sean's full English captions for this May 2026 conversation with Lawyer Tea, who acts for landlords in distress proceedings. The quoted answer is Lawyer Tea's own words; everything else is paraphrased. Fees are as quoted in the episode. This is general information, not legal advice for your case.

articles.title: My tenant wants to pay six months upfront. Will it hurt my next loan?
articles.excerpt: A 26-year-old in Kota Kinabalu bought a subsale condo below market value and rented it out the day renovation finished. Sean explains what he did right, and why rent paid six months at a time can cost him his next loan.

question.asker: From Mr J, a viewer who wrote in by email
question.context: Mr J is 26, self-employed in Kota Kinabalu and earns about RM10,000 a month net. His mother spotted a listing in the condo where he lives: RM520,000, partly furnished, with a market value of about RM580,000. The owner wanted a quick sale, so he negotiated it to RM500,000, and the bank valued it at RM650,000. He handled the paperwork himself, did minor renovations and rented it out for about RM200 a month more than his instalment. The tenant now offers to pay RM12,600 every six months for two years.
question.text: Will rent paid every six months, rather than monthly, affect his income assessment when he applies for a second property?

answer.quote: Luck is when opportunity meets preparation.
answer.summary: Yes, it will. Banks look at rental income month by month in your bank statements, so lump sums or uneven amounts may not be counted, and that can cost him the next property. Ask the tenant to pay the same amount every month instead.

reasons.title: Banks want steady monthly credits
reasons.body: When you apply for a loan, the banker reads your statements month by month. Rent that arrives every six months, or varies because repairs were deducted from it, looks inconsistent and may not be recognised as income.

reasons.title: Keep repairs separate from rent
reasons.body: Letting a tenant fix things and deduct the cost is common, but it breaks the pattern. Sean has repairs fixed and paid separately, while the full rent is still paid to him each month.

reasons.title: Subsale lets you negotiate
reasons.body: With a subsale or bulk purchase you can counter the asking price; a developer's retail price is fixed. Knowing his own building let Mr J judge a below-market listing and act quickly.

reasons.title: Stay ready for the deal
reasons.body: Sean checks his own CCRIS and loan eligibility regularly, because good-value listings go to whoever can commit first. A subsale needs about 18% of the price in cash, so savings must be in place before the chance appears.

actions: Decline lump-sum rent if you plan to apply for another loan soon.
Offer the tenant an auto-debit, or 12 post-dated cheques to bank in each month.
Pay for repairs separately rather than deducting them from the rent.
Keep your loan eligibility and CCRIS checked, so you can move when a below-market listing appears.
Ask for a better price or rate at every step, from the seller to the lawyer and the bank.
articles.caveat: If you don't need the rent counted for a loan in the next year or two, advance payment matters less; the issue is only how a bank reads your statements.
articles.sourceNote: Summarised from Sean's full English captions for Asking Sean #281. The quoted line is verbatim; everything else is paraphrased. Figures are as stated in April 2025. The episode is sponsored by The Makeover Guys, a renovation company Sean says furnishes and manages most of his investment units; it does not bear on this answer.

video.title: ASKING SEAN #281 | BUYING SUBSALE BELOW MARKET VALUE, THEN RENT OUT DURING RENOVATION

articles.title: Should my third property be subsale, auction, new or bulk purchase?
articles.excerpt: A 30-year-old with two landed homes and RM200,000 to RM300,000 in cash weighs subsale, auction, new and bulk purchase for her third. Sean says to keep her cash and let the deal decide.

question.asker: From YX, a viewer who wrote in by email
question.context: YX is 30 and single, earns about RM8,000 net from her job and declares about RM5,000 a month from her own marketing business. She shares the loan on a landed own-stay home with her sister and bought a second landed house at auction for RM560,000, financed by an insurer whose loans don't appear in CCRIS, so she still has one 90% loan left. She has RM200,000 to RM300,000 in cash and is a member of a property investment club.
question.text: For her third property, should she use cash on a subsale or auction unit with 10% down, or buy new or through bulk purchase, and save her cash?

answer.quote: Use as little of our money as possible.
answer.summary: Keep the cash and use credit. Sean has no favourite channel; he buys wherever the best deal is, but with her aim of letting the property pay for itself, new launches and bulk purchases fit better than subsale or auction, and her savings are worth more as runway for her business.

reasons.title: Less cash in means more options later
reasons.body: A subsale bought with a bigger down payment may give RM500 a month of positive cash flow, while a new unit with a larger loan may only break even. Sean still picks the one that ties up less money, and spends the difference on furnishing the unit so it stands out to the best tenants.

reasons.title: A bigger discount beats a standard one
reasons.body: Developers give everyone the same standard 10% or so. A bulk purchase with a 20% to 30% discount lets you own the unit, furnish it and still leave your savings untouched; any spare cash can sit in the loan to cut interest while staying available.

reasons.title: Auctions carry hidden problems
reasons.body: She was lucky with a landed auction house. Of ten auction units Sean has heard about, one or two had problems, and high-rise ones bring questions about arrears, whether the developer still exists and whether the strata title has been issued.

reasons.title: Her business may out-earn her job
reasons.body: If her side business grows from RM5,000 to RM15,000 a month, it may be time to focus on it. With living costs of about RM4,000, RM400,000 in savings would let her quit and build the business on her terms rather than take every job just to survive.

actions: Make sure the property itself makes sense before choosing how to buy it.
Compare the same project across all four channels when they overlap, such as just after completion when unsold, subsale and auction units all exist.
If you have paid for an investment club, use its research and advisers before comparing deals yourself.
Keep your savings as an emergency fund and business runway rather than spending them on down payments.
If you are a first-time buyer, stay away from auction high-rises until you understand their risks.
articles.caveat: If you dislike owing the bank a lot, Sean says it is fine to stop at two properties using both 90% loans. And financing from an insurer costs more: the rate is fixed and usually higher, and you must buy insurance from them.
articles.sourceNote: Summarised from Sean's full English captions for Asking Sean #306. The quoted answer is verbatim; everything else is paraphrased. Figures are as stated in January 2026. Sean is a customer of FAR Capital, the property investment club YX belongs to, not its owner, and he says he is biased towards its bulk-purchase deals. He also recommends a contact for insurer financing in the video.

video.title: ASKING SEAN #306 | DECIDING BETWEEN DIFFERENT CHANNELS OF BUYING

articles.title: Should I pick a low-floor three-bedroom or a high-floor two-bedroom?
articles.excerpt: In the same block and at the same price, a low-floor three-bedroom or a high-floor two-bedroom? Sean's answer depends on whether you will rent it out or live in it.

question.context: Buyers in the same project often face a choice at a similar price: an extra bedroom on a lower floor, or one fewer bedroom with a better view higher up.
question.text: In the same block, is a low-floor three-bedroom or a high-floor two-bedroom the better buy?

answer.quote: I'll go for the lowest floor three-bedroom
answer.summary: For a rental, take the low-floor three-bedroom: rents are set mainly by the number of rooms, not the height. For own stay it is personal, depending on how much you value the view, but check how low the low floor really is.

reasons.title: Rent follows the room count
reasons.body: The rental market is segmented by bedrooms: a one-bedroom rents for more than a studio, and a two-bedroom more than a one-bedroom. Converting a two-bedroom into a three-bedroom can be a smart move.

reasons.title: Few tenants pay for height
reasons.body: In the mid-market, a tenant won't pay much more to live on level 16 instead of level 6 with the same view. In the luxury segment, where rents run to RM16,000 or more, tenants do pay for a view.

reasons.title: How low is low
reasons.body: Level 3 next to a highway is noisy; level 17 against level 47 is a different comparison. Lower floors also complete earlier in the payment schedule, so you pay slightly more interest, though Sean calls it negligible.

actions: Decide first whether the unit is for rent or for your own stay.
For a rental, compare rents by room count in the area.
Check whether a two-bedroom layout could be converted to three.
Visit the low floor to hear road noise before you commit.
articles.caveat: Sean frames this as his own thought process rather than a rule; for a luxury unit or one you will live in, the view may be worth the trade.
articles.sourceNote: Summarised from Sean's English captions for this September 2019 video, a discussion with no right or wrong answer. The quoted line is verbatim; everything else is paraphrased.

video.title: 3-BEDROOM (LOW FLOOR LEVEL) VS 2 BEDROOM (HIGH FLOOR LEVEL)

articles.title: Three transit-linked condos, same cash flow. How do I choose?
articles.excerpt: A 40-year-old civil servant in Johor Bahru has shortlisted three new transit-linked serviced apartments in the Klang Valley for cash flow. Sean explains what to compare after cash flow, and why she must visit in person.

question.asker: From KD, a viewer from Johor Bahru who wrote in by email
question.context: KD is 40, single, a government servant earning RM9,100 a month net, with a car loan of RM944. She lives with her mother in a house transferred to her, and invests in shares, fixed deposits and money market funds, reaching half of her RM5,000-a-month passive income goal. For her first investment property she wants monthly cash flow and has shortlisted three new transit-oriented serviced apartments, in Kajang, Cheras and Petaling Jaya, buying new because she lives far away.
question.text: If all three give similar cash flow, what should decide it, how much does walkable convenience matter, why are some Mont Kiara subsales so cheap, and how should she judge bulk-purchase units near KLCC with cash back?

answer.quote: we should always look at pricing first then location then only timing
answer.summary: After cash flow, compare each project's price with the median of past transactions around it, and the cash each needs up front. Walkable shops and transit genuinely justify higher rent. And living in Johor is no reason to buy new: visit the sites, and consider subsales and bulk-purchase deals too.

reasons.title: Below-median prices leave room to grow
reasons.body: A unit that rents well but is priced above its neighbours has limited capital appreciation. A unit bought below the area's median that still covers its instalment is the better buy.

reasons.title: Upfront cash differs by deal
reasons.body: One project may need RM50,000 to own, another nothing, and some even pay cash back while still covering the instalment. Through his investment club, Sean buys units with positive cash flow and no money down.

reasons.title: Older units are cheap for a reason
reasons.body: Older Mont Kiara blocks sell at about RM600 per sq ft against about RM1,000 for new ones, because of lower ceilings and layouts, such as toilets along the facade, that cannot be changed.

reasons.title: Prime location is not enough
reasons.body: Units near KLCC with good shops still lose money if priced above market. A premium is fine when you know why you are paying it, such as a proven retail operator.

actions: Pull the past transacted prices for each project and its neighbours.
Compare how much cash each deal needs up front, not only the monthly cash flow.
Take a week to visit Klang Valley properties in person, about 20 if you can.
Check whether shops, transit, schools and clinics are within walking distance.
Consider subsale and bulk-purchase options alongside new launches.
articles.caveat: Rental income is not entirely passive; tenants and repairs still need managing unless you pay a management company. Buying new from a developer that sells only direct can be the best channel when early phases are priced low.
articles.sourceNote: Summarised from Sean's full English captions for Asking Sean #256. The quoted line is verbatim; everything else is paraphrased. Figures are as stated in June 2024. The episode is sponsored by PropertyGuru's Brickz transaction reports, which Sean recommends for checking prices. He is a VIP member of FAR Capital, a bulk-purchase club, not its owner, and his units are managed by Cozy Homes.

articles.title: At 21, should I buy a 430 sq ft suite in KL with RM80,000 cashback?
articles.excerpt: A 21-year-old wants a tiny dual-key suite on Jalan Ampang for Airbnb, financed with a big cashback. Sean lists the numbers he must check first, and says missing a deal beats a 35-year mistake.

question.asker: From A, a viewer who wrote in by email
question.context: A is 21 and new to the channel. He is considering a 430 sq ft dual-key suite on Jalan Ampang with a RM410,000 loan and RM80,000 cashback. He would use the cashback to furnish the unit and keep a reserve. He plans to run it on Airbnb, since he doubts anyone would live long-term in so small a space, and worries he can't otherwise afford a property.
question.text: Is this a good first investment, or is he making a mistake that will become a financial burden?

answer.quote: Would you rather have missed a deal or would you live with a mistake?
answer.summary: He hasn't done the homework yet, and at 21 he doesn't need to own property. He should first work out the real rents, nightly rates, occupancy and price per square foot against nearby projects, and check he could survive six months with no guest. Only buy if the numbers clearly cover the instalment.

reasons.title: Cheap is not the same as a good deal
reasons.body: A good deal is priced below market value and either earns cash flow, has strong potential to appreciate, or is structured for the cashback. After the cashback this unit costs about RM330,000, which may be RM900 to RM1,000 psf when neighbours sell at about RM700.

reasons.title: Airbnb needs its own maths
reasons.body: A RM410,000 loan costs about RM2,000 a month. He needs the nightly rate, an occupancy of perhaps 70% to 80%, and the operator's cut, and must check that the building still allows short stays, as some ban them.

reasons.title: Every property needs a plan B and C
reasons.body: If short stays fail, who would rent it long-term, and can a 430 sq ft unit be split further? Thousands of similar small units nearby, and auctions in the area, could push rents down.

reasons.title: At 21, flexibility is worth more
reasons.body: Start with an emergency fund of six months, insurance and a stable career. Starting at 25 or 28 with real data is no loss.

actions: Collect long-term rents and nightly rates for similar units on Jalan Ampang.
Ask operators about real occupancy and their profit split, and check the building's rules on short stays.
Compare the price per square foot with neighbouring projects.
Make sure you can pay the instalment for six months with no income from the unit.
View about 20 projects before booking any of them.
articles.caveat: Sean has nothing against small units or high risk. If the data shows the rent comfortably covers the instalment and he can afford six empty months, going ahead is a calculated risk.
articles.sourceNote: Summarised from Sean's full English captions for Asking Sean #197. The quoted line is verbatim; everything else is paraphrased. Figures are as the viewer and Sean stated them in January 2023.

articles.title: Is a condo linked to a train station a better buy?
articles.excerpt: Every new project near an MRT or LRT station now calls itself a TOD. Sean explains what transit-oriented development means, who it suits, and the trade-off between convenience and security.

question.context: With new MRT lines opening, developers market almost any project near a station as a transit-oriented development, or TOD. Mixed developments now combine homes, offices, serviced apartments, hotels and malls on one site, linked to rail.
question.text: What is a transit-oriented development, and is a home in one a better buy?

answer.quote: convenience doesn't really come with security
answer.summary: A TOD is built around public transport, so residents can live, work and shop without relying on a car. That makes it strong for rental to young workers, but the same accessibility brings crowds, noise and weaker security, so it suits investors and singles better than families who want privacy.

reasons.title: Young tenants want the link
reasons.body: Workers in their first few years of employment can barely make ends meet, and a direct rail link saves them time and the cost of a car. That demand supports rents.

reasons.title: Easy access cuts both ways
reasons.body: When a station's commuters pass through a development, privacy suffers. High-end residents have even objected to stations near them, which is why expensive projects tend to be less accessible.

reasons.title: Someone pays for the walkways
reasons.body: Public link bridges and walkways need lighting, cleaning and guards. In some projects, residents' maintenance fees cover areas used by every commuter.

reasons.title: Compartmentalisation matters
reasons.body: In a mixed development, the residential part should be well separated from the mall, offices and station, or residents share their lifts and lobbies with the public.

actions: Ask whether the project actually connects to a station, or is merely near one.
Ask who maintains and secures the public walkways, and whether your fees pay for them.
Check how the residential block is separated from retail and transit areas.
Match the project to its tenants: TODs suit young workers who commute by rail.
Choose a more private development if security for a family comes first.
articles.caveat: Some projects are both rail-linked and highly secure, but they command a premium. Sean also questions whether buyers of RM1.6 million units, who seldom commute by train, need a rail link at all.
articles.sourceNote: Summarised from Sean's English captions for this May 2018 video. The captions are of poor quality, so only points that are clear are included. The quoted line is verbatim; everything else is paraphrased.

articles.title: My uncle will pay RM80,000 if I buy a landed home. Should I take it?
articles.excerpt: A 32-year-old father renting in Ampang is offered RM80,000 by his uncle, but only for a landed home to live in. Sean shows the real cash needed and why he would politely decline.

question.asker: From H, a viewer who wrote in by email
question.context: H is 32, married with a two-year-old, earns RM6,500 a month and his wife about RM4,500. They rent a 900 sq ft unit in Ampang and have RM50,000 in ASB as an emergency fund. He owns one investment unit, completed in 2019, that costs him about RM400 a month above its rent. His uncle has offered up to RM80,000 for the down payment on a RM700,000 to RM800,000 landed home, but only for his own stay, with instalments of RM3,500 to RM4,500.
question.text: Should he accept and buy a landed home now, or keep renting and build investment properties first as planned?

answer.quote: My first property is not my only property.
answer.summary: Sean would decline. RM80,000 doesn't come close to covering a landed home, which would eat most of his income and block his loan eligibility for investments. Keep renting, keep building investment properties, and upgrade to a landed home in about ten years with his own money.

reasons.title: The real cash needed is far more than RM80,000
reasons.body: A RM700,000 subsale needs about 18% up front, roughly RM126,000 for the down payment, stamp duty and fees, plus at least RM50,000 to make it livable. He would still need about RM100,000 of his own.

reasons.title: It would leave no room for shocks
reasons.body: With RM3,500 to RM4,500 going on the loan before his car, insurance and family costs, every rate rise or family emergency would be stressful.

reasons.title: His loan eligibility would be tied up
reasons.body: A RM700,000 loan on his credit record would use up his debt service ratio, ending the plan of buying investment units whose rent eventually pays for his home.

reasons.title: A small monthly top-up can be acceptable
reasons.body: Paying RM400 a month still builds equity. Before selling his investment unit, check its market value against what he owes, and consider refreshing it to raise the rent.

actions: Work out the full cash needed for a landed home, including fees and renovation.
Check what is still owed on the investment unit and its current market value before selling.
Consider small improvements to raise its rent instead.
Plan to upgrade to a landed home once his investments and income can carry it.
Ask why the offer is only for a landed home, and what may be expected in return.
articles.caveat: If his only goal is one family home and he accepts five to ten years of tight finances, taking the gift is reasonable. Family dynamics differ, and Sean admits his preference for independence is personal.
articles.sourceNote: Summarised from Sean's full English captions for Asking Sean #189. The quoted line is verbatim; everything else is paraphrased. Figures are as the viewer and Sean stated them in September 2022. Sean says he, like the viewer, is a client of FAR Capital, a bulk-purchase company.

articles.title: Unsold units near completion: warning sign or better deal?
articles.excerpt: A first-time investor sees plenty of units still for sale in a project close to handover. Sean explains why developers end up with unsold stock, and when that works in a buyer's favour.

question.asker: From JJ, a viewer who wrote in by email
question.context: JJ is under 30, married with no children, and has no property or loans yet but a good credit score. Most of his money is in stocks, and he had avoided property because of the upfront cash it needs. He is looking at a bulk-purchase listing in Dutamas, near Mont Kiara, that is close to vacant possession but still has many units available, is already late enough for late-delivery damages to apply, and includes dual-key and tri-key layouts.
question.text: Do the unsold units signal a problem, does the delay matter to a buyer like him, and are dual-key and tri-key units worth it?

answer.quote: So, to me it's not a concern at all.
answer.summary: Not in this case. Few Malaysians can borrow for a unit above RM1 million, so slow sales near completion are expected, and a developer that keeps building through a delay is a financially strong one. Judge the unit on location, rent and long-term value, and treat any discount as a bonus.

reasons.title: Developers clear stock quietly
reasons.body: Banks pay developers stage by stage as the building goes up, so a developer still holding units near completion wants the cash. Open discounts would upset the first buyers, so stock is often cleared through bulk-purchase clubs, at prices kept confidential.

reasons.title: Price limits who can buy
reasons.body: To borrow RM1 million you need an income of about RM12,000 to RM15,000 a month, which Sean puts at roughly the top 20% of Malaysians. A unit above a million will naturally sell more slowly.

reasons.title: Delay hurts families more than investors
reasons.body: Late-delivery damages run from your own SPA date, so a later buyer's clock starts later than the first buyers'. For an investor the main cost of a delay is renovation: Sean says furnishing a unit that once cost RM28,000 now costs RM48,000 to RM50,000. A family waiting to move in loses far more.

reasons.title: Dual-key units stretch one loan slot
reasons.body: A single 90% residential loan can buy a dual-key or tri-key unit that rents as two or three, where buying separate studios would push the third onto a 70% loan. Sean says the format suits dense urban areas, and tri-key rooms can rent for less than a studio while giving more privacy than a shared flat.

actions: Visit the site before you buy: land cleared and foundations under way before launch are signs of a well-funded developer.
Check the late-delivery terms against your own SPA date, not the project's launch.
Compare the expected rent with the instalment at your discounted price, not the list price.
Consider completed unsold units: you see the finished building, the view and the neighbours before you pay, and still get the developer's packages.
Spend any cash back on renovation and buffers first, then put what remains towards the loan.
articles.caveat: This assumes a prime location and a developer able to finish; Sean says prime projects are rarely abandoned, but it can happen. If you bought early in such a project, unsold stock cuts the other way: buyers will compare your subsale unit with the developer's discounted ones.
articles.sourceNote: Summarised from Sean's full English captions for Asking Sean #313. The quoted answer is verbatim; everything else is paraphrased. Figures are as Sean stated them in June 2026. Sean says he is a client of the bulk-purchase club FAR Capital, not its owner, and has bought a unit in the project discussed.

articles.title: How do I use transaction data to check a project's price?
articles.excerpt: Asking prices are set by owners who want to sell high. Sean's three-part research ends with transacted prices: the median nearby, the outliers, and how often units actually change hands.

question.context: Viewers email Sean asking whether particular projects are good. Instead of answering each one, he explains his research process, which ends with checking what nearby properties have actually sold for.
question.text: How should I research a project's price before booking?

answer.quote: make that informed decision and take calculated risk
answer.summary: Research in three parts: the project and its sales gallery, the site and its surroundings, and then transacted prices nearby. Establish the median price and psf around the project, understand any outlier, and treat a location with few recent transactions as a warning.

reasons.title: Galleries are sales funnels
reasons.body: Everything in a gallery is curated: a scale model can show a sewage plant as greenery. Learn the current packages there, which change with sales, but hold off booking until you've seen about 20 properties and the site.

reasons.title: The site shows who lives there
reasons.body: Clinics and paediatricians, nurseries and tuition centres suggest families; pubs and snooker halls a different crowd. Ask where you or your tenants would eat, shop and catch a train.

reasons.title: Medians beat asking prices
reasons.body: Owners list high and buyers bid low, so check recorded transactions. Like comparing kailan prices at a supermarket, find the median, then ask why a project sits well above or below it.

reasons.title: Transaction pace shows demand
reasons.body: Many sales at rising prices in six months mean an area is heating up. If the last transaction was three years ago, prices are too high or demand is weak.

actions: Gather the project's details from its website, forums or reviews.
Visit the sales gallery to learn the current packages, but don't book yet.
Visit the site and its surroundings, and look at nearby competitors.
Check the median transacted price and psf for nearby projects.
Count how many units sold recently, and investigate any outliers.
articles.caveat: New launches sell at future prices to cover the years until handover, so they will usually sit above existing transactions. The paid report cost RM69 in 2024; free data shows medians without addresses.
articles.sourceNote: Summarised from Sean's full English captions for this May 2024 video, which was sponsored by PropertyGuru to introduce its Brickz transaction report. The quoted line is verbatim; everything else is paraphrased.

articles.title: Mum's paid-off flat is vandalised. Sell cheap, fix it up or rent it?
articles.excerpt: An 18-year-old asks what to do with his mother's paid-off, vandalised flat in Bukit Beruntung, offered at RM50,000. Sean says get repair costs and rents before deciding, then aim to sell.

question.asker: From Y, a viewer who wrote in on Instagram
question.context: Y is 18. His mother's first property, a fully paid apartment in Bukit Beruntung, has stood empty for years: people have broken in, the windows are smashed and it is full of rubbish, and the building has low occupancy. It costs about RM90 a month in fees. Units in move-in condition sell for about RM130,000 to RM140,000, but the best offer for theirs is about RM50,000. His father passed away two years ago and his mother has three children to support.
question.text: Should they sell it cheaply, fix it up to sell for more, or furnish it and rent it out?

answer.quote: What we need here is actually more data.
answer.summary: Get quotes for fixing the windows, cleaning and painting, and find out the rents for a basic and a fully furnished unit, before choosing. If a modest repair turns a RM50,000 sale into about RM150,000, it is worth doing. Either way, Sean would sell rather than hold, since he sees little room for the price to grow.

reasons.title: Announced infrastructure isn't a guarantee
reasons.body: The township drew buyers because major infrastructure was expected there, but the plans moved elsewhere and values fell. The same rush happened around proposed rail stations that were later cancelled.

reasons.title: Repair costs decide between selling cheap or later
reasons.body: If windows, labour, cleaning and paint come to maybe RM5,000 to RM15,000, spending that to sell nearer RM150,000 is worthwhile. If repairs cost RM30,000 to RM40,000 and the family doesn't have it, selling at RM50,000 may be the practical choice.

reasons.title: Renting may not be worth the trouble
reasons.body: A clean unit with basic fittings might rent for about RM800 a month, perhaps RM1,200 fully furnished with their own effort. Compare that with the repair cost and the work of managing tenants.

reasons.title: Holding brings little gain
reasons.body: With no real prospect of capital appreciation over the next five years, money released from the flat can work harder somewhere else.

actions: Ask a contractor, or a family friend, for quotes to replace the windows, clean and repaint.
Check what clean, basic and fully furnished units in the building rent for.
Decide with his mother how soon the family needs the cash.
If the numbers work, repair it, then sell close to the move-in median price.
articles.caveat: If the family urgently needs cash or can't fund repairs, accepting a low offer now is reasonable. The answer depends on their time and money, not just the potential profit.
articles.sourceNote: Summarised from Sean's full English captions for Asking Sean #194. The quoted line is verbatim; everything else is paraphrased. Figures are as the viewer and Sean stated them in December 2022; repair figures are Sean's rough examples.

video.title: ASKING SEAN #194 | STRATEGY FOR ABANDONED APARTMENT?

articles.title: What should I ask and check when I visit a sales gallery?
articles.excerpt: Show units are built to stir your emotions. Sean lists the questions to ask a sales team, what to check in a show unit, and why floor premiums make top floors hard to sell.

question.context: The big developers have refined the arrival at a sales gallery, from the landscaped drive to the guard who opens the door and the staff who brief you, and they spend heavily on show units.
question.text: How should a buyer approach a sales gallery and show unit?

answer.quote: always ask for more
answer.summary: Go to listen and to ask, and keep a realistic mind: the actual unit won't look like the show unit. Check what is really included, take package offers away to think about, and keep visiting other projects so you aren't swept along by one pitch.

reasons.title: Questions reveal the value
reasons.body: Ask the current sales status, why people are buying, what is special about the location, what will be built next, and how the developer will protect buyers' interests.

reasons.title: Show units aren't always the spec
reasons.body: Developers sometimes change the flooring, walls or sanitary fittings in a show unit to make it look its best. Check which finishes you will actually get.

reasons.title: Floor premiums add up
reasons.body: Prices often rise by RM1,000 or RM2,000 for every floor, which is why many projects struggle to sell their highest, most expensive floors.

actions: Prepare your questions on sales status, location and future plans before you go.
Ask which flooring, walls and fittings are included, and get it in writing.
Take any package offer away and think it over.
Visit a project on Saturday and another on Sunday to broaden your comparison.
Use show units for ideas for your own home, not as a promise.
articles.caveat: Some offers are genuinely good, and Sean warns against overthinking: if you never buy, prices may only be higher years later.
articles.sourceNote: Summarised from Sean's English captions for this November 2017 vlog, filmed at a developer's sales gallery where a salesperson he knows hosted him; he says he was not paid. The quoted line is verbatim; everything else is paraphrased. His explanation of price per square foot is covered in a separate guide.

articles.title: How do I know a location suits me before buying a home?
articles.excerpt: Viewers often ask Sean whether a home is worth buying. He can't know their lives, so he offers two tests to run first: affordability, then a weekday and a weekend in the new location.

question.context: The question Sean finds hardest is whether someone should buy a particular home to live in, because he can't know their needs. So he devised a test buyers can run themselves before booking.
question.text: How can you tell whether a home and its location will suit your life before you commit?

answer.quote: Imagine yourself living an entire weekday in the house.
answer.summary: Run two tests. First, can you carry the instalment for 30 to 35 years? Only then picture an ordinary weekday and weekend from that address, from the commute to school runs and errands, and see whether it still works.

reasons.title: The instalment shapes your whole life
reasons.body: A RM1 million home costs about RM4,500 to RM5,000 a month for 30 to 35 years. On a RM10,000 to RM12,000 salary that is half your income, or one partner working the whole month just for the house, and it can stop you joining a business opportunity later.

reasons.title: Weekdays are most of your life
reasons.body: Walk through a working day: where you work and how you get there, where you eat and buy groceries, and how far the daycare, school and tuition centres are. Newer, cheaper areas often come without schools and shops ready yet.

reasons.title: Don't buy for a once-a-month view
reasons.body: A golf course view you enjoy once a month may not be worth a traffic jam every weekday. Weigh weekend routines too, such as children's activities, a place of worship or your favourite brunch spot.

reasons.title: Bigger isn't always better
reasons.body: A 4,000 sq ft house means more to clean and maintain. Sean, who values time above all, would rather have a smaller home that serves him than become a slave to a big one.

actions: Work out the monthly instalment and what share of your income it takes.
If you are buying with a partner, talk honestly about whether you can afford it and whether you need to buy now.
Map a typical weekday from the new address: work, meals, groceries, and every drop-off and pick-up.
Map a typical weekend: activities, worship, family and friends.
Picture your life when you get the keys, possibly years away: marriage, children or a new job.
articles.caveat: These tests are for a home you will live in, not an investment. The answer is personal: if a trade-off, such as a longer drive for a view you love, is worth it to you, it can still be the right choice.
articles.sourceNote: Summarised from Sean's full English captions for this July 2020 episode. The quoted answer is verbatim; everything else is paraphrased. Figures are as stated in 2020.
