articles.title: What do seasoned property investors look for in a deal?
articles.excerpt: A big developer discount is not the same as buying below market value. Sean lists the four things experienced investors look for: a real discount, positive cash flow, data, and agents' news.

question.context: Developers advertise discounts of 30% or 40%, and many first-time investors take those as bargains. Experienced investors judge a deal differently.
question.text: What criteria do experienced investors use to judge a property deal?

answer.quote: always check for what's the current market value
answer.summary: They look for four things: a price below what neighbouring units actually transact at, rent that covers the instalment, decisions backed by data rather than emotion, and good relationships with agents who hear of deals first.

reasons.title: Below market means below transactions
reasons.body: A developer's 30% rebate on a marked-up price isn't below market. Buying at 700 psf where neighbours transact at about 800 psf is, perhaps through a bulk purchase or a quick sale.

reasons.title: Cash flow keeps you borrowing
reasons.body: Loans are usually 90% for your first two properties and 70% from the third. If the first two are fully covered by rent, banks look on you more favourably.

reasons.title: Data, not attachment
reasons.body: Sean says an investment he was emotionally attached to still holds him back. Check current values, rents, instalments and announced news, not speculation.

reasons.title: Agents hear first
reasons.body: Agents who work an area for years know which unit is selling well below value, and they call the investors they trust.

actions: Compare the price with recent transactions in the same building.
Check that rent covers the instalment before you buy.
List current value, rent, instalment and confirmed news for every deal.
Get to know the agents active in the areas you want to buy in.
articles.caveat: Sean says these relationships and this knowledge take years to build; new investors shouldn't expect to find such deals at once.
articles.sourceNote: Summarised from Sean's English captions for this September 2018 video, in which he also promotes an email list for deals from his industry contacts, including bulk purchases. The quoted line is verbatim; everything else is paraphrased.

video.title: 4 THINGS REAL PROPERTY INVESTOR LOOK FOR

articles.title: What is an APDL, and why can't I sign the SPA without it?
articles.excerpt: Agents often say a launch can't sign SPAs because it has no APDL yet. Sean explains the advertising permit and developer's licence, what an ad must show, and what pre-launch bookings really mean.

question.context: When buyers book a unit at a pre-launch, they are often told they can't sign the sale and purchase agreement yet because the developer has no APDL. Most don't know what that is.
question.text: What is an APDL, and what does it mean for a buyer?

answer.quote: this is to protect consumers like us
answer.summary: APDL stands for advertising permit and developer's licence, approved by the housing ministry. A developer can only apply after its building plans are approved, and can only sell once it has one, so until then you can't sign an SPA. Its details on every ad tell you a lot about a project.

reasons.title: Ads must show the licence details
reasons.body: Each ad lists the developer's licence and advertising permit numbers and validity, the building plan approval, the land tenure and any restriction in interest, the number of units, and the minimum and maximum prices.

reasons.title: It comes after plan approval
reasons.body: After buying land, a developer submits drawings to the local council and then building plans to many authorities, such as fire and landscape. Only once those are approved can it apply for an APDL.

reasons.title: Pre-launches come before it
reasons.body: Pre-booking or pre-launch campaigns offer rebates to collect interest early. You can't sign the SPA until the APDL is approved.

actions: Read the APDL details printed on a project's ad before calling in.
Note the land tenure, restriction in interest and the price range.
Ask when the APDL is expected if you book at a pre-launch.
Prepare your down payment for when the SPA can actually be signed.
Be extra careful with commercial projects, which lack the same buyer protection.
articles.caveat: Sean says booking fees for residential projects are generally not at risk, but rules on pre-launch bookings may have changed since 2018; check with your lawyer.
articles.sourceNote: Summarised from Sean's English captions for this April 2018 video. The quoted line is verbatim; everything else is paraphrased. The number of authorities that review building plans is unclear in the captions and is left out.

video.title: What is APDL?

articles.title: What should I actually check in my sale and purchase agreement?
articles.excerpt: Most buyers initial every page of their SPA without reading it. Sean goes through his own landed strata agreement and points out the clauses that protect a buyer of a new property.

question.context: Buyers of new properties sign and initial every page of the sale and purchase agreement, but few know what is in it. When there is a dispute, the agreement is what the developer and the housing tribunal go by, and developers know it inside out.
question.text: Which parts of a sale and purchase agreement should a buyer actually read and understand?

answer.quote: go and read through the entire agreement
answer.summary: Read the whole agreement, and know the clauses that give you leverage: the stated price, the payment schedule, the schedule of finishes, the conditions for vacant possession, area adjustments and the defect liability period.

reasons.title: Taxes follow the stated price and date
reasons.body: Stamp duty, legal fees and real property gains tax are based on the price in the SPA, not on what you pay after cash back. The date sets your holding period; in 2019, selling after five years cut the gains tax on residential property to 5%.

reasons.title: The payment schedule is fixed for homes
reasons.body: For residential titles, the law fixes how much a developer can claim at each construction stage, with the last 2.5% held for the defect period. Commercial titles have no such protection, so a developer can claim, say, 40% early and you pay interest on it for years.

reasons.title: Finishes are described, not branded
reasons.body: The schedule of finishes lists materials room by room, such as tiles or laminated timber, usually without grade or brand. It is still the only description of what you are owed.

reasons.title: Keys need a certificate, and facilities too
reasons.body: A developer can only hand over once a certificate of completion and compliance is issued. In strata projects, common facilities must be finished at the same time, or late-delivery damages run at 10% a year of the price.

actions: Check the stamping date and the stated purchase price.
Confirm whether your title is residential or commercial, and read the payment schedule.
Compare your plot or unit area with the plan; differences above 2% adjust the price.
Note restrictions on changing your facade or colours in a strata development.
Report defects within the 24-month defect liability period; if the developer doesn't fix them in 30 working days, a registered contractor's cost can be deducted from the 2.5% retention.
articles.caveat: Subsale and commercial agreements can differ from the standard form for new homes, and the tax rates mentioned date from 2019; check current rules with your lawyer.
articles.sourceNote: Summarised from Sean's full English captions for this 2019 video, in which he goes through his own SPA for a landed strata home. The quoted line is verbatim; everything else is paraphrased. Some figures in the captions were unclear and are left out.

video.title: WHAT'S IN YOUR SPA ?!

articles.title: Is it a good time to buy? What ten years of data says
articles.excerpt: Why did some Malaysians lose money on property over the past decade? Sean reads ten years of official data and swaps timing for a test you can actually apply.

question.context: Many Malaysians say they lost money on property over the past ten years, and with shares, crypto and other assets competing for their savings, people keep asking whether now is the moment to buy. Most decide on gut feel.
question.text: Why did some buyers lose money over the last decade, and how do you tell whether it is a good time to buy?

answer.quote: I don't encourage gut feel first.
answer.summary: Nobody can time the market, so stop trying. If your finances are ready, buy only below the location's past transacted median, with rent that gives a healthy yield. That limits the damage even if you happen to buy at a peak.

reasons.title: When you bought decided who lost
reasons.body: In 2015, GST and a rule limiting buyers to two 90% loans cooled demand sharply. People who bought in 2018 and 2019, near what should have been a peak, are behind if they sell today; those who bought amid the gloom of 2016 and 2020 are ahead. During COVID, door frames cost about six times more and labour three times more, so launches stayed low until 2023.

reasons.title: Property does not double every ten years
reasons.body: According to the official house price index, landed homes rose about 25% from 2015 to 2024, or 2 to 3% a year, while high-rise rose about 9 to 10% over the whole decade, through two crashes. Expecting prices to double is why so many owners feel they lost.

reasons.title: Nobody can call the bottom
reasons.body: Buying when everyone was pessimistic worked in 2016 and 2020, but nobody knows in advance whether prices will fall further. What does protect you is paying below the local median and having rent that carries the unit.

reasons.title: The outlook is positive, but supply is rising
reasons.body: The share of launched units sold rose from about 31% to 34% in 2024, and launches are back at 2017 levels. A rate cut from the 2.75% OPR or a build-then-sell rule could lift demand further. More launches also means more choice, so selection matters more than timing.

actions: Decide whether you are ready first: your finances, not the calendar, set the timing.
Compare against past transacted prices for the area, not the latest launch. A nearby launch at RM2,800 per sq ft does not make RM2,000 a bargain where sales have sat near RM1,600 for years.
Check the rental yield; Sean treats 6 to 7% as healthy, or rent covering the instalment on a 35-year loan.
Use as little of your own money as possible: borrow for property and invest your capital where you are confident.
Watch policy: interest rates, gains tax and launch rules all move demand.
articles.caveat: These are national averages from official statistics; a single project can do far better or worse. Landed homes have been the steadiest performer, and Sean says that with enough money, buying corner lots in established townships is hard to get wrong.
articles.sourceNote: Summarised from Sean's full English captions for this September 2025 episode, which draws on NAPIC data from 2015 to 2024. The quoted answer is verbatim; everything else is paraphrased. Market figures are as presented in the episode.

video.title: WHY SOME MALAYSIANS LOSE MONEY IN PROPERTY FOR THE PAST 10 YEARS? ALSO IS 2025 A GOOD TIME TO BUY?

articles.title: I just bought my first property. When can I buy the second?
articles.excerpt: A first-time buyer who prepared well wants a second property this year and worries banks or the tax office will object. Sean explains how rent counts as income, and why subsales speed things up.

question.asker: From C, a viewer who wrote in by email
question.context: C spent months watching Sean's videos, viewing projects, listing pros and cons and preparing his loan documents before signing the SPA for his first property two weeks ago; his loan offer came in three days. He now wants to buy a second property this year.
question.text: Will banks see a second purchase this year as too aggressive, will the tax office come asking, and how can he improve his chances?

answer.quote: We can declare rent that we collect as income.
answer.summary: Banks and the tax office don't mind how many properties you buy; they care whether you can repay and where your money comes from. If the first property is rented out, its rent can count as income for the next loan after about six months of records, so a rented subsale can lead to a second purchase quickly. If it's your home, the instalment simply reduces what you can borrow.

reasons.title: Rent can add to your borrowing power
reasons.body: With a tenancy agreement and at least six months of rent paid into your account, some banks count 100% of the rent as income and others 80%. A RM2,000 instalment with RM2,200 rent leaves you better off for the next loan, not worse.

reasons.title: Tax is on profit, not rent
reasons.body: Declared rent is taxable, but loan interest and other costs can be deducted, and in the first years most of the instalment is interest. The authorities mainly want to see where your money came from, such as an inheritance or gift.

reasons.title: Subsales move faster than new launches
reasons.body: A subsale completes in about four to six months and can be let straight away, so its rent starts counting sooner. A new launch takes four to five years to complete, which is a long wait before the next step.

reasons.title: The rules can tighten
reasons.body: Two 90% loans per person, low upfront payments and current RPGT rates are policies, not permanent features. Earlier rules differed and future ones could be stricter, which is a reason to act while the terms are favourable.

actions: Rent out the first property if you can live elsewhere cheaply, such as with family.
Keep the tenancy agreement and make sure rent is paid into your bank account every month.
Declare the rental income and keep records of interest and costs to deduct.
Budget about 18% of the price in cash for a subsale, plus about RM50,000 to RM80,000 to furnish it.
Keep six to eight months of expenses and your insurance in place before taking on a second loan.
articles.caveat: Sean thinks most people only need two or three properties in a lifetime, not dozens. If the first purchase is your home, expect to wait for your income to grow before the second.
articles.sourceNote: Summarised from Sean's full English captions for Asking Sean #211. The quoted line is verbatim; everything else is paraphrased. Figures and rules are as Sean stated them in May 2023; check current bank and EPF rules. The episode was sponsored by Dreame, an unrelated vacuum cleaner brand.

video.title: ASKING SEAN #211 | WHEN CAN WE BUY OUR 2ND PROPERTY?

articles.title: Where do discounted properties come from, and which are real deals?
articles.excerpt: A slow-selling project passes from the developer's own promotions to agents, then to group-buying clubs, and sometimes to auction. Sean traces the path, and what each discount really means.

question.context: Viewers were sending Sean properties with big advertised discounts and asking which to buy. He noticed most came through the same few channels.
question.text: Where can buyers find discounted property, and how genuine are the discounts?

answer.quote: you are the buyer you have the power
answer.summary: Discounts follow a project's struggle to sell: developer promotions, then agents, then group-buying clubs, and finally auctions. Many early discounts are applied after a price rise, while auctions often offer the most genuine value but need the most knowledge. First-time buyers are safest buying direct from a developer.

reasons.title: Developer discounts may follow a price rise
reasons.body: A unit priced at RM500,000 may be revised to RM600,000 and then offered at 10% off, which is close to where it started.

reasons.title: Agents step in when sales stall
reasons.body: Developers hand slow projects to agents who advertise aggressively online. Commissions are usually 2 to 3%, sometimes up to 7%; the harder a project is to sell, the higher it goes.

reasons.title: Group buys fill a building with investors
reasons.body: Gurus and clubs book blocks of units for members, with cash back of 15% up to 40% and an entry fee of a few thousand ringgit. A building full of investors and short stays can be unsettling for families who live there.

reasons.title: Auctions show the real value
reasons.body: When investors can't keep up their instalments, units go to auction at around 20 to 30% below market value, with the earlier gimmicks stripped out.

actions: Compare a discounted price with the price before any revision.
Get any agent's promises confirmed in writing in the agreement.
Before joining a club, check the entry fee and who else is buying in the block.
Learn the rules and process before bidding at auction.
If you're a first-time buyer, buy from an established developer.
articles.caveat: Sean questions some cash-back practices; buying with multiple loans through such schemes is risky unless you know exactly what you are doing.
articles.sourceNote: Summarised from Sean's English captions for this June 2019 video. The quoted line is verbatim; everything else is paraphrased.

video.title: 4 PLACES TO BUY DISCOUNTED PRICE PROPERTY

articles.title: Why invest in property instead of shares, gold or other options?
articles.excerpt: Shares, bonds, gold and savings plans all compete for your money. Sean gives three reasons he favours property, leverage, slow and visible trends, and rent along the way, while still urging diversification.

question.context: Investors can choose shares, bonds, insurance savings plans, gold, commodities or cryptocurrency. Sean has invested in shares and businesses too, and was asked why he still focuses on property.
question.text: Why choose property over other investments?

answer.quote: you use minimum to get maximum
answer.summary: Sean gives three reasons: banks lend you most of the price, property trends move slowly enough to see and act on, and the property pays rent while you hold it. But he still says not to put all your eggs in one basket.

reasons.title: Leverage from the bank
reasons.body: On a RM500,000 home you pay about RM50,000 and the bank lends RM450,000. Sell at RM600,000 and your RM50,000 has made RM100,000, with housing loans charging up to about 5%.

reasons.title: Trends move slowly
reasons.body: When a new rail line opens, you can watch people move along it over years. Share prices can fall overnight on news from abroad.

reasons.title: Rent while you wait
reasons.body: Gold just sits until you sell it. A property earns rent every month for years, and you can still sell it at the end.

actions: Compare how much of each investment you can finance with a loan.
Follow infrastructure and population moves to spot slow trends early.
Count rental income, not just the sale price, in your returns.
Spread your money: for RM1 million, Sean suggests about RM600,000 in property and the rest in shares, bonds, business and yourself.
Spread properties across price ranges and places, not one block.
articles.caveat: Sean says property suits his personality and work; other investors may do better with shares. The loan rate of up to about 5% is as he stated it in 2017.
articles.sourceNote: Summarised from Sean's English captions for this October 2017 video. The quoted line is verbatim; everything else is paraphrased. His example of buying a new launch with a 1% deposit is left out, as such schemes may no longer apply.

video.title: #Q14:  REAL ESTATE VS OTHER INVESTMENT OPTIONS

articles.title: What happens to my properties when I die?
articles.excerpt: Property owners spend decades building a portfolio but rarely plan how it passes on. Two succession lawyers explain what happens with and without a will, and how to prepare one.

question.context: Property investors spend decades building a portfolio but rarely plan how it will pass on. After visiting several retirement homes, Sean puts his own questions to Gary and Xin Hui, two succession lawyers. Their answers cover non-Muslim estates; Muslims follow Syariah principles.
question.text: What happens to your properties if you die, with or without a will, and how should a property owner prepare?

answer.quote: For me I think there must be some objective you want to achieve.
answer.summary: Without a will, the Distribution Act decides who inherits, and your family must go to court before anyone can act. A will lets you name an executor and decide who gets what, and the lawyers treat it as a plan for your family, not just a list of assets.

reasons.title: Without a will, the law picks your heirs
reasons.body: For non-Muslims, a spouse and parents with no children split the estate equally; with children, half goes to the children and a quarter each to the spouse and parents. Partners, friends and charities receive nothing unless a will names them.

reasons.title: Your family needs a court order first
reasons.body: No one can sign for a deceased owner. With a will, the named executor acts; without one, a family member must apply to court and be found fit to administer the estate. The lawyers describe one family whose dispute over an estate with no will dragged on for two years.

reasons.title: Loans don't fall due at once
reasons.body: If a property has no MRTA or MLTA, the executor can keep paying the instalments, and the bank won't recall the loan while they are paid. On a joint loan where each owner is insured for half, the insurer pays only the deceased's half; the survivor carries the rest, though banks may agree to restructure.

reasons.title: Executors must trace assets and debts first
reasons.body: Executors have a year to locate the assets and confirm the debts before distributing, and should file the deceased's final tax return with LHDN. An executor who pays out and then meets an unpaid debt can be held liable for it.

actions: Start with three questions: what you have, who should get it, and how, guided by the picture you want for your family ten years from now.
Keep an up-to-date list of assets and loans, including land titles and quit rent bills, so your executor isn't left on a treasure hunt.
Expect a simple will to cost from about RM300, with most between RM300 and RM1,500; complex estates can reach RM5,000 to RM10,000.
Review your will every year, and revisit what your children will need at least every five years.
Explain any unequal split in a letter kept with the will, and consider a trust protector to supervise the executor.
articles.caveat: This applies to non-Muslim estates; Muslims follow Syariah principles. Passing properties through a family company or a trust raises tax and control questions of its own, so take advice on your own situation.
articles.sourceNote: Summarised from Sean's full English captions for this May 2026 conversation with succession lawyers Gary and Xin Hui. The quote is one lawyer's own words; the captions don't show which of the two is speaking, so it is credited to both. Everything else is paraphrased, and fees are as quoted in the episode. This is general information, not legal advice for your situation.

articles.title: What mistakes do young buyers make in a slow market?
articles.excerpt: In 2019, with sales slow and developers offering ever more rebates, Sean's inbox filled with young buyers in trouble. He lists four: abandoned projects, signing before the loan, buying with a partner, and overgearing.

question.context: In 2019 property sales were weak, smaller developers were short of cash, and agents and speakers pushed generous promotions. Young buyers, anxious that prices would leave them behind, rushed in, and many wrote to Sean after things went wrong.
question.text: What are the most common mistakes young buyers make, and how can they be avoided?

answer.quote: don't buy things that you cannot afford
answer.summary: Four keep recurring: buying from developers who may abandon the project, signing the SPA before the loan is approved, buying with a boyfriend or girlfriend, and spending the cash back from heavily discounted deals. Be patient, check your loan eligibility first, and buy only what you can afford.

reasons.title: Abandoned projects still cost you
reasons.body: If a developer goes under after the structure is built, the bank has already paid out, say, 20% of a RM500,000 price, and you keep paying interest on RM100,000 for an unfinished building. Residential projects under the Housing Development Act have more protection; commercial ones don't.

reasons.title: Never sign the SPA before the loan
reasons.body: A booking fee is usually refundable, but once the SPA is signed you are bound. Developers offer an extra 1% to sign quickly; if the loan is then rejected, you can lose your deposit.

reasons.title: Don't buy with a partner
reasons.body: Sean gets many emails about properties shared with an ex. Share a purchase with siblings, parents or business-minded investors, not a boyfriend or girlfriend.

reasons.title: Cash back tempts overspending
reasons.body: Using cash back to cover the monthly shortfall is a valid strategy. The danger is the sudden sum in the bank going on a car or holidays, leaving nothing when the instalments bite.

actions: Check the developer's company records, track record and any blacklist before booking.
Find out how much you can borrow before you visit sales galleries.
Sign the SPA only after your loan is approved.
Keep cash back in a separate account for the property.
Take time to research rather than rushing out of fear of missing out.
articles.caveat: Some of the rebates Sean describes were expected to tighten after 2019. Buyers who understand the numbers can still use discounted deals, provided they can carry the commitment.
articles.sourceNote: Summarised from Sean's full English captions for this September 2019 video. The quoted line is verbatim; everything else is paraphrased.

video.title: WORST MISTAKES FOR YOUNG INVESTORS (2019)

articles.title: We're 26 and earn RM20,000 together. Is an RM800,000 home too much?
articles.excerpt: A debt-free couple of 26 with RM300,000 in savings want a new launch of RM700,000 to RM900,000 to start a family in. Sean says they can afford it, with two conditions, and how to judge a building before it exists.

question.asker: From Howard, a viewer who wrote in by email
question.context: Howard and his fiancée are 26, earn about RM20,000 a month gross between them and have about RM300,000 in liquid assets, with no debts. They live rent-free in a relative's apartment in Seri Kembangan, likely until 2027. They want a new launch of 1,100 sq ft or more at RM700,000 to RM900,000, an instalment of about RM3,500, to raise a family in. His fiancée does not want to rent, or to buy a worn subsale.
question.text: Is that price too high for their income, can he borrow in his name alone, should they buy new now or subsale later, and how can they judge a building's common areas before it is built?

answer.quote: I think it's a green light to go
answer.summary: They can afford it, and his RM10,000 income alone roughly qualifies at three times the instalment. Two conditions: don't pay much above the area's median price, and check that rent for similar units nearby covers about 85% of the instalment, so the home can be rented out when the family outgrows it.

reasons.title: The 85% rule protects the upgrade
reasons.body: With an instalment of RM3,500, nearby rents of about RM3,000 show demand for the space. Five to seven years on, with children and perhaps a helper, they will likely want more room and can rent out or sell without a loss.

reasons.title: Don't overpay for romance
reasons.body: Paying perhaps 10% above the median for a setting they truly value is fine as an informed choice; paying well above it simply because they love a concept is not.

reasons.title: Banks judge today's income
reasons.body: Banks lend on current income, not future raises. Interest during construction can be avoided with schemes such as HouseKEY, which has fewer developer rebates.

reasons.title: Learn to read a floor plate
reasons.body: Dimensions are fixed once approved, but finishes are not. Visit completed projects, walk from the car park through the lift lobby and corridor to a unit, and compare dark lobbies and corridors with ones that have voids or daylight.

actions: Compare the project's price per sq ft with the area's median.
Check rents for similar nearby units against 85% of your instalment.
Ask developers about completed, unsold units, which offer certainty with some launch perks.
Visit existing projects, not just sales galleries, and each list three likes and three dislikes.
Invest some of the RM300,000 rather than leaving it idle.
articles.caveat: In a project that sold well, buying early can pay off: Sean bought his own Bukit Jalil home's first phase at about RM700 per sq ft, and later phases sold above RM1,000. In a slow-selling project, waiting for completion carries less risk.
articles.sourceNote: Summarised from Sean's full English captions for Asking Sean #257. The quoted line is verbatim; everything else is paraphrased. Figures are as stated in July 2024. The episode is sponsored by The Makeover Guys, a renovation company.

video.title: ASKING SEAN #257 | DON'T OVERPAY FOR OWNSTAY PROPERTY

articles.title: I'm 25 and working in the UK. Should I buy a RM750,000 unit in KL Sentral?
articles.excerpt: A 25-year-old graduate in the UK has modelled a KL Sentral unit at over RM1,000 per sq ft. Sean suggests five years building his career first, and explains valuations, exit plans and how deals are crafted.

question.asker: From K, a viewer who wrote in by email
question.context: K, 25, started a job in the UK six months ago, earns about RM9,000 a month after tax and has no debts; he chose not to buy a car so he could invest. After comparing areas he has picked a new 650 sq ft unit in KL Sentral at about RM750,000, over RM1,000 per sq ft after incentives, with a bank valuation 10% to 15% above the price and expected rent of about RM4 per sq ft. He has budgeted to cover the instalment for a year if it stays empty.
question.text: Is the valuation margin a good sign, is this a good investment, and how can he make it cash-flow positive?

answer.quote: Best deals are crafted, not found.
answer.summary: There's no rush. At 25, Sean would spend the next five years raising his skills and income, then buy with more capital, more options and a clearer idea of where he will live. If he buys now, a higher valuation doesn't mean he has already made money, and cheaper areas may suit an overseas owner better.

reasons.title: A valuation isn't a sale price
reasons.body: If similar units sell for about RM750,000, that is the market price, whatever the bank's valuation. Many new condos in Kuala Lumpur sell at or even below their SPA price once completed, so a profit four years on isn't guaranteed.

reasons.title: Owning from abroad adds risk
reasons.body: Exchange rates can move against him, managing tenants and repairs from 12 hours away is stressful, and his plans may change if he settles in the UK. He needs an exit plan before he buys.

reasons.title: Cheaper areas are easier to carry
reasons.body: Units of about RM300,000 to RM400,000 in places like Subang Jaya and USJ rent for about RM1,400 to RM1,500. A vacant year there costs far less than at KL Sentral.

reasons.title: Good deals are made, not walked into
reasons.body: Sales galleries sell at the full retail price. Cash allows subsale negotiation, bulk purchase deals can be cheaper, and a well-furnished unit stands out: Sean pays RM100 more a month for a nicely done unit among 15 to 18 similar ones.

actions: Invest in your skills and qualifications for the next few years to raise your income.
Decide where you're likely to settle before buying in another country.
Compare each area's median price per square foot, and avoid paying well above it.
If you buy, choose a unit where the rent covers the instalment on a long loan.
Budget to furnish the unit well so it rents quickly against similar units.
articles.caveat: If he is sure he will return to Malaysia and the numbers work, buying young does get him a 35-year loan and a lower instalment. Sean's own strategy accepts a small monthly top-up while the tenant pays down the loan.
articles.sourceNote: Summarised from Sean's full English captions for Asking Sean #212. The quoted line is verbatim; everything else is paraphrased. Figures are as the viewer and Sean stated them in May 2023. The episode was sponsored by Dreame, an unrelated vacuum cleaner brand.
